events.title: Cramer’s week ahead: Earnings kick off as banks and chipmakers face big tests
events.summary: CNBC’s Jim Cramer said next week’s earnings reports will give investors a clearer picture of corporate performance and the strength of the AI trade. Major banks and chipmakers headline, while key inflation reports and rising Treasury yields remain in focus. CNBC's Jim Cramer on Friday said the start of earnings season next week will give investors a clearer picture of corporate performance and the strength of the artificial intelligence trade. "No more guesswork," the " Mad Money " host said. "We're about to go into the wide world of earnings season, so we don't need to hang on every little data point to figure out where to put money into the market." Stocks rose on Friday , led by the tech sector, as traders rebounded from a volatile week marked by elevated Treasury yields and oil prices, and declines in AI stocks. With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead, when major banks kick off earnings season alongside key semiconductor reports and inflation data. Tuesday brings earnings from Goldman Sachs , Wells Fargo , JPMorgan Chase and Citigroup . Cramer said recent weakness in bank stocks could set the stage for a rally if results exceed expectations. He remains bullish on Charitable Trust holdings Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo. Goldman's strength in bond issuance and trading could offset slower deal-making, while Wells Fargo's attractive valuation and potential for improving metrics make it particularly appealing. Cramer was more cautious on JPMorgan, which he said is priced for near-perfect execution, and wants to see whether Citigroup can rebound. Club holding Johnson & Johnson also reports Tuesday. Cramer said the stock often sells off during its earnings call despite strong underlying results, creating a potential buying opportunity. "With 18 potential blockbuster drugs in the pipeline and among the best cardio and oncology franchises, J&J needs to be bought when it gets crushed," he said. The consumer price index is released Wednesday morning, with Cramer looking for signs that inflation is easing outside of energy. Semiconductor equipment maker ASML also reports. "If ASML raises guidance and talks about solid demand, then you need to be ready to do some buying, picking up some Lam Research or Applied Materials , my two favorite semiconductor capital equipment stocks." Bank of America , Morgan Stanley and BlackRock round out Wednesday's financial earnings. Cramer especially likes Morgan Stanley's growing wealth management business, which provides an important growth driver beyond investment banking. Thursday could be the biggest day for semiconductor stocks, with chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing reporting earnings. "If it's strong, then we could have a rally of immense proportions," Cramer said. The producer price index and retail sales figures, also Thursday, will offer fresh clues on inflation and consumer spending. Brokerage firm Charles Schwab reports and holds an analyst meeting Thursday. Cramer said the events could shed light on the growing influence of individual investors in the market. Despite the busy earnings calendar, Cramer warned that rising bond yields remain a major risk. "We have earnings, we have to worry about oil, and we have to start accepting that we'll have a plus 6% long bond because of demand for money, from both the Treasury department and private enterprise, chiefly data center investments," Cramer said. "When it comes to bonds, there's too much supply and not enough demand for the moment. It's coloring everything and we need to respect how challenging the market can be when interest rates head inexorably higher." events.title: Long live the mechanical keyboard
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For a writer, the mechanical keyboard is a beautiful thing. It’s certainly not necessary for everyone, but a well-designed mechanical keyboard can turn a tedious day of typing into an aesthetically pleasing experience. Given that most of my days involve sitting at a desk for hours, having a keyboard that I enjoy using is a necessity. I first got a mechanical keyboard about two years ago — the Keychron K2 — and I’ve never looked back. Keychron is one of the most prominent brands within the mechanical keyboard industry, having made a name for itself after initially launching via Kickstarter back in 2017. The company has since produced dozens of different keyboards (as well as keypads) and a variety of mouse models . Unlike other electronics, there isn’t a whole lot to owning a mechanical keyboard. The simplicity is part of the appeal. You unbox them, set them up (the K2 comes with little tilt legs that give you a slightly better angle from which to type), and plug them in. From here, you have a couple of different options. The K2 comes with a simple USB cable, but there’s also an option for Bluetooth connection. If you value a clean, minimalist workspace, Bluetooth is probably the way to go. While I am loyal to my older Keychron K2, there are a few upgraded and newer versions to consider. Keychron has released a variety of new models over the past two years, with a broad range of features and price tags. In many cases, the form factor is the draw. One of the more interesting releases, called the Keychron K8 HE Wireless Magnetic Switch Custom Keyboard, comes with an all-wood body and is equipped with an LED backlight. That one is substantially more expensive at around $200. The K2, meanwhile, costs $60. But if you’re into the look, maybe it’s worth it. If you’re a gamer, there’s also Keychron’s C0 HE One-Handed 8K Keyboard , which is a keypad built for convenience and speed and has an industrial aesthetic to it. However, interested gamers will have to wait — as it’s currently sold out. The company has also updated its K, Q, and V series keyboards, with many of those ranging in price from $100 to $200, depending on the features and model. One of the appealing elements of owning a mechanical keyboard is the versatility. You can swap out the key caps for a wide variety of others (indeed, there’s a whole submarket devoted to this) or make your own custom caps (I’ve never gone that overboard). There is also the sound, of course. Some people balk at the accentuated noise of loudly clacking keys, but I’m a fan. In fact, the sound is one of the key selling points for a lot of consumers. The distinct auditory experience produced by said keyboards has even made its way into ASMR videos . For me, the Keychron’s biggest selling point is its retro form factor. I get really nostalgic for old school electronics, and Keychron scratches this itch pretty well. It’s a beautiful-looking device, which brings to mind a different era of computing, when the style was more workman-like, less minimalist. As far as home office purchases go, you could do a lot worse than to pick yourself up a piece of hardware that makes your desk look like it just time-traveled from the 1990s. events.title: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Friday he won't watch a potential livestream of the convicted Fort Hood shooter's execution, which President Trump told reporters he had approved. Why it matters: Vance questioned whether the execution would actually be public but joined a small chorus of Republicans opposed to watching the execution, which is set to be conducted by a firing squad in December. What they're saying: "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters on Friday. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it." Yes, but: Trump's comments came during a separate press gaggle on Friday, where he was asked if he had authorized or approved the execution. "Did I approve? Absolutely, I approve." Driving the news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview Thursday that Americans would be able to watch the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it...people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said. The AP later reported that the execution would be livestreamed. If it goes forward, Hasan's execution will be the first public one in 90 years, and the first military execution since 1961. Zoom in: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) condemned plans to make the execution public in a Thursday night X post . "Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," the outgoing senator said. Utah Sen. John Curtis (R) said in an X post that "[b]roadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity." The other side: Some GOP politicians, like Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.), welcomed the livestream. "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves. We will be watching," he said in a post on X. Editor's note: This story was updated with comments from President Trump.

events.title: Exclusive: Zelensky tells Axios Trump's diesel deal with Putin "not fair and not honest"
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in a phone interview on Friday that President Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was "not fair and not honest." "You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible," Zelensky said in frustration, referring to the Russian president's birthday earlier this week. Why it matters: Trump's announcement after a call with Putin shocked Ukraine and many European governments and created a new crisis between the U.S. and its Western allies. During the 15-minute interview, Zelensky sounded exasperated and dismayed and even expressed a sense of betrayal by the news of the diesel deal. Trump was asked several times by reporters on Friday about Zelensky's criticism but declined to comment and said he was happy about the deal with Putin. Driving the news: Trump announced the deal with Putin as his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting in Miami with the Ukrainian negotiating team along with senior diplomats from Germany, France, the UK, the EU and NATO to discuss new U.S. ideas for ending the war. Zelensky said he spoke several days ago with Witkoff about the need to continue efforts to reach a diplomatic breakthrough before winter and the midterm elections. "Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss," Zelensky said. At no point during his talks with Witkoff and Kushner did the U.S. suggest that a diesel deal with Russia was on the table, Zelensky stressed. He said he understood from Witkoff that the U.S. envoys planned to take messages from the Florida talks to the Russians and then potentially travel to Kyiv to try to seal a peace deal. Behind the scenes: Zelensky said that an hour before Trump's statement, his negotiators, who were meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Florida, informed him that Trump planned to speak with Putin. They said an announcement regarding U.S. sanctions on Russia might be forthcoming, without elaborating. "It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way," he said. "It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this." What he's saying: The Ukrainian president said he would have supported easing sanctions on Russian energy if it was done in the context of a deal to halt attacks on energy facilities in Ukraine and Russia during the winter. "If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good," Zelensky said. But he argued that Trump presumably would have announced such a breakthrough if Putin had agreed to it. "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world," Zelensky said. Zelensky compared the current deal to the Anchorage summit between Trump and Putin last year, which ended with the U.S. president agreeing to many of the Russian demands regarding the war in Ukraine without getting anything in return. "It looks like Alaska number two," he said. Between the lines: Despite his anger, Zelensky stopped short of saying the episode meant Washington could no longer mediate between Kyiv and Moscow. "It's not simple. We need the Americans," he said. "We need the Americans to try to stop this war." But he questioned whether rewarding Moscow without an apparent Russian concession would make further diplomacy more difficult. "This decision will not help us in any way," Zelensky said. "But what is bad, I think that this decision will not help Americans." What's next: Zelensky said he plans to speak with his negotiating team to get a full readout of its talks with Witkoff and Kushner. Zelensky said he also wanted to understand whether the diesel agreement was connected to a trip Trump's envoys planned to take to Russia. "If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting," Zelensky said, while stressing that he did not know whether that was actually Trump's intention. "Maybe I'm not right," Zelensky said. "But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"

events.title: ‘Piece by piece’: Trump administration vows to dismantle the International Criminal Court with sweeping new sanctions
events.summary: The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay , a former judge at the ICC and other international courts. Trump has coveted that prize for himself. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.” The sanctions cut the court off from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and even using U.S. dollars. They set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down. The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens. “It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do,” the court said in a statement. “It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.” ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” She also appealed to other ICC members for support. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law.” Rights groups also denounced the sanctions. “This existential attack must fail,” said Erika Guevara Rosas, an Amnesty International senior director. “States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures and actively protect the Court.” The court’s host country of the Netherlands has been preparing for weeks for the move. One possible measure to mitigate sanctions is the EU “blocking statute,” which could be used to protect European court staff by preventing European companies from complying with the U.S. measures. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has called the blocking statute the “nuclear option” in countering possible sanctions, but said the Netherlands has been in talks with the European Commission to ensure that if it is necessary it can be quickly enacted. In a joint statement, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom expressed strong disagreement with the U.S. sanctions. “We will continue to work together to support the court’s vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability,” the statement said. “If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families. They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims.” Rubio said U.S. allies should join in the U.S. actions. “If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer,” he said. A number of countries have withdrawn from the court this year, including Venezuela and Chad. The South Pacific island nation of Naoero was the most recent to announce it would quit. ___ Quell reported from The Hague, Netherlands. Associated Press writer Mike Corder contributed from The Hague. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

President Donald Trump has offered the job of White House press secretary to Katie Zacharia. Bush's second term. The James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House. Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images What is Katie Zacharia's educational background? Zacharia earned a Bachelor's degree in political science and government from Pepperdine University and a law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, per her LinkedIn. Zacharia is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia, who has produced movies such as "Young Washington" and "David" with Angel Studios, a production company specializing in faith-based films. He also served as an executive producer of the 2019 movie "The Irishman" starring Robert De Niro and Al Pacino, according to his  IMDb page . They wed in 2011 and share four children. events.title: ‘I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen’: Vance doubts plan to livestream of execution of Fort Hood shooter after Pentagon’s announcement
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.” The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009. “So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said. “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added. Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment. Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution. “It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution,” Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the conference, said in a statement. He added that the decision was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.” Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting “the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it.” Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, called him “a maniac.” The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions in that state this year. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging. Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn’t mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it. ___ This story has been corrected to show the military base’s name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood. ___ Associated Press writers Will Weissert in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee contributed to this report. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin just weeks after signing Russia sanctions. Zelenskyy calls it ‘a weak decision’
events.summary: Zelenskyy calls US-Russia diesel deal ‘a weak decision’ and says negotiators are being ‘used as a smokescreen.’ THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story is below. President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Trump’s shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reacted sharply in a social media post, saying that the Russian leader was trying to strike “backroom deals” to buy time in the war. “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” he said. Trump’s move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas. Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.” Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3. Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday’s news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during his call with his U.S. counterpart, he and Trump dedicated “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and also discussed “the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations.” Russia “confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets,” Putin said. “I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy.” The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement. Trump and Putin’s deal draws immediate backlash Zelenskyy, in his lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy.” He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. “It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump’s announcement “infuriating.” “This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” Beyer said in a statement on X. “Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he’s lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels.” The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt. It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market. This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war. The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year. The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow’s ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine. Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine’s repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%. ___ Associated Press writers Will Weissert and Konstantin Toropin in Washington and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Katie Zacharia tapped as next White House press secretary
events.summary: Katie Zacharia, a former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, will be the next White House press secretary, President Trump said Friday. The big picture: Zacharia will take over the podium from Karoline Leavitt, a tenacious Trump loyalist who announced her departure from the administration in August. What they're saying: "It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration." Zoom in: Zacharia thanked Trump for the appointment in a Friday post on X. "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime. President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day," she wrote. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting." Catch up quick: Zacharia is a conservative lawyer and commentator who works as a senior communications advisor at Trump Media & Technology Group, which oversees Truth Social. She also served for about two months as the Department of Homeland Security's deputy assistant secretary for Public Affairs and spokesperson. Zacharia left DHS in April and said in a post on X that she hoped to continue supporting the president's agenda "in other capacities." Zacharia has worked as a commentator on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News, and other outlets. She holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, where she currently serves on the school's Dean's Council. The intrigue: Zacharia is less well known than some of her predecessors, but she is a vocal defender of the administration on TV and online. Trump also noted Friday that Zacharia had been involved in his 2024 presidential campaign "assisting in key Swing States." She also previously worked for Trump ally Richard Grenell at Fix California, an advocacy group that works to advance conservative values in the state. Zacharia has previously described herself as a "native Californian and lifelong conservative." She told CNN in April that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol" and praised Border Czar Tom Homan's work on immigration. Axios' Avery Lotz contributed to this reporting. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

events.title: Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs
events.summary: Spreads in high yield recently widened to levels not seen since April. Investors are demanding more compensation for taking on the riskiest credit. Experts lay out the warning signs that could signal broader trouble ahead. Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs. High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis . Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier. Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%. The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps. Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management. It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said. Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week. "The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said. He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning. That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards. "There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning." While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape. In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. "We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said. The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research. The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market." In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps. The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said. "It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now." For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised. "We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said. Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market. But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort.

events.title: Chuck Schumer has a 2028 problem that's not even in New York
events.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is going to have his hands full next Congress, even without a threat to his leadership or a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Why it matters: Schumer (D-N.Y.) will have to grapple with the presidential ambitions of up to eight of his senators who may care more about winning the White House than following their leader. Roughly one in six Democratic senators eyeing the campaign trail would add a degree of difficulty to a job that rarely lacks challenges, as former President Obama acknowledged this week. "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said of Schumer at a fundraiser Wednesday. Flashback: This year's ICE funding fights gave Schumer a taste of how presidential ambitions can complicate governing. Potential 2028 contenders competed to take the toughest stance against ICE funding, even at the risk of a government shutdown. Zoom in: The tension between individual ambition and party unity could surface early in Schumer's tenure if he becomes majority leader. Democrats are promising to lower costs and govern responsibly, while insisting they'll challenge and investigate the Trump administration at every turn. Schumer and President Trump have a long, complicated relationship — and each other's cell numbers. Between the lines: Democrats could control majorities in both chambers, giving them immense power against Trump. But majority power is dependent on members being present and unified. Presidential contenders have incentives to spend time outside Washington and show how they differ from their fellow 2028 hopefuls in the Senate. They also may want to pick high-profile fights with the party establishment to prove their progressive bona fides. But Schumer faced a similar challenge during the 2020 presidential cycle, when he was minority leader and seven sitting senators sought the Democratic nomination. Attendance was the biggest headache as candidates crisscrossed the country, complicating Senate scheduling. But Democrats didn't lose any major votes despite their presidential hopefuls being on the campaign trail. Who we're watching: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) has visited South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada (twice). Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.): South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.): South Carolina (twice), Nevada and Michigan. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.): South Carolina. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.): Iowa and Nevada. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.): Iowa and New Hampshire (twice). Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.): Nevada (twice) and New Hampshire. Honorable mention: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is focused on winning reelection, so he has no documented early-primary-state visits yet. That hasn't stopped presidential rumors from swirling. Zoom out: First, Schumer needs to get to at least 51 seats in November, navigate a high-stakes lame-duck session, and then win a secret-ballot election to reclaim his title as majority leader. Some of his potential new members — especially if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3 — aren't overly enthusiastic about supporting him. Candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas have not committed to voting for him. The bottom line: Presidential candidates want to stand out. Senate majority leaders need their members to blend in — and fall in line.

events.title: Wall Street posts weekly gains with earnings, inflation data on tap
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City. Wall Street ended higher and posted weekly gains as investors looked ahead to third-quarter earnings and inflation data that could shape the Federal Reserve’s next move. Big banks, including Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase, are due to report, while analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to rise 30.6% and energy and technology to lead. Stocks were mixed by sector and company news, with AI shares rising, telecom firms falling after SpaceX’s spectrum deal, Humana jumping on Medicare ratings, and Apple slipping on weaker demand. NEW YORK - Wall Street ended higher on Oct 9 as investors shifted their focus to next week, with third-quarter earnings season set to start and inflation data expected, which could shed light on the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision. All three major US stock indexes advanced on the day, logging weekly gains. The small-cap Russell 2000, however, ended lower than Oct 2’s close. “It’s the kind of back-and-forth market we’ve been in where we have the reversal of sentiment around Iran,” said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. “With conflicting headlines coming out of the White House and parties in the Middle East, there’s just no edge there.” “That’s why it’s a fairly tepid rally,” Mayfield added. Crude prices initially retreated after President Donald Trump said the US will not launch any attacks on Iran before the midterm elections, adding that talks between Washington and Tehran aimed at ending the market-rattling Iran war were “productive.” Front-month West Texas Intermediate oil and Brent crude both settled up 0.4%. Benchmark Treasury yields edged higher, but remained below Oct 7’s 24-year high. Third-quarter reporting season begins in earnest next week, with big US banks Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley scheduled to release results. Analysts estimate S&P 500 annual earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-September period, with energy and technology posting the largest year-on-year earnings growth of 123% and 66.5%, respectively, according to LSEG data. The mood of American consumers, who shoulder about 70% of the US economy, has soured this month, according to the University of Michigan, with near-term expectations deteriorating to an all-time low. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423.31 points, or 0.83%, to 51,654.95, the S&P 500 gained 46.15 points, or 0.59%, to 7,811.51 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 172.83 points, or 0.64%, to 27,366.17. Among the 11 major sectors of the S&P 500, communication services was the lone percentage loser. AI-related momentum stocks were generally higher, with the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF up 1% as the US bull market, largely driven by the AI boom, approaches its four-year anniversary. “Chips have been this year’s story,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs in Dallas. “(It’s) a multi-decade technological change and just at the beginning of whatever’s happening, not at the end.” Elon Musk’s SpaceX struck a deal to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, posing a direct challenge to US wireless companies. Telecom firms T-Mobile US, AT&T, and Verizon dropped between 8.8% and 13.3%. Humana jumped 11.6% after US government data showed 95% of the health insurer’s members were in Medicare Advantage plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. Apple slid 1.1% after a media report that the iPhone maker has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its newly launched iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, as soaring memory chip costs and price increases dampen consumer demand. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.65-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 141 new highs and 183 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,756 stocks rose and 1,997 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.38-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 14 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 41 new highs and 209 new lows. events.title: Nvidia's head of corporate communications has left after roughly four months
events.summary: Nvidia. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Nvidia's head of corporate communications has left after roughly four months. Anna Soellner joined the chip giant from Reddit around June. Her brief tenure coincided with Nvidia's deal with Hugging Face. Nvidia's head of corporate communications has left the company after roughly four months on the job, Business Insider has learned. Anna Soellner joined the chip giant around June, per her Linkedin profile, amid a period of explosive growth. During her brief tenure, the company announced a nearly $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and reported quarterly revenue of $96 billion. "I'm honored to help tell the story of one of the world's most consequential companies alongside an extraordinary communications and marketing team," Soellner wrote on LinkedIn when announcing her hiring. She was tapped to help oversee communications as Nvidia navigated heightened public scrutiny through the AI boom. She reported to Mylene Mangalindan, Nvidia's vice president of corporate communications, Axios reported in July. Before joining Nvidia, Soellner spent over eight years at Reddit as vice president of communications, helping lead communications strategy, including through its 2024 initial public offering . Before that, she held senior communications roles at the Motion Picture Association and the Center for American Progress, and served as a senior advisor at the US Treasury Department. events.title: Trump announces major diesel deal with Putin, infuriating Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump announced Friday that he's reached a deal with Russia to increase the supply of diesel to the U.S. and global markets — angering Ukraine, which called it a gift to Vladimir Putin in the midst of their war. Why it matters: The announcement, which includes a waiver on some U.S. energy sanctions against Russia, took place as Ukrainian and European diplomats arrived in Miami for talks on ending the war with Russia. What he's saying: "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump added that Russia will deliver," within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel." Combine with oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, Trump wrote, "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" "Today, at President Trump's direction, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market," the Treasury Department said in a statement. Friction point: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky responded angrily to Trump's announcement, writing on X that any sanctions relief for Russia outside of a "lasting de-escalation agreement ... is an obvious weakness." "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," Zelensky wrote. Zelensky added that Ukraine told Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff that it is "ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps" with Russia. "Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the U.S. has enough power to achieve such a compromise," he said. The other side: The Kremlin said in a statement that during Putin's call with Trump, "significant attention was devoted to prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis." The Kremlin said the two leaders discussed the situation in global energy markets. "The Russian side confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets. I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the global economy as a whole," Putin said during the call, according to the Kremlin. Putin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who worked on the deal, wrote on X that "Russia-US energy and economic cooperation will continue and benefit global markets and the world." By the numbers: Ukrainian strikes cut Russia's available refining capacity by as much as 60% over the summer, though the effect varies month to month, per an analysis by two Dallas Fed researchers this week. Through a combination of Middle East refinery outages, shipping constraints, damaged Russian refineries and curtailed Chinese refining, the global fuels market has seen reduction of as much as 6 million to 8 million barrels per day of capacity since late spring, or up to 10% of global refining. Ben Geman contributed to this report.

events.title: Trump lifts US sanctions on Russian diesel amid price surge
events.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russia had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The move comes as Mr Trump faces growing domestic political pressure to bring down rising diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries , before November's midterm elections. Mr Trump said in a social media post that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”. The US President said that, “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia would deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”. “Between our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian energy, diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be coming, in record numbers down, and fast!” Mr Trump wrote. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control released a licence allowing the immediate “sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation” of Russian origin-diesel fuel into the US until April 2027. The department said it did not authorise any debit to an account on the books of a US financial institution of Russia's central bank, its national wealth fund, or its finance ministry. The move drew quick condemnation from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”. “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Mr Zelenskyy said. Trump is doing a deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes from the shockingly high diesel prices caused by his own reckless, illegal war in the Middle East. This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target… https://t.co/lEILjnE38R — Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) October 9, 2026 US Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer and other members of the Democratic Party expressed dismay at the announcement. “This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” he said on X. Russia was the second-largest diesel exporter in the world after the US before imposing curbs to protect its domestic market. Those supplies have been further hampered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, including what Kyiv claimed to be an attack on the country's largest oil refinery on Thursday. It is unclear how Russia will supply the diesel amounts announced by Mr Trump. Russia's fossil fuel export revenue fell 8 per cent on a monthly basis in August to €604 million ($676 million) per day, with export volumes falling 7 per cent, according to the Centre for Research on Clean Air, a think tank that has previously condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine . Mr Trump has recently acknowledged the diesel fuel crisis. In September, he publicly called on Mr Zelenskyy to halt its attacks on Russia's oil facilities “because he's causing a shortage of diesel fuel”. G7 member countries last week said they had agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other products through the International Energy Agency to help stabilise markets following pressure from the Trump administration, which had threatened to impose a diesel export ban. IEA members on Wednesday said they had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks and accelerate the release of roughly 100 million barrels of emergency oil reserves. The IEA's members in March agreed to release 425 barrels of reserves to markets as prices surged after the Iran war broke out on February 28, with roughly 325 million barrels having been released so far. Friday's surprise move also appears to defy a Russian sanctions law championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham , which Mr Trump signed into law on September 18. The law codifies the existing US sanctions regime targeting Russia and introduced new tariff authorities with a particular focus on energy exports. Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives Joint Economic Committee who opposed the legislation, called the deal “infuriating”. “Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake,” he wrote on X. The average cost of diesel in the US on Friday was $6.27 per gallon, compared to $3.67 this time last year.

events.title: Verizon posts worst day since 2002 as SpaceX U.S. network plans whack cell provider stocks
events.summary: Telecom stocks sank on Friday after Elon Musk's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio. Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T all sold off while SpaceX climbed slightly. FCC Chair Brendan Carr told CNBC that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers." Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk 's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio , aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service. Verizon closed down 8.75% on the news, its worst day since July 2002. Shares of T-Mobile dropped 13.27% while AT&T fell 9.81%, each notching their own worst days since 2013 and 2000, respectively. SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day. The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," in a Thursday statement. FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers" in a CNBC interview. "We're probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we're seeing a lot of competition," Carr told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Friday. "There's going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that's great. We're going to see how this plays out. It's not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers," he added. Multiple SpaceX analysts lauded the new spectrum deal, with Evercore ISI writing that the rocket maker "now has the outline of a real network" alongside its existing satellite capabilities. JPMorgan wrote that the acquisition made Starlink Mobile's long-term opportunity "more credible." "That said, we continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network," analysts added in a Friday note. events.title: New York Plans Stronger Sports Betting Regulation to Curb Gambling Addiction
events.summary: DraftKings sent extensive promotional offers to ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson while he was testing the company’s safety guardrails for problem gamblers. Recreation of notifications by Chris Alcantara/ProPublica Gambling regulators in New York on Friday formally proposed two rules that they say will help curb gambling addiction in the state. The move adds the country’s largest sports betting market to a growing list of places that are seeking online gambling reforms as states that have legalized wagering on sports in recent years deal with the harmful side effects, including rising addiction diagnoses there. While the drafts have been months in the making, their official introduction follows mounting media scrutiny, including a ProPublica investigation last month that showed weaknesses in the guardrails that companies like DraftKings have erected to address problem gamblers on their platforms. That system is called “responsible gaming.” The commission’s chair, Brian O’Dwyer, said that the proposed rules “provide an opportunity for the industry to illustrate its commitment” to protecting its customers.  “The industry is on notice by me and this commission that they need to solve this problem,” O’Dwyer said. “If the industry does not address it, then we will address it and they may not like the solution that we come up with.” One of the new rules would effectively adopt guidelines that New Jersey already uses, requiring sportsbooks to follow specific thresholds to identify at-risk bettors. The company would then be mandated to check in with those users. Another rule would bar companies from using artificial intelligence to customize bonuses or wagers. DraftKings, one of the country’s largest sports betting companies, has said it already follows the New Jersey trigger thresholds. Among them: depositing more than $10,000 in a 24-hour period or wagering more than $1 million in a 90-day period. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience But as ProPublica recently reported, problem gambling can manifest in much smaller amounts. With the advice of recovering addicts, addiction specialists and professional sports bettors, a reporter deposited $21,600 into his DraftKings account in less than eight weeks and purposefully bet compulsively, exhibiting the hallmark signs of problem gambling throughout that time. The behavior didn’t qualify for a company review or interventions beyond responsible gaming notices, including in-app pop-ups. Some advocates for gambling reforms said that’s one big reason why the proposed rules don’t go far enough. New York and New Jersey “are clearly complacent in the status quo by endorsing and prescribing regulations that are nothing more than giving the appearance of reform and not effectuating actual change,” said Brianne Doura-Schawohl, a gambling reform advocate who lobbies for consumer and public health protections. After the commission advanced the rules unanimously on Friday, O’Dwyer said he recognized “the limitations of this proposal” and urged the state’s nine licensed mobile sports betting companies to share data so that problem gamblers can’t elude intervention by bouncing between them.  The introduction of the rules is a key step toward formal adoption. There will be a 60-day comment period for the public to weigh in on them. Barring major changes, the rules will then go back before the commission. Though the plans were first published in March and received dozens of public comments, their official introduction at the gaming commission comes on the heels of reporting by The New York Times, which found that DraftKings used artificial intelligence and data scientists to target its promotions to losing bettors , and ProPublica, which found that promotions far outweighed the responsible gaming notices sent to a reporter exhibiting problematic behavior. DraftKings made that journalist a VIP after he displayed red flags of problem gambling. Since those articles were published last month, regulators in Maine and Michigan have also said that they are reviewing some of the issues raised in the stories. Read More I Deliberately Bet Like a Problem Gambler. DraftKings Made Me a VIP. A spokesperson for Maine’s Public Safety Department said the Gambling Control Unit is “monitoring the use of AI locally and nationally” but has no rules or laws addressing the issue and declined to provide any additional information “regarding the scope of that monitoring or specific operations.” A spokesperson for Michigan regulators hasn’t responded to requests for comment. Massachusetts regulators, who have been looking into the use of AI by gambling companies, said they were also taking a look. The governor of Maryland has separately said he’d like to limit gambling companies’ use of AI to “identify and target users showing problem-gambling patterns.” Asked for comment on the New York regulations, a FanDuel spokesperson said the company “welcomes the opportunity to engage with regulators and work collaboratively to establish best practices for the industry.” A spokesperson for DraftKings referred ProPublica to its prior comments. In statements and interviews, the company has defended its responsible gaming program and disputed any characterization that it targets addicts or those prone to addiction with inducements. In an interview with ProPublica, Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, said that, overall, “the system worked the way it was supposed to” during our gambling investigation, citing the more than 30 messages it sent our reporter. She added that “as a business, as an industry, we’re doing a good job of educating people, of raising awareness, of making tools and resources available, of monitoring accounts.” DraftKings told the Times it “rejects any implication that its marketing practices are unfair or improperly targets customers” and said its perks were delivered to “customers who demonstrated sustained, engaged use on our platform, not toward customers based on their losses.” The rules presented on Friday were made in response to a call by Gov. Kathy Hochul this year to address problem gambling. The Democrat, who is running for reelection, has announced a 10-year survey of residents’ gambling behavior to help “guide smart, targeted investments that protect New Yorkers and strengthen access to care.” But the commission’s proposed rules are a relatively moderate step in that direction. The measures would require a sports betting company to do more due diligence into a user’s “financial vulnerability” under certain conditions. events.title: Shop owners ramp up security due to rise in Pokémon card thefts
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Game shop owners ramp up security due to rise in Pokémon card thefts Collectable retailers are concerned about recent break-ins and thefts targeting valuable Pokémon cards. ( ABC News: Sharne Wakefield ) Game and collectibles shop owners are bolstering their security because of a rise in Pokémon card thefts. One card store owner says almost $20,000 worth of Pokémon and other trading cards were allegedly stolen from his shop. Another trader says these cards have a high resale value. When Benjamin Hill went to his collectables store one day, he was shocked to find the ceiling smashed through and almost $20,000 worth of Pokémon and other trading cards gone. "It was pretty confronting to be honest … I was aware this could happen, but you never think it would be you," the shop owner said. "I was shaking a little bit as well; it took me a few days to get over it." Mr Hill said the alleged thief had sneaked through the back toilet door and crawled through the ceiling at his Blair Athol shop in early September. Pokémon trading cards were allegedly stolen and a store ceiling was damaged at a Blair Athol store in early September. ( Supplied: Benjamin Hill ) He said Pokémon trading cards could have been the target, as they generally cost between 50 cents and $50 but some rare cards were being auctioned for millions of dollars. Mr Hill said these trading cards were high in value, untraceable and easy to resell. "It's just a little bit of cardboard that can fit in your pocket. You could have $1,000 in your pocket," he said. Benjamin Hill's trading card store was allegedly broken into last month. ( ABC News: Sharne Wakefield ) SA Police told ABC News a 47-year-old man was this week arrested and charged with serious criminal trespassing, theft and property damage over the alleged break-in at Mr Hill's store. Mr Hill said he had since upgraded his security and taken all expensive items off site. In recent months, tens of thousands of dollars' worth of trading cards were stolen from collectables shops in Brisbane, Perth and Melbourne. Pokemon trading cards have been the target of thieves because some are of high value. ( ABC News: Sharne Wakefield ) SA Police arrested a 29-year-old man who allegedly smashed a glass cabinet at a Noarlunga toy store and stole Pokémon cards last month. ABC News spoke to several Adelaide shop owners, including one who was spending about $20,000, to bolster security measures such as installing bollards, fog alarms, roller shutters and new CCTV. Trading cards were allegedly stolen from Benjamin Hill's store. ( Supplied: Benjamin Hill ) Card shop owner Hung Nguyen is one of those taking extra precautions. "What's happening around Melbourne and Queensland, it's just made us think twice about looking into our security a bit more," he said. "I guess there's nothing stopping us from comparing ourselves to a jewellery shop." Hung Nguyen has installed bollards and security alarm at his store. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie ) The Japanese game is 30 years old but Pokémon trading cards have seen a global resurgence in recent years, prompting its government to consider a clampdown on the industry. Due to a lack of supply, high demand and influx of investors, Pokémon cards are soaring in price, with an American YouTuber selling an ultra-rare card for a record $22.6 million this year. Recently, these Japanese cards have been outperforming Bitcoin and the S&P 500 on the stock market. Hung Nguyen says he has increased security at his game store. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie ) "Like a box that was worth $100 to $200 is now worth $8,000," Mr Nguyen said. The trader said most of these cards were being resold for more than double their retail price. "You could say the return on investment is 100 per cent, which is crazy," Mr Nguyen said. "So for them, it's, 'Why wouldn't I get into it and make a quick flip?

events.title: I spent a week eating my way through one of the world's largest cruise ships. Years later, I still crave these 10 dishes.
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter dined at several restaurants during her cruise on board Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My seven-day cruise started with tiger shrimp. It ended with fluffy French toast and a berry compote. These are just two of the 10 best things I ate on Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas. I thought I'd get sick of the food by the end of my seven-day voyage in April 2022. I'd never been on a cruise before, but I imagined my dining options would be limited at sea. And they might have been if I weren't on board Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas , one of the largest cruise ships in the world. The megaship has 20 eateries, from coffee shops and buffets to fast-food joints and upscale restaurants. I was overwhelmed with options every time I got hungry on my Caribbean cruise . I ate at as many different restaurants as I could — more than half of them. There were 10 standout dishes that I still think about when my stomach grumbles. Some of the best meals were included in the cruise rate. Others came from specialty restaurants. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Wonder of the Seas has some restaurants that are complimentary as part of the cruise rate , while specialty dining incurs an additional cost. For the latter, guests often pay a cover charge for a three-course meal. I made reservations at five specialty restaurants . I recommend booking your reservation as soon as possible, because the cost tends to rise the longer you wait. Two of my favorite dishes came from the main dining room. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The main dining room is complimentary for guests and serves breakfast and a three-course dinner each day. One was a dinner entrée — garlic tiger shrimp with jasmine rice, seasonal veggies, and herb butter. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The shrimp was juicy and had great flavor. The rice was sticky, which I like, and the asparagus and tomatoes were well-seasoned. The other was a French toast breakfast. The bread was thick, crispy on the outside, and fluffy on the inside. Joey Hadden/Business Insider A delicious berry compote on top paired nicely with maple syrup. Two crispy strips of bacon added a savory crunch to each bite. This was my favorite breakfast of the whole trip. I also particularly enjoyed El Loco Fresh, an outdoor DIY taco bar. Joey Hadden/Business Insider It's included for guests and serves a selection of meats, cheeses, and toppings, like pico de gallo, guacamole, and sour cream. I grabbed a bowl of chips and made myself some nachos. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The queso had great texture and flavor. The bar had every topping I could want, satisfying my Tex-Mex craving on the ship. When I wanted an upscale meal, I splurged on dinner at Chops Grille, a steakhouse. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I paid $55 for a three-course dinner here. The highlight was the appetizer — a crispy goat cheese salad with green apples, candied walnuts, cranberries, and balsamic dressing. Joey Hadden/Business Insider It was an eclectic mix of textures and flavors, yet it blended perfectly in my mouth. I treated myself to another fancy dinner at 150 Central Park. Joey Hadden/Business Insider On a plant-filled outdoor deck, 150 Central Park served a variety of meat, seafood, and other "locally sourced ingredients," according to Royal Caribbean. I had a three-course dinner for $50. My favorite dish was the fried cheesecake for dessert. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The dessert was soft, fluffy, and light, with a cream cheese filling. Caramelized popcorn, whipped cream, and a Nutella drizzle complemented it perfectly, making it even more satisfying than the main course. To get my seafood fix, I went to the New England-style Hooked Seafood restaurant. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The menu draws inspiration from Maine to Maryland. I paid $53 for a three-course dinner. The lobster roll was fantastic. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The toasted roll was generously loaded with thick chunks of lobster and a layer of crisp lettuce. I squeezed the grilled lemon across the top and bit into the refreshing mess of a sandwich. It reminded me of lobster rolls I've had back home on the East Coast. For dessert, I went with the chef's suggestion: a lemon tart. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I took one bite, and it was easy to see why it came highly recommended. The lemon custard was tangy with a bit of sweetness, and it filled up a flaky, buttery crust. It was the best lemon tart I've ever had. The Mason Jar serves southern comfort food. It ended up being my favorite restaurant on the ship. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I booked a three-course dinner at the Mason Jar for $40, and everything I ordered made my top 10 list. I'm glad I booked it for a three-course dinner, which started with crab beignets. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I ordered the crab beignets appetizer at the Mason Jar. Although I'd never had one before, I love crab, and I love beignets. So I gave it a try. They were the perfect texture — soft and fluffy with a crisp outer layer. The crab flavor was subtle, with cinnamon on top for an interesting twist. The accompanying crap dip was refreshing, too. For my main, I ordered fried chicken with mashed potatoes and mac and cheese. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The chicken was tender and well-seasoned, with a crispy outer layer. The sides had good flavor as well. My dessert at The Mason Jar was served in one. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Called "Gone Bananas," the dessert consisted of layers of vanilla pudding and graham cracker crumbs inside a jar. It was topped with brûléed bananas, whipped cream, and toffee. The dessert was fluffy, light, and rich in banana flavor. It was a fitting ending to my favorite meal of the trip. If I were to cruise with Wonder of the Seas again, I'd spend less money on specialty restaurants and more evenings in the main dining room. Joey Hadden/Business Insider While the specialty restaurants served delicious dishes, I thought the food quality was just as high in the main dining room, where I ate only twice. But I'd absolutely pay to go back to The Mason Jar for all three standout courses. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I'm 61 and can't find a job. I've drained my savings and started a GoFundMe to help pay the bills.
events.summary: Gautam Dev turned to gig work after struggling to find another full-time tech job. Gautam Dev Gautam Dev worked in tech for more than two decades before quitting his job in 2024. Two years of job hunting later, he's still without a full-time role. The 61-year-old is struggling to afford rent and is considering leaving the US. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Gautam Dev, a 61-year-old job seeker in Dallas. He previously worked as a software engineer before resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In 2024, while working as a software engineer for an IT company in Dallas, I was told I'd have to relocate to another state to keep my job. That September, I decided to quit my job, stay in Dallas, and look for a new role . That decision became a disaster. I didn't realize how difficult finding another job would be I'd worked in the IT industry for more than two decades and had gaps of a few months between jobs before, but I was always able to find another one. This time has been completely different. I never expected to still be without full-time work nearly two years later. After I resigned, I didn't immediately start seriously searching for another job, but I soon began applying, mostly to jobs through LinkedIn. I also tried networking, but it wasn't much help. Most of the people I talked to said their companies weren't hiring . Some told me their jobs had gotten tougher, but that they were afraid to quit because they might not find another one. Still, I've managed to land some interviews over the course of my search, including multiple with the same company. I thought some went well, but I never received an offer. I thought my significant experience in the IT industry would help me find a job. However, I think being in my 60s could be working against me. And after being out of work for so long, I also think the employment gap is making things even more difficult. It seems like AI can do some of the things software engineers used to do manually. I've seen job postings for AI engineering positions , but I don't have much of an AI background, so I'm not sure they're a good fit. Between my age, the long gap, and the state of the IT industry, my expectations for finding another job have fallen. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I've largely stopped applying for jobs For a while, I kept applying and applying, but most applications received no response. Eventually, I reached a point where I didn't see much use in continuing to spend so much time applying. I've largely stopped now. I need to spend that time earning money instead. For a while, I tried day trading to earn some income. It was going well for a while, but then my luck turned. Earlier this year, I started doing gig work through platforms like Uber , DoorDash, and Walmart Spark. I wish I'd started doing it earlier, though I haven't been able to make as much as I'd hoped. Still, it's some money. It's not zero. My options are also limited. I can't carry heavy items, which rules out some gig work options . My long job search has drained my finances Even with gig work, it's become difficult to keep paying the bills. I've had to drain my savings and take on a lot of credit card debt. My rent in Dallas is high, and I'd like to move somewhere cheaper. Right now, though, I feel stuck. I worry that if I tried to rent another apartment, a landlord would ask for proof of employment and income. Without a full-time job, I don't know whether I'd qualify. Even if I could move, the process would take time away from doing deliveries and earning money. In January, I started a GoFundMe and received more than $9,000. It's all gone toward paying my bills. It was hard to ask people for money, and not everyone has been supportive. But some people have been really nice and generous. For now, my plan is to keep doing gig work. I'm eligible to start receiving Social Security when I turn 62 in January. Once that begins, I'm hoping it, combined with whatever I can earn through gig work, will make my situation a little easier. Until then, it'll be tough. I've also strongly considered moving back to India, where I lived before moving to the US more than two decades ago and eventually becoming a citizen. But I'm not in a rush to do so, and it would take some time to make the move happen. I never imagined I'd end up in this situation, but here I am. Do you have a story to share?
