events.title: Money & Me: 'I went from The X Factor to having to sell my car to pay staff but now earn Dh130,000 a month’
events.summary: JJ Thompson has a very varied CV. He came ninth on The X Factor in 2013 as part of a boy band, spent years as a radio presenter before launching a podcast production company during Covid, which ultimately failed. Then, in June 2024, he walked away from a job offer at one of the UAE's biggest radio networks to start from scratch in real estate with no salary. More than two years later, he's earning an average of Dh130,000 a month at Dubai -based property brokerage Strada. How did money feature in your childhood? I think I have some financial trauma. My dad was a business owner and we seemed to have a little bit and then very little. I've always had a bit of an issue with finances. I don't know if it's through ADHD or childhood, but I'm good at spending money. I'm learning to get a hold of money and get rid of it as quickly as possible – forcing myself to buy property, which is weird to say, because either I’ll spend the money or I'll invest in property to make sure it doesn't get spent. What was your first job? What did you earn? A waiter when I was 16 years old, £4.50 an hour. I moved to London from Coventry when I was 19 and had random bar jobs for those three years. I worked for my dad doing roofing but he fired me after a couple of months. When I moved to London, I worked in Harrods, spraying perfume on the ground floor. That's where I met my now-wife. Then I worked in a call centre selling Grazia and Heat magazines for about £6 an hour. Then I got into a boy band, and I did The X Factor . We came ninth in 2013 when I was 22. How did you end up in Dubai? After the band, I did radio in the UK, for Capital Radio, then I moved over to the UAE in 2016 to do it full time for Channel 4. I did the evening show, then the breakfast show. During Covid, there weren't many people advertising, so we didn't get paid. I went down from around Dh18,000 a month to about Dh2,500. I started a podcast company to try to bridge that gap. We got an investor but it failed dramatically – I had to sell my car to pay staff. I gave the business to the investor and said: “I'm going to go into real estate.” It was called a midlife crisis by a few people, which added fuel in the fire. It's gone well. I'm very happy I took the leap and took the risk. What do you earn now? It's month to month, but it's around Dh130,000 a month. My max in radio was Dh19,000. When [the money] came – and it happened so quickly – it was a bit of a Will Smith Pursuit of Happyness moment. I wasn't mentally ready because I was so used to having very little, but always wanting more, always knowing one day I'd get it somehow because I'm very financially ambitious. We had a baby, and I'd turned down a stable job for something where I didn't know if I would earn anything for six months. But I landed my first deal within six days and that got me about Dh150,000. I burst into tears looking at my child. I thought: “We're on to something here and all the risk paid off.” How do you grow your wealth? Mainly real estate. I've invested in two off-plan properties in Abu Dhabi with a client. We've got a property in the UK and we're looking to expand that to three as an Airbnb business in Scotland with my wife. I prefer off-plan investments. I look for higher-risk investments for higher reward rather than safe rental income from a ready property that will net me six per cent. What has been your best investment? They haven't come into fruition yet because they're off-plan, but I would like to think my investment in Hudayriyat Golf Estates in Hudayriyat Island, Abu Dhabi, will probably yield the best return by 2030. Any cherished purchases? I bought a nicer car and then I bought a Rolex, which was always a bit of a goal of mine. What luxuries are important to you? Travel and holidays – that's the most important thing for me, and the most expensive. I've been away once a month this year. My favourite thing is to go away with the family. What financial advice would you give your younger self? I was right in always thinking it's going to be all right. Keep working, keep being ambitious, keep allowing people to laugh at your goals because they're bigger than theirs. Keep going, it will all be all right.

events.title: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
events.summary: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. AI-generated avatars explain concepts The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material. Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions. Modeling expert reasoning through dialogue The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance. Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development. The program goes further by interrupting the dialogue at key moments and inviting the learner to step in. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team. A new standard for advanced engineering education By merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. It captures the complexity of real‑world problem‑solving, humanizes the learning experience, and challenges participants to think like the engineers who are defining the future of AI hardware. It is not simply a new course; it is a new way of learning. For individual access, visit the IEEE Learning Network . For customized organizational options , contact a content specialist to discuss volume pricing.

events.title: Firmus valued itself 'way too high' and paid the price
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How Firmus's plans for the biggest IPO in three decades fell over Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis, the co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) It was supposed to be the second-biggest stock float in Australian history. Sydney-based AI startup Firmus Technologies was close to listing on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) at a $43.7 billion market capitalisation. It would have been the biggest IPO since Telstra listed in 1997. The company, founded in 2019 by Oliver Curtis, Tim Rosenfield and Jonathan Levee, had planned to raise about $7 billion by going public. The intention was to list and then borrow more to build data centres across Australia, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. By Wednesday night, the IPO plans began to unravel and reports emerged that bankers were considering lowering the share price and valuation towards $30 billion. On Thursday morning, as Firmus scrambled to save the IPO, it withdrew from appearing at a federal parliamentary inquiry into AI. By Friday, the founders's grand plans had fallen apart and the float was pulled . Tim Rosenfield, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (centre) and Oliver Curtis (right) at the Firmus Technologies site in Launceston. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Despite being backed by global AI giant Nvidia, investors had grown anxious. Firmus had previously said it secured $US2 billion ($2.86 billion) in commitments from investors, including Nvidia and Blackstone. Other potential investors felt the company's share price offer was overpriced, some felt there was not enough detailed information in the IPO prospectus, and many were spooked that the rapid growth of AI and data centres would soon stop. The founders are now hoping to pursue further private funding and Firmus will attempt to list on the Nasdaq next year. What caused the Firmus float to fail? A mixture of factors led to the float's demise, including the high per-share price offer, which by Thursday had reportedly fallen from $11 to $8.25. The company was being given a similar valuation to Woolworths, according to Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway. "The economics look good now and the growth is very fast now, but what that looks like again in five or 10 years is the big question mark," he said. Lochlan Halloway says the company had been given a similar valuation to Woolworths, while making the revenue of a startup. ( ABC News ) The timing of the IPO was also wrong. Commentators say fears of an AI bubble, set against a backdrop of mounting concerns from politicians and the community about the rapid rise of data centres, also played a part. "Firmus ran into a wall of AI anxiety right at the time that they had planned to list," Philip Wool from Reliance Investment Research said. And then there was some angst over Mr Curtis's colourful past. He served a year in jail in 2016-17 for insider trading before co-founding Firmus as a bitcoin mining company in 2019. Mr Wool said Firmus's assertion that it was market volatility that prevented it listing at its desired price was "a euphemistic way of describing exactly what happened". "The market is more uncertain now when it comes to AI hardware and, given the perhaps aggressive pricing that they were targeting, they really didn't see the demand," he said. 'They do have to come back to the market' Ten Cap Investment co-founder and lead portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said the IPO was overpriced, but thought a second attempt was on the cards. Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors. "The valuation for the company was way too high to start with," she said. "It is almost three times what the valuation was when they raised money just a few months ago. "At some stage they do have to come back to the market simply because it's a very capital-intensive business. It requires listed shares." Floodline Research founder Anna Wu said the founders should have tried to list in the United States because the Nasdaq was a bigger and more accepting market than the ASX for emerging tech. "The downside is much tougher competition and, as an Australian company, Firmus may struggle to attract the same attention and valuation as its US peers," she said. The Nasdaq has recently hit record highs and is up 43 per cent in the past year, but Australia's tech sector has faltered by comparison. The ASX All Technology Index, which tracks the share prices of 42 tech-linked stocks on the ASX, has dropped almost 18 per cent this year, including 9 per cent in September alone.

events.title: Trump appoints committee to investigate statements by the Fed's Lisa Cook
events.summary: President Donald Trump established a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements related to mortgages, the White House said. Trump tried to fire Cook, a nominee of former President Joe Biden, but the Supreme Court blocked his first attempt. The committee consists of three members, all hired by Trump for administration positions. President Donald Trump formally established a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements related to "one or more mortgage instruments," the White House announced Friday. The extraordinary announcement is the latest development in Trump's long-running effort to fire Cook, a nominee of former President Joe Biden , from the central bank's board. Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, recently said the failure to do so by his handpicked chair, Kevin Warsh , is the fault of a "hostile" board. The committee comprises three executive branch officials, including Kevin Hassett , Trump's top economic aide and a chief defender of the administration's economic record, according to a presidential memorandum posted on the White House website and shared Friday on social media. The other two members are Keith Sonderling, Labor secretary and acting head of the Office of Government Ethics, and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas, according to the notice, which is dated Wednesday. No outside, independent arbiters are mentioned. The highly unusual move, which hasn't been used in nearly a century, is bound to fuel new accusations that Trump and his aides are eroding the Fed's long-maintained independence while once again wielding government power against the president's enemies. Congressional Democrats quickly slammed the announcement, while Cook's lawyers expressed deep skepticism about the panel's validity. There is no modern precedent for such a committee, though past presidents have convened similar panels. President William Taft in 1912 appointed a committee to investigate the Board of United States General Appraisers, and President Herbert Hoover did the same in 1931 to probe statements by the president of the Navy League. The Supreme Court, in its June ruling temporarily blocking Trump from his first attempt to fire Cook, cited Taft's committee. Trump's panel and Cook are scheduled to appear for an in-person hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm election, the memo states. Its members can consult with the Department of Justice and other agencies "to aid in its inquiry," the notice says. Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, sharply questioned the legitimacy of the inquiry, but nevertheless said the governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name." "In light of the President's repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook – regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law," the lawyers told CNBC in a statement. "But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they said. "We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise. Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her," Lowell and Eisen said. Trump first tried to fire Cook last year, after administration officials raised allegations that she made false statements on at least one mortgage-related document. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing and filed a lawsuit to block her dismissal. A federal court temporarily barred Trump from firing her, and the Supreme Court in June narrowly upheld that ruling. But the high court did not stop Trump from trying again for Cook's removal. Rather, it rejected Trump's first bid because Cook was not given proper legal due process, and said any new attempt to fire her would require additional steps. Under the Federal Reserve Act, a president can remove a Fed governor only "for cause." Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' In August, White House aide Dan Scavino told Cook in a letter that Trump was once again "considering" firing her in connection with the mortgage allegations. "As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump states in the memo establishing the committee of inquiry, which is addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

events.title: Why buying Chipotle would be a mistake for Starbucks, even with Brian Niccol in charge
events.summary: If Starbucks bought Chipotle Mexican Grill, a possibility the Financial Times reported this week was being explored by the coffee giant, it would be the largest purchase of one restaurant chain by another ever in the U.S. It would also almost certainly be one of the biggest missteps, given the limited synergies between the two brands, the size of the deal, and the potential distraction as Starbucks brass works on its turnaround. Chipotle investors initially reacted well to the report, with shares rising as much as 8% on Thursday after the report was published. They are now back down to roughly where they were before the article. It’s easy to understand their enthusiasm: Starbucks’ Brian Niccol is the star CEO who knows Chipotle intimately after turning it around in his six years leading the burrito chain, before leaving in 2024 to fix Starbucks. On his watch, Niccol led Chipotle out of a food safety crisis; improved its restaurants and operations; built a leading app; and ultimately helped Chipotle double annual sales to $10 billion. But more recently Chipotle has struggled, and its shares have fallen by almost half since his successor took the reins almost two years ago. (Chipotle did not respond to a request for comment.) Starbucks investors reacted rather differently to the report, sending shares down on fears a transaction like that would be a big distraction, even for a CEO as well regarded as Niccol who is being credited with getting Starbucks out of a long slump and back to growth and in the good graces of its customers.  “Starbucks is still executing its turnaround strategy, and acquiring Chipotle could consume significant senior management time on financing, integration, organizational design, systems, and personnel,” BTIG analyst Pete Saleh wrote in a note. Starbucks itself told Fortune in a statement it was “laser focused” on that turnaround. The fact that shares in both companies have essentially returned to where they were before the FT article suggests the stock market has concluded the deal is unlikely to happen. Chipotle’s market capitalization is about $40 billion, meaning Starbucks would likely have to offer $50 billion (or half of Starbucks’ current valuation) with the standard 20% acquisition premium.  That enormous sum in turn would require Starbucks to borrow tens of billions of dollars, with interest expense damaging its profitability and potentially diverting money away from the investments it is making to upgrade its coffee shops. Investors are already watching Starbucks’ capital spending closely given how pricey café makeovers and store equipment to improve its service can be and how they eat into profit margins. The company could also use equity but that would have undesirable effects and pressure shares. Ultimately, a Starbucks-Chipotle deal offers little in terms of improving both companies’ performances. Wall Street firm William Blair estimated about $300 million in potential annual corporate and technology savings, to be sure, but that hardly justifies a $50 billion deal. What’s more, Starbucks is focused on beverages, and the food it does sell is largely premade, while Chipotle makes freshly prepared foods. Many observers are concluding that the initial appeal of the deal had to do with the regard the market holds for Niccol as a leader. “The clear anchor to why this would make any sense is management,” Citi analyst Jon Tower wrote in a note. But even someone as talented as Niccol can only do so much at once. Focus is core to delivering a turnaround. And indeed, some of Niccol’s moves at Starbucks have involved getting rid of some complexity and distractions, notably selling majority control of Starbucks’ China business last year. Niccol has little experience integrating other brands or dealing with M&A. He was enormously successful at Taco Bell, then at Chipotle, and now at Starbucks by being relentlessly focused on restaurant operations and customer experience. And with this deal apparently unlikely to happen, he can continue to be. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The used car market is stagnant. Here's how to profit anyway
events.summary: There's an old but useful expression used for buying cars: Kick the tires and light the fires. The phrase, which started in aviation but bled its way into automobiles, is a reminder to look under the hood and poke around before purchasing a car. The same advice would work for shares of CarMax . On the surface, the stock looks fairly priced. CarMax is trading at roughly 17x fiscal-year expected earnings of $3.16/share. That's roughly in line with its 10-year historical forward multiple. While that valuation may not look stretched, the underlying fundamentals reflect a sharp squeeze on used-car affordability. Middle-market consumers, already pressured by high new and used car prices, see that compounded (literally) by severe financing headwinds. St. Louis Federal Reserve data puts average used auto loan APRs at 15.9% with an average loan term of 68 months. Even with used vehicle prices softening slightly, high borrowing costs keep monthly payments out of reach for many prospective buyers. Operational metrics used to evaluate a car dealership's performance show the impact. The cash conversion cycle has lengthened, inventory turnover has slowed, and average days on the lot have crept higher. Because borrowing rates are unlikely to drop precipitously in the near term, a catalyst for an auto sales boom remains elusive. However, given the fair multiple and stable cash generation, an abrupt collapse is also not the base case. The setup favors a range-bound stock with a capped upside ceiling. The strategy: November (hedged) short strangle Investors expecting KMX to stay within a defined channel can sell a wide strangle and buy an out-of-the-money call to neutralize upside tail risk. Buy the November 67.50 Call for $0.20 (Upside Hedge) Key trade metrics & risk parameters As a package, this three-legged structure collects a net credit of roughly $2.30/share ($230 per spread, since each contract represents 100 shares), or about 4.3% of the current share price, over 6 weeks (42 calendar days), or more than 37% annualized. Downside breakeven: $47.70, 12% below current price. Upside breakeven $62.30, 16.5% above current price. Maximum upside risk is $5.20/share ($520 per spread); that risk is capped above $67.50 ($7.50 spread width – $2.30 credit). Ideal Target Profit Zone: between the short strikes of $50.00 to $60.00, in which case you retain the full $2.30 credit if held to expiration. The sweet spot is between $50 and $60 at November expiration, where all three options expire worthless, and you keep the full $2.30 credit. On the downside, the structure provides a nearly 11% buffer. If KMX breaches $47.70, the position carries standard put-assignment risk, allowing an investor who doesn't mind owning the shares to acquire them at an effective net basis of $47.70 (roughly 15x forward earnings).On the upside, standard short strangles leave the trader exposed to unlimited risk associated with a short stock position. By buying the November 67.50 call for a small portion of the premium received, upside risk is capped at $5.20 above $67.50, guarding against short-covering spikes or a sudden, unanticipated macro easing/rate decline, while still maintaining attractive yields. events.title: Celebrity deaths in 2026: Remembering the famous people we lost this year
events.summary: Mike Ditka. George Gojkovich/Getty Images Actors James Van Der Beek, Hayden Panettiere, Robert Duvall, Chuck Norris, and Eva Marie Saint died in 2026. So did musicians Dolly Parton and Duncan Sheik. Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, activist Gloria Steinem, and NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka also died this year. Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Scott Adams, 68 Scott Adams. Michael Macor/Getty Images Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert." By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips. At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons. Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams. Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer . Brad Arnold, 47 Brad Arnold. Scott Gries/ImageDirect/Getty Images The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year. The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom. Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer. Afrika Bambaataa, 68 Afrika Bambaataa. Paul Natkin/WireImage/Getty A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx. He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career. Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse . Bambaataa denied all claims. He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer . Rob Bass, 59 Rob Bass. Al Pereira/Michael Osche Archives/Getty Images One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstream, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock. The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine. Bass died on May 22 following cancer . Nicholas Brendon, 54 Nicholas Brendon. Getty Images Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential." Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement. In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries. "While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart." Peabo Bryson, 75 Peabo Bryson. ABC Photo Archives/Getty Images Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads. Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain." Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin." Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given. James Burrows, 85 James Burrows. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier." Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes. Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given. Kyle Busch, 41 Kyle Busch. Sean Gardner/Getty Images Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time. Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead. Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis. Robert Carradine, 71 Robert Carradine. Bobby Bank/WireImage/Getty Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds." As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career. He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series. Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness. "We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness." Carradine died by suicide on February 23. If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline . Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US. Bud Cort, 77 Bud Cort. events.title: The release of Sarah J. Maas' 6th 'ACOTAR' book is just weeks away. Here's everything we know.
events.summary: Sarah J. Maas is publishing the sixth "A Court of Thorns and Roses" book. Alexandra Genova / SAINT LUCY Represents Sarah J. Maas is returning to the "ACOTAR" world with two new books. The sixth book will be released on October 27, 2026, and the seventh on January 12, 2027. Teasers shared ahead of its release confirmed three characters who will return in book six. Sarah J. Maas fans, gather round. We finally know what's coming in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series (sort of). On August 17, 2026, Maas announced the titles of the sixth and seventh "ACOTAR" books, along with initial descriptions of the novels. Book six is called "A Court of Splintered Harmony" and will be released on October 27, 2026, and book seven is "A Court of Forgotten Melody," hitting shelves on January 12, 2027. Maas first announced she would publish the sixth and seventh installments of her series in March 2026, remaining tight-lipped about them until the title announcement in August. The books are eagerly awaited not only by fans but also by Maas' publisher, Bloomsbury. The company's sales fell 10% for the 2025-2026 fiscal year because Maas didn't release a new book, Publishers Weekly reported . And in recent weeks, Bloomsbury has been sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony" on social media, building hype for the novel and teasing what's to come. Here's everything we know about "ACOTAR" six so far. Warning: Some spoilers for Maas' work — including "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City" — ahead. Maas is releasing the sixth 'A Court of Thorns and Roses' story in multiple volumes In March 2023, Bloomsbury announced that Maas had signed a deal for three more books with the publisher. At the time, she was already under contract for four titles, including "House of Flame and Shadow," the third installment in her "Crescent City" series , published in January 2024. Readers didn't find out what the next book she would write would be until her March 2026 appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast with Alex Cooper. She told Cooper she finished the sixth "ACOTAR" book while writing in Montana over the summer of 2025, but she didn't share details about it because of its nontraditional release structure. "This book's coming out October 27, and then on January 12, like two months later, I can't do math, whatever that is, the next ACOTAR book will be coming out," Maas said. "So there will be two books within, like, a very short span." Sarah J. Maas for "Call Her Daddy." Call Her Daddy As her fans will know, Maas' books are typically split into parts, separating different sections of the story she is telling. However, when it comes to the sixth "ACOTAR" story, Maas said the individual parts became longer than she anticipated as she started writing, with part one coming in at 400 pages at one point. As she continued writing, Maas decided the parts didn't have to be in a single physical book. "What if this book was really long?" she said. "What if it took me more than a thousand pages to tell the story that needed to be told, the arc that I wanted to create from start to finish?" Maas said the story for "ACOTAR" six was ultimately divided into four parts, though it is still one cohesive story. Part one is the novel Bloomsbury will publish  on October 27, 2026, and parts two and three will be published together on January 12, 2027. Maas has yet to write or give a publication date for part four, but she told Cooper all three volumes would be published "in a very short time." "It's meant to be read, ideally, as one massive, massive story as opposed to in a trilogy," she said. "It's not a trilogy. Like, arcs aren't wrapped up." Maas finally shared some details about the books in August 2026 On August 16, Maas cleared her Instagram of all its posts, changing her profile photo to a black-and-white illustration of a monster and a spider. Then, on August 17, she shared the covers and titles of books six, "A Court of Splintered Harmony," and seven, "A Court of Forgotten Melody," on her wiped Instagram. The "Splintered Harmony" cover features a pink-and-orange backdrop with a sketched drawing of a monster with teeth and bones, and the subtitle is "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movement I." The Valkyrie were introduced to "ACOTAR" in "A Court of Silver Flames," when Nesta Archeron brought the legendary all-female fighting squad back to life alongside her friends Gwyn and Emerie. "A Court of Splintered Harmony." Bloomsbury Maas posted the book alongside the tagline, "What was broken will be remade." The blurb shared on booksellers' websites reveals that the Night Court is facing new threats when book six opens: Koschei the Deathless, one of three legendary monster siblings introduced throughout "ACOTAR," and those willing to ally with him to claim the newly freed human lands. The description also notes that there is tension among the members of the Night Court because of "recent betrayals and revealed truths," which they must work through if they want to defeat Koschei. "A Court of Splintered Harmony" will be 352 pages and will include three bonus chapters from the "ACOTAR" series. Those bonus chapters were previously published in specific editions of Maas' novels, but they will be in all copies of "ACOSH," as the publisher shared on its social media on September 24. One chapter focuses on Feyre and Rhysand, one on Cassian and Nesta, and one on Azriel's experience on the Winter Solstice that takes place in "A Court of Silver Flames." Teasers from the new book In mid-September, Bloomsbury began sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony," offering more insight into the novel than the vague blurbs. It released six quotes in total, and the first, shared on September 17, revealed that at least some of the novel will be told from Lucien Vanserra's perspective. "Lucien's heart thundered, throat drying out," the quote read . "Maybe this had been a terrible idea." Lucien has only played a supporting role in the "ACOTAR" books so far, but Maas has been teeing up his expanded role in her books through his unaccepted mating bond with Elain Archeron, Feyre's middle sister, and his connection to Koschei. He serves as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court in "ACOSF," alongside Jurian and Vassa, a human queen who was sold to Koschei and cursed to turn into a firebird each day. It would be surprising if Vassa — and by extension Lucien — weren't involved in fighting against Koschei in book six. Likewise, the final quote Bloomsbury shared on October 9 appeared to confirm that Azriel will narrate some of "ACOSH." The quote didn't include his name, but the unnamed narrator was communicating with shadows: "'We are here,' the shadows whispered in his ear. 'We are always here.'" Azriel is a Shadowsinger in the "ACOTAR" world, with his shadows being described as keeping him company and whispering to him as he serves as the Night Court's spymaster. events.title: DHS faces blowback over its attack on a Democratic House candidate
events.summary: The Department of Homeland Security is coming under fire for publicly attacking Democratic congressional candidate Janelle Stelson less than a month before the midterm election . Why it matters: The Stelson campaign is threatening a lawsuit over the allegations, while a watchdog group is seeking an investigation into whether an ICE official violated restrictions on partisan political activity by federal employees. "We are likely to take legal action to combat the blatant lies and coordinated misinformation campaign," Stelson campaign manager Alma Baker said in a statement to Axios. The campaign said Friday it has sent out cease and desist letters, viewed by Axios, to several news outlets that reported DHS's claims as fact. The race between Stelson and Republican Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania's 10th district is one of the most competitive and expensive House elections in the country, attracting more than $26 million in spending, according to AdImpact. Driving the news: DHS published a press release on Wednesday announcing the arrest of what it said was an "illegal alien from Nigeria who exposed himself in public while working for congressional campaign in Pennsylvania." The migrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, was arrested by ICE on Oct. 1 after pleading guilty to disorderly conduct last month, according to the press release. The release included a statement from ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall saying: "It's unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public." Stelson herself quickly batted down the claim: "He's not an employee. He's not a volunteer," she said at an event on Wednesday. Nobody named Igbojekwe was paid by the Stelson campaign as of Sept. 30, according to disbursements tracked by the Federal Election Commission. The campaign also showed Axios a search of its volunteer database that turned up no results for the name. In its cease-and-desist letter, the campaign said Igbojekwe has also "never been employed by any vendors of the campaign." Asked Thursday for comment on this story, DHS sent Axios its initial press release. The agency did not respond to multiple follow-up emails requesting comment on the Stelson campaign's threat of legal action. Between the lines: DHS cited a New Jersey-based news outlet called "Shore News Network" as its source for the claim that Igbojekwe was a Stelson canvasser. That outlet cited a social media post from conservative activist Scott Presler. "A canvasser for democrat Janelle Stelson ... was reportedly charged for indecent exposure," Presler wrote in a post on X , which included a photo of a court document that did not make reference to the Stelson campaign. Presler did not respond to a request for comment from Axios. Axios obtained an affidavit in which Trevor Jeffers, the East Pennsboro, Pa., police officer who made the initial arrest, testified that Igbojekwe was sitting in a parked car in a residential neighborhood "wearing nothing but a shirt" with his "genitals ... exposed." "Igbojekwe advised that he was in the neighborhood for work and that he was waiting to hand out flyers for Janelle Stelson's political campaign," Jeffers said in the affidavit, adding that Igbojekwe "was able to provide a stack of flyers showing he was there for work." The East Pennsboro Police did not provide a comment and denied Axios' public records request for documents related to the case. Several news outlets that covered the initial arrest or the DHS press release have since deleted their stories and posts. None responded to Axios' requests for comment. The Stelson campaign, asked about the affidavit, referred Axios to Baker's statement on Wednesday saying Igbojekwe had "never been employed" by them and that they had "never heard of him prior to the news of his arrest." Zoom in: Igbojekwe was charged with indecent exposure and disorderly conduct, later pleading guilty to a single count of disorderly conduct, according to court records. The attorney listed as his representative in court documents, Cumberland County first assistant public defender Arla Waller, did not return multiple phone calls seeking comment. Igbojekwe did not respond to a request for comment sent to an email address listed under his name. The latest: The Office of Special Counsel "will open a file" in response to questions about whether Wall violated the Hatch Act, which prohibits mixing federal government work with political campaigning, according to emails shared with Axios. Donald Sherman, the executive director of ethics watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, wrote in an email to OSC that Wall's statement was "gratuitous partisanship that constitutes prohibited political activity." An OSC staffer replied to Sherman: "We received your complaint and will open a file to address this matter." An OSC spokesperson confirmed the authenticity of the emails but declined to comment further. Wall did not respond to a request for comment. What they're saying: Deborah Fleischaker, a former acting ICE chief of staff under the Biden administration, told Axios that legal counsel at the agency during her tenure "almost certainly would have recommended not to say something like" what Wall did in his statement. Directly referencing an election in an official statement "really is seen as a no no," she told Axios. Fleischaker acknowledged that federal ethics rules aren't the deterrent they used to be . The bottom line: Cook Political Report rates the race between Stelson and Perry for the Harrisburg-based House seat as a toss-up. The Freedom Caucus Fund, a hybrid PAC dedicated to electing and supporting House Freedom Caucus members, released a digital ad on Thursday calling Igbojekwe a "Nigerian illegal alien campaigning for Democrat Janelle Stelson."

events.title: Hurricane Isaias disrupts U.S. oil production in Gulf of Mexico, threatens refineries
events.summary: Hurricane Isaias is disrupting U.S. crude oil production in the Gulf of Mexico. As of Thursday, oil companies shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or around 63% of total U.S. production in the Gulf. The hurricane's path could affect Chevron's refinery in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Vertex's refinery in Saraland, Alabama. Hurricane Isaias is disrupting U.S. crude oil production in the Gulf of Mexico and could limit about 2% of the country's refining capacity, at a time when fuel markets are already tight around the world. Isaias is churning toward Mississippi, Alabama and the Florida panhandle as a Category 3 storm with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center , and is expected to make landfall Friday night or early Saturday. As of Thursday, oil companies had shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or roughly 63% of total U.S. production in the Gulf, according to the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement . The hurricane appeared to be veering away from the dense refining region in southern Louisiana near New Orleans and Baton Rouge. But the storm could affect Chevron 's refinery in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and a Vertex Energy refinery in Saraland, Alabama. Both areas are under hurricane warnings. The facilities there can produce a combined 466,000 bpd, or 2.4% of U.S. refining capacity, said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "Of course, losing any refinery capacity when diesel supplies are at their lowest level for this time of year since the EIA began reporting in 1982 is not a good thing," Lipow wrote in a Friday note, referring to the Energy Information Administration. Chevron's refinery at Pascagoula remains operational, spokesperson Ross Allen said Thursday. Vertex officials weren't immediately available for comment about its Saraland refinery. " The biggest risk to these two refineries are a loss of electricity or flooding damage," Lipow wrote in a note Friday. If the refineries do shut down, it would take one to two weeks to restart them if they did not sustain damage, he said. Refineries on the Gulf Coast are running at 95% of their capacity, so there is no slack in the system to make up for lost production, Lipow said. Diesel prices have soared as the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East knock out refining capacity . Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to ban diesel exports. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East. U.S. refiners have stepped in to take advantage of wide profit margins to export diesel around the world, particularly to Europe. In the past, fuel prices rose while crude prices fell during outages at Gulf refineries, said Kevin Book, managing director at ClearView Energy Partners. That's a result of those refineries not demanding crude and not producing fuel for consumers, Book told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Thursday. Lipow warned that tanker traffic will also be disrupted. "Tankers will be delayed delivering crude oil to the refineries while other tankers are delayed loading gasoline, jet fuel and diesel out of the refineries," the analyst said. "Florida will experience delays in receiving gasoline, jet fuel and diesel."

events.title: Delta CEO says there's no Elon Musk feud: 'I drive a Tesla'
events.summary: Elon Musk said Delta's CEO, Ed Bastian, should lose his job on X. Bastian said there's no drama between the businessmen. Getty Images/Business Insider Ed Bastian said there's no feud with Elon Musk — and he's a big fan of the trillionaire's projects. "I drive a Tesla," he told CNBC. Musk has ramped up his criticism of Delta after some unconfirmed comments from the airline CEO. Delta CEO Ed Bastian said he doesn't have a public feud with the world's richest man. "There's no tit-for-tat, as far as I'm concerned," he said during a Friday interview with CNBC when asked about Elon Musk's recent X offensive against the airline. "I'm a big fan of Starlink. I'm a fan of what Elon does. I drive a Tesla. OK? So there's nothing. All this nonsense about being personal is not true at all." The apparently one-sided battle appears to have started in March, when the airline chose Amazon's Leo as its next-generation satellite internet provider over SpaceX's Starlink. At the time, Musk made one post , warning the airline "doesn't realize how much this will affect them." Musk has stepped up his criticisms of Bastian and Delta in the past two weeks after aviation-industry X account, JonNYC , posted unconfirmed quotes from Bastian, including a comment warning that, "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me." The same day, Musk reposted an article with the unverified comments, saying that Bastian would "lose his job over this." @garyleff @Delta He will lose his job over this — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) September 30, 2026 Musk has posted several other times about Delta since the unconfirmed comment, making fun of the airline's internet choice: "Best way to sandbox an AI is to put it on a Delta flight," he wrote in late September. Bastian is not the first airline CEO to draw Musk's ire. In January, Musk and Michael O'Leary, the CEO of the European budget airline Ryanair, exchanged jabs on X because the company didn't install Starlink on its planes over what it said were cost issues. At the time, Musk polled X users, asking if he should buy RyanAir and find someone named Ryan to take over as the main boss. O'Leary, who has fashioned himself as an outspoken chief executive, launched a "great idiots" seat sale in response. Delta's Bastian is taking a very different tack. "I don't pay any attention," he said when asked about the feud on CNBC. "Everyone is entitled to their own opinion." Delta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. events.title: I tried every item in Joanna Gaines' line of frozen baked goods. Here's how I'd rank them from worst to best.
events.summary: Joanna Gaines and Magnolia Table released a line of frozen baked goods. Samantha Pettyjohn Joanna Gaines' Magnolia Table brand released a line of frozen baked goods. I tried the eight items and ranked them from worst to best. The frozen version of Jo's Buttermilk Biscuit was my favorite of the bunch. It's hard to say what Joanna Gaines is more famous for at this point: her home designs or her food. Gaines and her husband became household names through "Fixer Upper," but over a decade later, they're full-blown moguls who are constantly expanding their Magnolia empire . For Gaines, that has meant leaning into new food ventures, from the Magnolia Table restaurant in Waco to her ever-growing list of cookbooks. And last year, she entered the frozen food game. In October 2025, Gaines launched a line of frozen baked goods through her Magnolia Table brand. I decided to try every item in the line so I could rank them. Here's what I thought. Joanna Gaines launched a line of frozen baked goods in 2025. Christopher Willard/Disney via Getty Images Magnolia Table's line of baked goods was first sold exclusively at Target , like the Hearth & Hand with Magnolia brand. Now, shoppers can also buy the line at HEB and Central Market. All of the baked goods in the collection were inspired by food Joanna Gaines makes at home, or that's served at Silos Baking Co. or Magnolia Table in Waco, Texas. The line originally featured six items: Chocolate Chip Cookies Classic Sugar Cookies Silo Cookies Classic Cinnamon Rolls Jo's Buttermilk Biscuits After School Banana Bread And Gaines later added two more products in recent months: Brownie Cookies Prize Big Biscuits As of October 2026, each item costs $10.99, except for the biscuits, which are $9.99. I'm no stranger to Gaines' food offerings, having dined at Magnolia Table in Waco and made her homemade biscuit recipe . When I saw the news of Magnolia Table's frozen line, I knew I had to try it. After grabbing the collection through a pickup order at Target , I spent an afternoon baking the original six items, and a year later, I grabbed the Brownie Cookies and Prize Pig Biscuits after they were released to review them as well. Here's my ranking from worst to best. 8. After School Banana Bread Samantha Pettyjohn/Business Insider When I first glanced at the box of the After School Banana Bread, I saw "ready to enjoy in minutes" written on the front. However, about an hour into my baking endeavors, I looked more closely and realized the bread required more preparation than I had thought. The directions said to thaw the bread in its bakeable tray for three to four hours before baking it at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 minutes. There was an option to microwave the bread from frozen, but I wanted to bake it for the best possible result. Thawing the banana bread wasn't a huge deal, but remembering to take it out of the freezer hours before baking didn't seem particularly convenient. When I asked the brand about the timing, Magnolia Table said, "We know so many families love our After School Banana Bread recipe, and we wanted to give them a way to recreate that same warm, cozy aroma at home by baking it in the oven." "At the same time, we know life gets busy, so we also included a quicker option for those moments when convenience matters most," the brand added. "If you're warming from frozen, you can simply place the loaf in the microwave and enjoy it in just a few minutes. Both methods are there to make sure families can experience that homemade comfort, whether it's a weekend bake or a weekday treat." The banana bread didn't stand out. Samantha Pettyjohn/Business Insider I'm not generally a huge banana bread fan, but the Magnolia Table iteration was fairly tasty. It wasn't too banana-forward and had a comforting taste when I took a bite fresh from the oven. The bread offered easy eating, and as its name indicates, it seems like a good option for an afternoon snack for kids. The flavor didn't really stand out, though, especially compared to other items in the line, and I don't think it was worth the hours of thawing. I would probably make it in the microwave next time, though I'm unsure how that would change the texture. 7. The Classic Cinnamon Rolls Samantha Pettyjohn/Business Insider I've always loved a good cinnamon roll , and although homemade rolls are particularly good, I have no problem with frozen options. I spent most Saturdays of my childhood begging my mom to make the Pillsbury or Sister Schubert brand of refrigerated rolls. As a frozen cinnamon roll connoisseur, I was excited to try Gaines' take on the classic pastry. In Magnolia Table's pack, four rolls come in a bakeable tray sealed inside plastic wrap. I was a bit surprised by the small number of cinnamon rolls, but when I asked Magnolia Table about it, it said "a great deal of consideration" went into deciding how many of each baked good to include in its packs. "Some decisions were guided by simple kitchen logic — like including a dozen cookies, which naturally feels right when baking at home," Magnolia Table said. "We also relied on research and consumer insights to ensure each product offers both exceptional quality and convenience. Ultimately, every package was designed to feel intentional and familiar, much like something made in your own kitchen." The directions on the box instruct you to remove the rolls from the plastic wrap and then let them rest for 45 minutes to an hour before baking at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for 23 to 25 minutes. The resting wasn't my favorite, but I liked that you could throw the rolls into the oven in the tray. A packet of icing was also included, but the directions didn't specify what to do with it while the rolls rested. I left my packet on my kitchen counter. The cinnamon rolls were fine, but I probably wouldn't pick them over another brand at the grocery store. Samantha Pettyjohn/Business Insider My cinnamon rolls were ready in about 25 minutes, with the edges slightly crispy and the center gooey. I poured my icing — which had softened from sitting on the counter — over the cinnamon rolls, and it spread out fairly thin. The icing might have had a better consistency if I had kept it in the refrigerator while the rolls thawed, but the directions didn't indicate that I should have done so. I informed Magnolia Table about my icing consistency issues. The brand expressed appreciation for the feedback and clarified that the icing could be left out without compromising safety. "Our icing is completely safe to leave out while the rolls thaw and bake, but for those who prefer a thicker consistency, placing it in the fridge is a great option," Magnolia Table said. Despite my issues with the icing, the cinnamon rolls smelled inviting, so I was optimistic when I took a bite. It wasn't bad, but it reminded me of cinnamon rolls I've had at the mall. events.title: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work. “The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch. After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts. The result is LumenUs , the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden. “I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said. While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation. “We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said. From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available. “We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said. Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product. LumenUs, a participant in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 — the annual showcase of promising early-stage startups at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco — will launch in early access in October. events.summary: All-robotic airborne assaults have become a new operational reality in Ukraine. Courtesy of NC13 Ukrainian forces recently used heavy bomber drones to air-drop armed robots behind enemy lines. Traditional airborne assaults have been rare. All-robotic ones, however, are becoming an operational reality. This tactic has triggered growing attention across the military and defense industry. Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, made a highly unusual disclosure late last month, revealing that his forces had become the "first in the world" to air-drop ground robots from drones in combat. Heavy bomber drones had carried the armed robots roughly six miles deep into Russian territory and dropped them there as part of Operation Vivaldi , an assault that is still unfolding in eastern Ukraine and has already seen Kyiv reclaim large swaths of territory from Moscow. The tactic is called "Gryphon" and is named after a soldier who went missing in action near Andriivka, said Mykola Zinkevych, commander of NC13, the world's first strike uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) unit. Rather than driving explosive-laden robots across the front line, heavy drones dropped the bots in the Russian rear, creating an unexpected new direction of attack. NC13, a unit within the Third Assault Brigade of the Third Army Corps, has played a leading role in Operation Vivaldi. Zinkevych, who goes by the call sign "Makar," spoke to Business Insider through a translator this week to discuss his unit's participation. Traditional airborne assaults have been very rare in this conflict as dense air-defense networks threaten air operations. Operation Vivaldi, however, has demonstrated the potential for entirely uncrewed airborne assaults. Rather than risking helicopters, transport aircraft, or paratroopers, drones can drop robots behind enemy lines, and Ukraine's booming defense industry is working on solutions to advance this concept, as are military units. Brave1 , Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, said several days after the Third Army Corps' airborne assault reveal that another combat unit, the "Alter Ego" robot battalion of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade, had developed and deployed similar technology. The view from a heavy bomber drone as it drops a UGV. Courtesy of NC13 The unit engineered a specialized robot called "Desantnyk," as well as a mechanism that allows its heavy bomber drones to carry and drop the robot deep behind the front lines. It has already been used to attack Russian positions, Brave1 said, adding that the entire process, from initial concept to combat deployment, took just 10 days. Without an off-the-shelf robot on the market that bomber drones could readily carry and drop, especially at long ranges, the Alter Ego unit could only develop one itself, a Brave1 representative told Business Insider, relaying information from the unit. "This is an asymmetrical solution that the enemy does not expect — delivering mobility and the capability to conduct operations far behind enemy lines," the representative said. From the robot's combat experience, Alter Ego now understands that the UGVs must balance mobility, range, and payload, while also maintaining resilient communications with operators. Brave1 said it helped the unit find a manufacturer so they could turn the prototype into serial production. Other Ukrainian defense companies, likewise, see value in these systems. Volodymyr Zinovskyi, the CEO of the Ukrainian defense firm TAF Industries, told Business Insider in London recently that his company has developed both robots and heavy bomber drones and could easily combine the two for a mission. The concept of using robotic systems to carry each other into battle is not necessarily new. Earlier this year, for instance, Business Insider reported that a Ukrainian defense manufacturer said soldiers surprised them by dropping one of its robots from a drone. A heavy bomber drone carries a UGV in this system engineered by Alter Ego. Courtesy of Brave1/Screengrab And motherships have become increasingly popular. Ukrainian firms have engineered new ways to launch drones from autonomous platforms, such as uncrewed boats and ground robots, significantly increasing their operational range. Using drones to air-drop robots into battle — a tactic Brave1 said is unique to Ukraine and that only a few units are able to pull off right now — is Kyiv's latest homemade mothership concept. The development comes amid broader efforts by Ukraine to replace soldiers with robotic systems for dangerous front-line missions, especially logistics runs and casualty evacuation. "During assault operations, ahead of the infantry, UAVs and loitering munitions always go first," Biletskyi, the Third Army Corps commander, said on September 20 while sharing Operation Vivaldi details on social media. Ukrainian defense companies and soldiers told Business Insider that mothership ideas like air-dropped robots — combining technologies in creative and effective ways — underscore the direction that war is headed. Zinovskyi, the TAF Industries CEO, said that defense companies were previously focused primarily on producing drones. The next challenge is systems integration, where mixed systems work together to complete missions. Zinkevych, the NC13 commander, said that he's pleased to see multiple firms developing bomber drones capable of carrying UGVs and described these efforts as a key example of industry scaling a system that has already proven effective on the battlefield. events.title: ‘Trojan horse’: California’s top 1% pay nearly half the state’s income taxes. Prop 40 opponents warn the billionaire tax could reach everyone else
events.summary: California’s revenue is notoriously top heavy, leaving state coffers vulnerable to boom-and-bust cycles as the wealthiest residents see their incomes rise and fall with the stock market. In recent years, the top 1% of California households have accounted for about 40% to 50% of all personal income tax revenue, according to the conservative Hoover Institution . In fact, the top 1% paid more than $60 billion in California personal income taxes in 2021, when the stock market soared. The flip side is that the state suffers crippling deficits when the market tanks, as during the Global Financial Crisis. Now, California’s Proposition 40 seeks to tax billionaires’ wealth in addition to their incomes, and opponents have launched a full-court press, calling it a “Trojan horse” that will eventually come for all Californians. The ballot initiative calls for residents worth more than $1 billion to pay a one-time tax equivalent to 5% of their assets. The union pushing Prop 40, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, has said the wealth tax could raise $100 billion in revenue and help offset federal cuts to health spending. Prop 40 includes a provision that says the state legislature could modify it with a two-thirds vote—but only “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Prop 40 backers insist it’s only aimed at billionaires. Still, any changes would be up to state lawmakers, though courts would also weigh in on any attempts to stretch the scope to all taxpayers or to extend it beyond a one-time levy. According to CalMatters , there have been numerous instances in which the state legislature has amended other ballot measures after they have passed. There have also been times when the courts have upheld the changes and when they have struck them down. In 1995, the state Supreme Court ruled lawmakers can make changes if they advance voters’ original intent “by any reasonable construction,” the report said. But in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal rejected an attempt to amend the Political Reform Act, saying it “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the law. Of course, there’s nothing that would prevent another ballot initiative in the future from taxing wealth to fund other spending priorities. And if Prop 40 succeeds, similar initiatives could pop up elsewhere. A group of Nobel laureate economists who support Prop 40 have said the ballot measure could “ kick-start a movement ” that spreads well beyond California. In a  letter signed by Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman, and Joseph Stiglitz, the economists argued that while billionaires have “made important contributions,” they have also been “amply rewarded” and have used loopholes to avoid taxes on capital returns, allowing their wealth to compound further. “As Californians head to the polls, their vote may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy,” the letter added. Prop 40’s critics have warned the tax is unlikely to be a one-time deal and also raised alarms about the forms of wealth that would be targeted, such as unrealized capital gains and privately held stock that’s key for startups. Supporters point to the AI boom and say California’s ultrarich would still be among the world’s wealthiest. And the Nobel laureates contend the tax will not doom Silicon Valley, saying California has attracted 80% of all new venture capital funding in the U.S. since the start of 2026, up from about 50% before 2025. Prop 40 has split the state’s political and business leaders. Gov. Gavin Newsom is against it, while U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna is for it. But even the congressman has conceded he doesn’t want illiquid stakes or voting shares to be taxed. Some unions have also come out in opposition, saying other areas of state spending should be priorities, too. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he’s “ perfectly fine ” with it, while Google cofounder Sergey Brin  contributed over $100 million  toward opposing the billionaire tax. Further complicating the matter is competition from other ballot measures that would nullify Prop 40. Proposition 41 would make any new taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit, while Proposition 42 would prohibit taxes on financial assets and personal property other than real estate. A recent  poll from the Public Policy Institute of California  found all three have support from a majority of voters. “Supporters of Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax initiative, have a lot of work to do,” Mark Baldassare, the survey’s director, told KQED . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The biggest changes Anthropic just made to Claude’s rules
events.summary: Anthropic's new usage policy for Claude takes effect next month. Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images Anthropic updated Claude's usage policy with several new provisions. The changes include clarifications around deceptive campaigns, weapons, and surveillance. The updated policy takes effect on November 12. Anthropic's new rule against abusing Claude wasn't the only update to its revised usage policy for the AI chatbot. The artificial intelligence lab has also spelled out a series of new usage provisions about deceptive campaigns, elections, weapons development, surveillance, law enforcement, and Claude-connected hardware. Anthropic said this week that most of the changes in the latest version of its usage policy were intended to clarify existing rules. The updated policy takes effect on November 12. Deceptive campaigns Anthropic added a new section to its AI rules titled, "Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity," which the company said applies to deceptive activity of any kind, political or commercial. "It covers efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts, along with building the tools and infrastructure for running influence operation campaigns," Anthropic said. Elections The company refined its political content restrictions and sharpened its elections section, focusing it on "disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections." That section was renamed "Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes" and includes using Anthropic's products to "generate or disseminate false or misleading information in political and electoral contexts." Weapons Anthropic said its usage policy has always barred the use of Claude to make weapons. However, its new rules make explicit that the chatbot cannot be used to develop the software or components that make weapons work, "as well as actions like arming drones or other autonomous vehicles." The company said it has recently seen users attempt to use its models to "build guidance and control software for weapons." Surveillance and law enforcement Anthropic tightened its usage policy's surveillance and criminal justice section to more specifically lay out banned activity. That includes tracking people without their consent as well as doxxing. Under the new policy, Claude also cannot be used to "decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process," or to build or improve tools designed for surveillance. Claude-connected hardware Anthropic updated its policy to reflect new requirements for its models when they're connected to hardware that "takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury." "A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected," Anthropic said.
