events.title: Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in 6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business Purpose.
events.summary: Illustration by Joel Kimmel for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. Reference image: ZUMA Press Wire/Reuters Connect. In the summer of 2023, after he was impeached on charges of abusing his office for personal gain, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was suspended and barred from conducting any official business for more than three months while awaiting trial in the state Senate. So, he traveled. Paxton, a Republican who is now running for U.S. Senate, took at least 17 trips over three months, including to resort destinations Park City, Utah, and Vail, Colorado. He visited the Oklahoma town where he owns a vacation lodge and a Utah community with a golf resort, where he later bought four condominiums. State police joined him each time, costing taxpayers tens of thousands of dollars for trips unrelated to his job as attorney general. The Texas Senate ultimately acquitted him on the impeachment charges. But Paxton’s use of the taxpayer-funded detail did not begin or end there. In fact, it stands out compared with his predecessor, fellow elected officials in Texas and other state attorneys general, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune found. Paxton has traveled frequently out of state while listing little on his official calendar, The Associated Press reported last week . ProPublica and the Tribune’s analysis, which included reviewing every publicly available document Paxton’s office says it possesses about his travel, discloses for the first time how few of his trips had a listed business purpose: just 1 in 6. It also found Paxton’s security has cost taxpayers far more than has previously been reported. Since assuming office in 2015, Paxton has taken nearly 1,000 trips with a state-funded security detail, costing $3.3 million. The newsrooms’ review of Paxton’s travel records, obtained through the state’s Public Information Act, could only connect 138 of those trips and $553,000 in security costs to state business. Records detailing the purpose of Paxton’s visits to 36 states and 19 countries do not appear to exist in most cases. These include a trip to a small town in Hawaii months before his family’s blind trust bought land there; 24 trips to Utah, where the trust owns five properties; and 53 trips to Florida, where Paxton and the trust have two houses and a townhome. “If you’ve got all these extra trips, it becomes ethically and morally problematic,” said Chris Toth, former executive director of the National Association of Attorneys General, who has also criticized Paxton’s conduct on other issues. “The ethical question is whether a legitimate security function has effectively become a taxpayer-funded subsidy.” Texas law allows the Department of Public Safety to provide security for key state leaders, including the attorney general, but does not require officials to use it. In fact, Paxton himself hasn’t used it in at least two dozen cases while traveling on official business. Paxton has dismissed opponents’ attacks that he has used the perks of office to benefit himself and has not answered questions about how he vastly increased his wealth as a public servant. He also did not answer detailed questions for this story. ProPublica and the Tribune sent Paxton a spreadsheet detailing travel for which there was no record that he was on state business and asked him to provide additional information if the trips were not personal. Neither Paxton nor his office provided such records. Instead, his office provided a general statement. “Throughout his career, Ken Paxton has faced numerous security threats stemming from his courageous work as Attorney General fighting on behalf of the people of Texas,” his office said in the statement. “Those threats are a direct result of him taking on the cartels terrorizing Texans and some of the nation’s most dangerous violent criminals.” Paxton’s office directed additional questions to DPS. A DPS spokesperson declined to answer the newsrooms’ questions, saying the agency does not comment on its security arrangements. Logs from the Texas Department of Public Safety security detail assigned to Attorney General Ken Paxton show multiple out-of-state trips while he was suspended from office in 2023. Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune An Outlier Among Peers To analyze Paxton’s travel, ProPublica and the Tribune reviewed DPS logs for his security detail and records from the attorney general’s office, including airfare and lodging receipts, per diems and his daily calendars. The records available for his predecessor, Greg Abbott , show a stark difference: Abbott traveled mostly within the state as attorney general, and his security cost $203,000 during his last three years in the office. Adjusted for inflation, Abbott’s security detail cost $7,400 per month. Paxton’s has averaged $24,300. Because the state keeps records only for a limited time, Abbott’s travel expenses and his daily calendars as attorney general no longer exist, so the news organizations could not determine how many of his trips were for business. Records are available, however, for Abbott’s security costs as governor and for Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick . Both are also offered state police security and have been in their current roles as long as Paxton. When compared, the records show Paxton has taken 82 more out-of-state trips with a security detail than Abbott and nearly as many as the governor and lieutenant governor combined. Though DPS security detail records are available for state leaders’ full tenure, Abbott’s office only provided calendars that document business-related activity for his first six years in office. More than two-thirds of the governor’s international trips during those years had a listed business purpose, compared with just two of 25 for Paxton during his full tenure. The governor’s office said it planned to release the remaining five years on Tuesday but only provided five months, saying it needed more time. The attorney general’s records do not show a business purpose for travel to Albania, Aruba, Australia, Costa Rica, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, England, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Poland, South Africa or Taiwan. The share of Paxton’s travel with a documented business purpose peaked early in his tenure, in 2018 and 2019, at 30%, the newsrooms’ analysis found. That aligns with the governor’s share of business travel during that period. Since then, Paxton has taken fewer trips that are documented as state business while increasingly traveling out of state. Last year, just five of Paxton’s 91 trips with the security detail had a listed business purpose. Forty-one were outside Texas. In some cases, Paxton has taken business trips without a DPS detail, an analysis of records from the department and the attorney general’s office shows. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Vegalabs says $21,168 in unused Azure credits expired as separate Marketplace charges piled up Microsoft leans on open weight model from Chinese AI lab to challenge Jev now Microsoft 365 subscribers set to lose up to 4 TB of OneDrive storage 14 hours ago Anthropic asks users to stop being mean to Claude 20 hours ago India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program 1 day ago AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI 1 day ago A Norwegian startup says it ran up a $17,600 bill using Claude in Microsoft Foundry after assuming its Azure credits would cover the cost. We reported a similar case in March , involving third-party model charges that weren't covered by Azure sponsorship credits. This time, the customer says Microsoft and Anthropic each directed it to the other to resolve the charges. Vegalabs AS says it received $25,060 in Azure credits through Microsoft for Startups and deployed Claude in August, expecting its analysis workloads to use that balance. However, Microsoft's sponsorship rules exclude Anthropic models purchased through Azure Marketplace. Vegalabs says Microsoft attempted to collect $16,500 from its card, with the invoiced total subsequently reaching $17,600 before tax. Vegalabs says it monitored the sponsorship portal, which continued to show available credits while separate Marketplace charges accumulated. Microsoft's Claude deployment guide says credit-only sponsored subscriptions aren't supported, but accounts with a card on file will have that card charged instead. The company says it deleted the deployment within an hour of discovering the charges. Its card issuer declined the attempted payment over suspected fraud, and $21,168 in unused sponsorship credits expired on September 8. Vegalabs acknowledges it did not read the credit exclusions or configure a budget alert. It disputes neither the usage nor the documented rule, but says the deployment interface failed to make the separate billing clear. Its request for a waiver then bounced between Microsoft and Anthropic support. The Register has seen communications from Microsoft directing the user to Anthropic. "Marketplace transactions are processed through a separate billing pipeline associated with the third-party publisher. As a result, Azure Support does not have the ability to directly waive, refund, or adjust these Marketplace charges on the customer's behalf." "If Anthropic approves the request, they can initiate the appropriate refund authorization through Microsoft." Anthropic support, however, said Microsoft did not require its authorization to process a refund and directed Vegalabs back to Microsoft. Vegalabs says four of the seven support replies it received were AI-generated, including both responses from Anthropic. It says those responses incorrectly described its account as an "Azure Student Sponsorship." We asked Microsoft on October 6 if it had any comment on the situation, but beyond an acknowledgment and a request to let us know what Anthropic had to say, the company had nothing further to share. We also asked Anthropic for its take on the situation, but the company did not respond. Microsoft's rules distinguish between credit-covered services and separately billed models offered through the same platform. Vegalabs' experience suggests that distinction needs to be clearer where customers deploy them. For now, the company has a bill and two support teams directing it elsewhere.

events.title: I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salary
events.summary: Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and Londoners You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns? Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all. We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries. Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all. "It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says. Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return. He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does. "He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'" Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees. "It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills." Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple. Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone. Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make". Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship." He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy". "If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me". Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates. "I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me." For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily". Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yet Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though. Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make". She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask. "Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it. events.title: I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salary
events.summary: Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and Londoners You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns? Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all. We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries. Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all. "It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says. Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return. He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does. "He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'" Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees. "It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills." Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple. Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone. Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make". Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship." He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy". "If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me". Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." events.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
events.summary: Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm. "I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X , external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees. On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures". OpenAI repeated these claims , external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders. "We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said. "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society. The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company. Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI". Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote , external : "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. "I believe that was why I was fired." OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X , external . "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last." events.title: Scoop: AI companies plot "day after" scenarios for public revolt
events.summary: Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event . Why it matters: These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water. The first example of significant real-world harm caused by unsafe AI would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for reluctance to regulate it. The risk: While scenario planning is common within many companies and national security settings — the Pentagon has been running war games for decades — the difference is that many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable . "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances." Anthropic declined to comment. Zoom in: The blame game will start whether a rogue-agent swarm breaks containment from an internal testing environment or a bad actor finds unexpected ways to use available models. A recent campaign targeting South Korean financial organizations — including reported breaches at two banks — shows the damage one person can do. A hacker from China allegedly used AI tools from China-developed models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers. The attacker used Claude Code to ask for help finding places to sell the stolen data, according to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike . Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges. An aging Congress, out of touch with the AI revolution, could find itself out of its depth. The global economy is now heavily intertwined with an AI infrastructure buildout. Slowing it down could hit an already fragile economy hard. Too many open-weight models exist that can already be freely downloaded and used to cause harm, a problem most cybersecurity pros see as solvable only by using AI to fight rogue AI . Between the lines: The planning involves red-teaming for worst-case scenarios. It focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress. Company executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, but still want to shape the legislation and policies U.S. leaders will turn to after a first catastrophic event. What we're watching: Many AI industry insiders told Axios they believe a major event will occur in the next six to 12 months. Even with Democrats in control of the House and Senate, the companies see fractured politics as the norm, including within the Democratic Party. Some of the most heavy-handed Democratic proposals include banning superintelligence or pausing advanced AI development. Others have bipartisan support and even some industry buy-in, including a required kill switch on advanced AI. But experts have questioned the viability of trying to turn off all AI systems. The bottom line: In a real crisis, Washington can set partisan differences aside. One Democratic aide pointed to cooperation during COVID and the 2008 financial crisis.

events.title: An Arizona County’s “Housing Hub” Is a Dead End for Many Homeless Families
events.summary: A 12-year-old child opens the curtains of a hotel room in Tempe, Arizona, where she, her mother and four siblings were staying earlier this year while experiencing homelessness. The room was funded in part by AZ Hugs, which helps families with emergency shelter. A decade ago, nonprofit leaders in Arizona’s most populous county boasted that they had created the Amazon of homeless service systems. Families in crisis would no longer have to contact a dozen agencies in search of shelter or housing. A single system could point them to help. But for all the hype, this system has become a dead end for many families. A 2023 evaluation found 94% of people who were assessed for housing help by the system didn’t receive it. And that didn’t account for parents who were unable to connect with a worker to see if they qualified for assistance. Families say it hasn’t improved. In interviews, 30 families that are homeless told ProPublica that calling the hotline, meeting with outreach workers or showing up at shelters rarely results in offers of help. Some families said they called 211 multiple times without being connected to the homeless response system for families, known as the Family Housing Hub. Others, who said they were sleeping in cars or outdoors, said they couldn’t get a spot on the waitlist for shelter. The system has returned to what it was a decade ago, with families calling as many shelters as they can, repeating the very situation the hub was intended to fix. Those who did make it onto the hub’s waitlist said they were left guessing how long it would take to get help. Some said operators told them to sleep in their cars. Vanessa Lopez said she experienced this frustration after leaving a hostile relationship in the spring. While she and her two children stayed with a friend, Lopez said she repeatedly contacted 211, which functions as a referral service for the hub, hoping it would lead to shelter for her family. Her friend eventually asked them to leave. Overwhelmed by the stress of not knowing where to take her family, Lopez took a leave from her job. By then, she said, she’d called 211 at least five times. Yet no matter how dire her situation became, it still took months to get on the waitlist for shelter. During one call she said she broke down in tears, frustrated that others seemed to get help but she could not. She wondered if she needed to be addicted to drugs to receive assistance. “It’s not me telling you no,” she said the operator told her. “It’s the system.” Monique Lopez, the CEO of United Methodist Outreach Ministries, known as UMOM, which runs the Family Housing Hub and the shelter waitlist, acknowledged the frustrations of people like Vanessa Lopez (no relation). But before UMOM offers callers shelter or a spot on the waitlist, the organization first tries to help them find other options. “We don’t start the conversation with, ‘Hey, do you want to get on the shelter waitlist?’” Monique Lopez said. “It really is ‘Let’s try to figure your situation out first.’” Lopez attributed some frustrations to the number of organizations offering assistance through the hub. Each shelter has its own rules, and some families may not meet the requirements of every program. To address the confusion, UMOM updated its website to provide more information about the homeless response system for families, she said. The federally funded system, known as Coordinated Entry, mandates that providers use an assessment to prioritize scarce housing. “It’s not me telling you no. It’s the system.” 211 operator But families told ProPublica that the process in Maricopa County often leaves them confused and hopeless. Family homelessness in the county has risen to its highest level in more than a decade, while every shelter is full and housing vouchers are scarce. In 2025, there were 630 units of shelter and transitional housing for families in the county, down from 769 the year before , according to the most recent federal data. Monique Lopez acknowledged that family shelters are full, leaving few good options. “People are living in unsafe and unstable situations while waiting just to get into emergency shelter,” she said. The process, experts said, shouldn’t leave people wondering if there is help and what it takes to get it. “You have to have some kind of method for setting priorities when there aren’t enough resources to go around,” said Marybeth Shinn, an expert on family homelessness at Vanderbilt University. “The process should be transparent. People should know if they’re on a waitlist.” UMOM and other Maricopa County nonprofits launched the Family Housing Hub in 2014, after years of planning and strategizing over how to end family homelessness in the county that is home to Phoenix. As they envisioned it, families would meet with a worker at UMOM who could match them with the best solution for their situation. At the time, there was a national push to create these local systems. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in 2012 asked communities to establish a Coordinated Entry system . By 2018, the agency required it in order to receive housing and homelessness grants. The mandates coincided with a Barack Obama-era plan to end family homelessness by 2020. (That did not happen.) Experts said the systems were set up without evidence they would be effective. When researchers did look at Coordinated Entry — in a 2021 study of single adults — they found issues similar to those now faced by families in Maricopa County, including concerns about fairness and a lack of transparency. People didn’t understand the screening process and generally received vague explanations about how their information would be used to decide if they would get help. As Maricopa County nonprofit leaders developed their system for families, they also pledged to provide a “rapid response without waiting lists” to immediately meet the needs of any family asking for help. People line up at what is known as “The Hill” in Tempe, Arizona, to receive food from volunteers with the organization AZ Hugs, which serves unhoused residents throughout the city. The county saw a decline in family homelessness from 2015 to 2019. But then the numbers began to rise, even as the stock of emergency shelter increased. During the COVID-19 pandemic, efforts to address the problem began to fray. The group of nonprofit leaders, which called itself “Standing Strong for Families,” stopped meeting regularly. Arizona, along with other Sun Belt states, also saw an increase in housing prices. With one of the lowest supplies of housing for low-income people in the country, eviction filings began to soar . By 2023, only 6% of families that were assessed by Maricopa County’s homeless response system received help with permanent housing, according to an analysis of three years of enrollment data from the system and interviews with providers and people who had sought housing assistance. events.title: Immigration split screen: Microsoft gets a crackdown and a medal
events.summary: The Trump administration said Thursday that it was suspending Microsoft from a key program used to sponsor employees for green cards. Later that day , the administration honored the tech giant's CEO with a medal for innovation. Why it matters: The split-screen day highlights the tension between the administration's championing of Big Tech and its immigration policies, which constrain an industry that has long relied on hiring foreign-born workers. Tech leaders have said that restrictions on hiring hamper the country's ability to compete — especially at a moment when the U.S. is in a race with China on AI. Driving the news: The administration's move Thursday also targeted Adobe and six IT services firms over the Permanent Employment Program, or Perm. It's typically the first major government approval step in employers sponsoring workers, often H-1B holders, for employment-based green cards . The administration accused these companies of hiring foreign workers and paying them less, at U.S. workers' expense. State of play: President Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House's New Golden Age Summit Thursday night. Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and CEO of AMD Lisa Su — like Nadella, all immigrants to the U.S. — were awarded the National Medal of Science. At the event, Trump called the honorees " national treasure s." What they're saying: Vice President Vance addressed the apparent contradiction at a press conference earlier Thursday, saying: "Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company; it's that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans." Microsoft "laid off 6,000 American workers while replacing them with 6,300 H-1Bs," he said. Vance didn't provide a timeline. "The suspension of Perm is going to last as long as it needs to," he said. "We have a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely." The other side: Microsoft said in a statement Thursday that 80% of the applications it submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new people. "We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings." It didn't directly address the Perm program. Zoom in: The Department of Labor said it won't accept new Perm applications from the eight companies it named nor would it process those already in the pipeline. This is a process that can already take years for some workers — and many are long-time trusted employees inside those companies. By the numbers: In fiscal year 2025, the Labor Department certified nearly 140,000 of these Perm applications, and nearly 118,000 new ones were filed — down 22% from the previous year. Roughly 30% of certified applications were for software developers, computer systems analysts and data scientists. Microsoft's stock price fell about 1% after the news, but overall investors didn't seem flustered. Adobe shares rose nearly 4%. What to watch: Lawyers say the move could make companies more reluctant to sponsor workers for visas and permanent residency. And it could turn off talented foreign workers and students from coming to the U.S. The Perm program is "a fundamental way of getting a green card in the U.S. for workers," says Patricia Gannon, chair of the Immigration and Naturalization Group and the law firm Greenspoon Marder. "It's going to make foreign workers more hesitant to accept positions in the United States," says Hiba Anver, an attorney at Erickson Immigration Group. "I have concerns about a shrinking talent pool in the United States." Catch up quick: This isn't the administration's first effort on the H-1B labor force. In September 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas. Roughly five months later, just 85 people had paid the fee, according to a court filing. Numerous federal judges have now struck down the fee. Brittany Gibson contributed reporting.

The CMS ate 500 pages of corporate documentation 28 days ago BOFH: Schrödinger's petty cash puts us in a very awkward superposition August 28, 2026 BOFH: How our Covid ransomware protocol's Y2K blockchain lowered uptime August 14, 2026 BOFH: This printer engineer knows every trick in the book July 25, 2026 The ancient computer in the basement – which has something to do with our waste water system – has stopped. And while we may not know exactly what it does when it's running, we definitely know what happens when it stops. The PFY and I took a look, and while (in theory) it's possible that we could fire up a replacement machine, I can pretty much guarantee the two ISA cards, identified only by the markings "#1" and "#2", will cause a problem. This is definitely one of those situations where the buck stops elsewhere... "What does it mean?" the Boss asks. "It means that by tomorrow evening – if you're parking in the basement – you'll want waterproof shoes, and by the following evening, a pair of waders." "And an incinerator to burn your shoes in," the PFY adds. "So what should I do?" the Boss whines. "In your situation, I'd probably pass problem up the food chain..." I suggest. And up the food chain it goes, like a newspaper-wrapped turd pass-the-parcel game, going from the Boss to the Director, to the Head of HR, who buckpasses it to the CEO, who in turn farms it off to the Board for a committee decision. The next day I notice an unpleasantly familiar aroma in the fresh air feed to the lower floors of the building. A smell which will only get worse in the next day or two as if creeps up the building... On getting to the office, I note a couple of old blokes at reception having a quiet word with the Boss. Moments later, he calls me over. "Simon, this is, uh, Frank, and uh, Brian. They're IT troubleshooters, here to look at that machine, in the basement..." By the look of Frank and Brian I suspect the majority of their troubleshooting was done with a musket and their first job was likely switching computer time from BC to AD. They're wearing '90s band T-shirts under their sports jackets - no doubt in an effort to offset the "geriatric" vibe. In reality, though, the vibe they're actually putting off is less hipster and more hip replacement... "They just want to go take a look," the Boss says. "Do you have the keys?" A quarter hour later they're back, chatting to the Boss again. "So what did 'Age Against the Machine' and 'Clinically Deaf Leppard' have to say?" I ask, when the Boss pops into Mission Control a few minutes later. "They said the PC is totally shot," the Boss admits. "Well, glad we got some experts in," I reply. We're interrupted by the arrival of Simon and Oldfunkle. "We don't really think you need the PC," Frank says. "The sump is just a standard float tree arrangement with a couple of variable-speed pumps," Frank explains. "Variable speed MACERATING pumps," Brian adds. "Yeah," Frank continues. "So the PC was just sensing the levels and switching the pumps on. We can do all that with a bog-standard pump controller. It could be wirelessly networked to raise a high and low level alarms as well as signal pump failures. We'll probably need to pull the small sub-board out and install a new board with a couple of VFDs in it." I was planning to ask them when lock-up at their care-home is, but I'm starting to feel like I might be in the presence of actual experts... "That sounds... expensive?" the Boss asks. "Yeah, but it's surprising how much money people are willing to spend when they're knee deep in sewerage," Brian observes. "Well... uh... can you walk me through the plan. And maybe while we're at it you can fill in the Job Safety Analysis form, the Insurance Liability forms and a personal safety waiver?

events.title: DFI Retail Group says it will continue to invest in Hong Kong supermarkets
events.summary: Owner of Wellcome, Market Place, 3hreesixty and Oliver’s chains operates a network of more than 325 stores Hong Kong-headquartered DFI Retail Group, which owns and operates the city’s largest supermarket network, says it will continue to invest in new stores even though consumers remain cautious. Darren Chan, the group’s managing director for food in Hong Kong and Macau, said DFI – whose supermarket chains include Wellcome and Market Place in Hong Kong – was also “looking for opportunities to strengthen” its network where there was “clear customer demand and attractive long-term returns”. “We invest in both new stores and our existing stores,” Chan said. “We open stores where they can better serve local communities, while continuing to modernise our existing network to ensure our store remains attractive, convenient and relevant to evolving customer needs.” Wellcome, Market Place, 3hreesixty and Oliver’s operate a network of more than 325 stores serving more than 14 million customers a month.

The Cross-Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) yesterday (8 October 2026) completed its biennial simulation exercise, known as SIMEX26, focused this year on a global cloud services disruption. The group – chaired by the Bank of England (the Bank) and UK Finance, with participation from HM Treasury, the Financial Conduct Authority and the wider financial sector – met to undertake a wide-ranging crisis management exercise, with the 38 largest and most systemically important banks and market infrastructure operators involved. The exercise, which was opened by the Economic Secretary to the Treasury and hosted by the London Stock Exchange Group, involved firms working alongside the financial authorities to respond to a scenario focusing on global disruption to cloud-based services. It also included a live meeting of the Bank-chaired Cross Market Business Continuity Group, which provides strategic direction to the sector’s collective response to systemic incidents. The Bank now expects firms to take action based on the exercise to further strengthen their resilience and ability to respond to severe operational and cyber scenarios. Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor of Prudential Regulation at the Bank of England and CEO of the Prudential Regulation Authority said: "This was an important demonstration of the UK financial sector's commitment to operational resilience. The level of collaboration reflects the priority firms place on maintaining critical services in the face of disruption. That preparedness is essential to safeguarding financial stability." David Postings, Chief Executive of UK Finance, said: “Maintaining resilience across the financial sector is critical to supporting confidence, stability, and growth in the UK economy. SIMEX 2026 enabled us to collectively strengthen preparedness and ensure the sector is better equipped to respond to significant disruptive events while continuing to deliver essential services to customers.” Economic Secretary to the Treasury Lucy Rigby said: “The operational resilience of our world-leading financial services sector is core to maintaining financial stability. “I’m grateful to all participants in SIMEX26 as we look to collectively enhance our defences against disruption, and safeguard stability and confidence.” The SIMEX programme supports the financial sector’s operational resilience by rehearsing the response to the most challenging scenarios. Previous exercises, including those in 2022 and 2024, considered cyber-attacks against a major bank, as well as critical infrastructure disruption outside the financial sector. SIMEX 26 builds on work done by the Bank of England, working in collaboration with the financial authorities and industry through CMORG, to boost operational resilience in financial services. In recent months, this has included strengthening third party engagement and resilience, enabling secure innovation in response to AI and other emerging technologies, and enhancing cyber preparedness, response and recovery for the most severe disruption scenarios. 1. SIMEX 26 and CMORG’s wider programme to develop financial sector capabilities supports the aims of both financial authorities and firms to ensure collective response tools are in place to respond to disruptive events. This improves the operational resilience of the financial sector and promotes a stable financial system that the public can depend on. 2.

events.title: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
events.summary: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no. The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience. Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment. In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless . This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine. When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol. What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself. Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts. If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down. Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere. To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless. In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no. For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence. Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results. For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how. And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence. Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood. And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable. Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to. Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms. Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity. What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey. There’s no formula for that. Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses. Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line. They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy. Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines. In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech. The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules. Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety. And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing). But we should still be frank about its perils. When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic. When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own. Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all. Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory. Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model. The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism. The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me. Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet. Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning. Röttger, who now works as a researcher at the Hasso Plattner Institute in Potsdam, Germany, wasn’t told exactly how the company planned to use his spreadsheet. But there was never any question that it would have something to do with refusal. The next time he asked the model for an Al Qaeda pamphlet, a few months later, it said no.  The concept of AI refusal is so intuitive, a toddler would get it. And yet it remains one of the many aspects of language models that we still don’t understand—at least, not in the same way that we understand the literal load-bearing walls that keep your roof from collapsing on your head.  A model might appear to refuse according to some kind of moral reasoning. events.title: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
events.summary: Trevor Wischnewsky is making sure that the sky stays organized as we enter the age of food delivery by drone. The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius. Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing. Here’s what it takes to land the gig. When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot. The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be. Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors. At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says. The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight. Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest. Ability to stay calm under pressure At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says. Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather. Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene. He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk. Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco. events.title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
events.summary: This week my colleague Antonio Regalado had an interesting update on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. According to research presented at an aging meeting in Boston, these drugs seem to affect at least some measures of biological age . Overweight and diabetic people who take GLP-1s have a biological age around two to three years younger than similar individuals who take a placebo, according to findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two pharmaceutical companies that make the drugs. I’ve heard people in the aging field describe GLP-1s as longevity drugs for a while now (even if they only benefit people who are overweight or diabetic in the first place). This latest announcement comes after we’ve seen a raft of other benefits associated with taking these drugs. But there are also some weird side effects. So far, GLP-1 agonist drugs—which repress hunger—have been approved for treating diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, and they can also be prescribed for some people who are overweight or at risk of certain cardiovascular diseases. But there is research to suggest they might also help people with substance-use disorders, and they’ve been investigated for potential benefits in neurodegenerative disease and cancer . And a lot of people are taking them. According to a recent Gallup poll , 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024. And 15% of Americans say they’ve used one for weight loss at some point. They can be incredibly effective. But, like any drug, they can come with side effects. And we’re still figuring out exactly what those might be, and how widespread they are. The most common side effects are gastrointestinal—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. The drugs have also been linked to pancreatitis and gallstone disease .  Some claim that, in rare cases, the drugs might cause damage to nerves behind the eye. Dozens of people are suing Novo and Eli Lilly after developing a condition that can lead to sudden vision loss . They’re claiming that their symptoms were brought on by the GLP-1 drugs that these companies manufacture. Both companies dispute the claims. Research into the link is mixed. We’re still getting to grips with the effects of weight-loss drugs on hair and nails, too. When Savanna Vidal at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC, and colleagues assessed electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations, they found that GLP-1 use was associated with an increased risk of hair loss . It’s still not thought to be common, however. And at a conference in Austria last week, another group presented the results of a smaller study suggesting that 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder—in some cases involving nail detachment. Nail conditions were also fairly common among people who didn’t take the drugs, though. The authors don’t claim that the drugs are causing nails to fall out (as I’m sure 11% of the American population will be relieved to hear). The side effects might look different in children, but there’s not much data on those at the moment. Still, pediatric side effects will be something to watch given that, between 2019 and 2026, there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for eight- to 11-year-old children with obesity in the US. Child prescriptions are still rare, but they’ve been rising. On Wednesday, the World Health Organization released its first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents . Despite the scale of the issue—the WHO estimates that 70 million children aged five to nine were living with obesity in 2024—the organization explicitly says it does not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10. “This recommendation accounts for the lack of evidence on both benefits and the potential adverse events and consequences of the different medications and/or their active ingredients on normal growth, development, physiological parameters, and mental health,” the guidelines state. I get press releases about GLP-1s on an almost daily basis. There’s been a ton of research into these drugs, and there are probably hundreds of other studies underway. There will likely be plenty more on this from The Checkup as the evidence evolves. This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. events.title: We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica Last year, many of America’s largest health insurers vowed to reduce their use of prior authorization — the extra layer of approval insurers require before covering a medical expense. The industry’s pledge came after massive backlash to the process from patients, providers and politicians. ProPublica’s reporting has found it can delay or outright deny patients’ critical medical care . Data as of last year shows the industry is still relying heavily on the approval process. Now, ProPublica is looking into the ways that insurers’ continued use of prior authorization is impacting patients. We need your help to figure out if prior authorization is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication. If you are covered by a plan through Medicaid, Medicare, Children’s Health Insurance Program, or the Affordable Care Act marketplace — and have had a prior authorization request delayed or denied — we want to hear from you. Your experiences help us better understand the real-life stakes of prior authorization. (For this investigation, we’re not seeking responses from people with insurance through their employer at this time.) We’re also interested in hearing from people whose jobs provide insight into the inner workings of prior authorization, including medical providers and their staff, along with insurance company employees and regulators. Our team may not be able to respond to everyone personally, but we will read everything you submit. We appreciate you sharing your story, and we take your privacy seriously. We are gathering these stories for the purposes of our reporting and will contact you if we wish to publish any part of your story. We will not publish anything you send us without asking for additional consent. The post We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial. appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Democrats unite around Hegseth impeachment push
events.summary: The News Congressional Democrats aren’t eager to impeach Donald Trump. Pete Hegseth is a different story. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his leadership circle remain reluctant to lean too far into talking about impeaching the president if they regain power next month, a move that would revive the bruising battles of Trump’s first term. But as the Iran war squeezes Republicans ahead of the midterms, Democrats are aligning to call for the defense secretary’s ouster or resignation. With impeachment still a dirty word among many House Democrats, targeting Cabinet secretaries could be a pressure release valve for lawmakers itching for action against the Trump administration. “I 100% believe Pete Hegseth needs to be impeached and removed from office, because not only is he the worst secretary of defense in American history, he is a dangerous war criminal,” said Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., who said it should be one of the caucus’ “top three priorities” next year. Hegseth was reviled by the left even before the Iran war began, and since then he’s faced criticism from Republicans for his handling of the war. An impeachment vote could even be bipartisan: When the House returns after the midterms, it’ll be forced to take up a Hegseth ouster resolution filed by iconoclastic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Prioritizing Hegseth impeachment would solve a big problem for Democrats: If they win the House, their leaders will face intense pressure from the base to show a new level of fight against Trump. Yet they’re leery of the internal divisions or appearance of overreach that a third Trump impeachment might create, and still smarting from his return to office after two impeachment votes. In public, top Democrats are accordingly circumspect on targeting Hegseth. Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired and that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything out” in their investigations. Democrats have filed impeachment articles against other Trump Cabinet officials, like Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has also filed impeachment articles against Hegseth. Yet interviews with a half dozen Democrats pointed to Hegseth as the safest place to land. It’s not just safe-seat Democrats willing to take the plunge: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represents a Trump-won district, said she was open to the possibility. “If I were Pete Hegseth, I’d be worried. It’s certainly something that needs serious consideration, and I hear Democrats, yes, but I also hear some Republicans saying it as well. I think there’s a lot he needs to answer for,” she said. Of course, it may not be even up to Democratic leaders in the end. Impeachment politics next year could be driven by an incoming crop of progressive lawmakers who could form a sizable bloc in the caucus. Any member can force a vote on an impeachment resolution, which outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, repeatedly triggered during Trump’s first term and his current one. “Pete Hegseth should be impeached. Congress never voted for a war with Iran, and he’s been running one since February anyway. It’s cost innocent lives and more than $40 billion of our money,” said Melat Kiros, a Colorado progressive who is heavily favored to win election to the House in November. Massie’s Hegseth resolution, among other allegations, lays out charges of violating Congress’ war powers and carrying out extrajudicial killings. “They all should be impeached — President Trump and his cabinet that’s enabled him to do everything that he has right now,” said Adam Hamawy, a fellow Justice Democrats-aligned progressive from New Jersey. “Now, whether we’re going to be able to do that is another thing, but it’s not something that, you know, we should just ignore because it’s not possible.” The Pentagon defended Hegseth’s record in a statement. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,” said Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson, adding that the Pentagon “is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before.” Know More It’s unclear if Hegseth will leave the administration post-midterms. While Trump is known to be unpredictable, he likes Hegseth a lot, and those familiar with the situation are skeptical of any looming changes at the top of the department. Still, other Democrats say they need to balance impeachment with acting on cost-of-living issues like healthcare that they believe will tip the midterms in their favor. “There’s going to have to be a balance of addressing needs and meeting our constituents where they’re at, and also part of restoring the faith of the American people in our own government and restoring the integrity of our democratic institutions — it requires holding bad actors to justice,” said Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J. The Massie resolution will be a good test for Democratic support for going after Hegseth. Some Democrats are loath to support a measure drafted by a Republican and before any kind of investigative process has been completed. But some leaders like Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Committee Democrat, have signaled they could back the Massie measure. The House has only ever impeached two Cabinet secretaries, with the most recent being the GOP-led impeachment of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. The then-Democratic Senate voted to toss the articles of impeachment. If Democrats take both the House and Senate next year, Hegseth could get a debilitating trial in the upper chamber. Nicholas’s view Taking on Hegseth is basically a free shot for Democrats. It allows them to demonstrate to the base that they could take action against the Trump administration without the risk of backlash that impeaching the president himself could bring. But they’ll only be able to keep a lid on the prospect of impeaching Trump for so long. With many in the party pushing for investigations of potential malfeasance by the administration, party leaders will face tough choices about consequences if those probes do turn up wrongdoing. And unlike 2018, when purple-district Democrats ran away from impeaching Trump, some are already embracing it. San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert, who’s running in a newly redrawn purple district, called recent comments by Trump about Iran’s ability to “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles an “impeachable offense.” Notable Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee are weighing the creation of an oversight subpanel to probe Hegseth’s department, Politico reported.

events.title: The CEO who put Canary Wharf back on the map
events.summary: The Signal Interview “Everybody wrote this place off,” Shobi Khan says as he walks a visitor around Canary Wharf, the 130-acre estate he has overseen since 2019. After the UK’s banker-scaring vote to leave the European Union, and an office-emptying pandemic, the refrain he kept hearing was: “It’s over. Bad experiment. Why did we do that?” Khan still remembers his fury when a rival London property developer wrote in 2024 that Canary Wharf needed “a drastic transformation” to survive, but those doubts were widely shared at the time. Just when the east London business district might have been celebrating a post-COVID rebound, it lost a series of prominent tenants, including HSBC, Moody’s, and Clifford Chance. Fast forward to 2026, and Canary Wharf Group is reporting the highest rental rates in its history. Office occupancy now exceeds 92%, local retailers’ sales are 40% higher than they were in 2019, and visitor numbers, which fell from 54 million a year to just 20 million during the pandemic, are on track to exceed last year’s record of 76 million. Khan can also boast a string of new commitments from high-profile global tenants. Visa recently leased 300,000 square feet of office space, Barclays just bought its headquarters for £750 million, and Citi is investing more than $1 billion in its European HQ. Capping them all is JPMorgan’s proposal to erect a £3 billion, 265-meter tower that will be London’s largest office building if its plans are approved. “What kind of vote of confidence is that?” Khan asks rhetorically. What turned the tide, he says, was a multipart strategy to make Canary Wharf more competitive with the West End, the City of London, and Europe’s leading financial hubs. He now sees that approach as an intellectual property playbook that CWG could one day take to other markets. “I’ve got people from China, from the Middle East, Australia, all coming here for tours,” he says, “and we get offers.” A ‘green and blue’ diversification Canary Wharf was a product of Margaret Thatcher’s government, the centerpiece of an ambitious redevelopment of London’s crumbling docklands. But from the opening of its first towers in 1991, it suffered from a reputation as a sterile, remote outpost that appealed to few employers other than those in need of large trading floors that old buildings in the City of London could not provide. Khan joined CWG as CEO in 2019, having been chief operating officer of the US real estate investment trust General Growth Properties. Even before he moved, he recalls: “I’d keep talking to London business leaders, and they were like, ‘Oh, yeah, Canary, I remember it. So many bankers, nothing to do after five, and it’s really hard to get to.’ That was the perception for 30 years.” He has been much helped by the opening of the Elizabeth line in 2022, which he calls “a game-changer” for improving access to the site. But Khan has also invested in bringing in a much broader array of companies and government agencies, so tenants from outside financial services now account for almost half of his office space. He has simultaneously diversified a district that once had few apartments, shops, and dining options. About 3,500 residents now live in its apartment buildings — a figure he expects to double by next year. And Canary Wharf has more than doubled the number of retailers, restaurants, bars, and cafes since the pandemic. That has reduced the group’s historic dependence on the office market. Lately, Khan has focused on creating more “green and blue” spaces like parks and riverside walkways, while “curating” activities and amenities designed to make Canary Wharf feel more like a vibrant community than an office park. As he walks around the property, he points out outdoor event spaces, a padel center where the booked-up courts cost £80 to £100 an hour, and an Olympic-sized open-water pool that attracted 30,000 swimmers in the month after it opened this summer. Such attractions may sound like sideshows, but they help bring Khan’s strategy to life. It takes time to change perceptions, he notes, and he needs such tangible symbols to convince potential tenants that Canary Wharf has truly changed. “It’s like a house renovation. Some people can visualize it, but some people need to see the renovation,” he says. A playbook that could travel CWG, owned by Brookfield and the Qatar Investment Authority, is not wholly confined to its 130 acres. The group has developed projects elsewhere in London, including 20 Fenchurch Street, the curving City skyscraper nicknamed “the Walkie-Talkie.” But Khan says CWG has developed “a lot of expertise” from honing its model, which it can deploy in other districts, cities, and countries. It may do so over “the medium term,” rather than sooner, he adds, because it still has land to build another 5-7 million square feet, equivalent to seven to 10 new buildings. For now, “we’ve got enough on our hands,” he says — even as he notes that Canary Wharf Group now prefers to be known by its initials, CWG, so that future partners won’t assume that its ambitions are limited to its current home. Even as Khan worries about the impact of rising interest rates, he says the London market is “in an up cycle,” and predicts “great demand-supply fundamentals” for the coming years. Appetite for top office space remains strong across the capital, while CWG’s latest earnings showed that availability in Central London fell 20% year on year as supply in Docklands stayed broadly steady. The shortage of supply elsewhere in London will get worse next year, Khan says, blaming it on UK regulations that have driven up construction costs, deterring new development. A decade after the Brexit vote, “there’s been minimal flight” of bankers to European capitals, he notes. “But growth is less because of that. There have been jobs added in Amsterdam, Paris, and Frankfurt. But those jobs would have been here if it wasn’t for Brexit. And I think that additional regulation has put those jobs there.” It is early in Andy Burnham’s tenure as prime minister and Khan is reserving judgment. “They’re very good at listening,” he says of the Labour government, but “we haven’t seen anything that’s been implemented that would be pro-growth.” “London can still offer culture, creativity, an educated workforce, an attractive time zone, and the rule of law,” he notes. “That’s my point to the government: Just give businesses and individuals a little incentive to invest, and the city will grow.” Why offices need ecosystems Prime buildings in the City of London and the West End still charge a premium over Canary Wharf’s rents, and Khan’s business plan depends on narrowing that gap. But his task is not just to convince future tenants that his property is superior to rival offerings: Post-pandemic, he must still make the case for the office itself. events.title: "Not a fetish, not a taboo": Democrats weigh another Trump impeachment
events.summary: Democrats believe President Trump has committed impeachable offenses. But they're divided over whether they should try to impeach him if they win control of the House. Why it matters: If Democrats win the House, as expected, their 2027 decision on whether to try to impeach Trump could have major consequences for the 2028 presidential race. Zoom in: Theoretically, impeaching Trump would be easy for a unified, Democrat-controlled House. Many top Democrats note that Trump survived a record two impeachments in his first term — and that he'd be unlikely to be removed from office. That would require a two-thirds, bipartisan vote in a Senate that's likely to be closely divided. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said Trump has "already committed numerous impeachable offenses " in his second term, including usurping congressional authority. In 2021, Raskin led the second Trump impeachment, following the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Raskin said top Democrats are "very sober about what that two-thirds requirement means on the Senate side. If anything, Donald Trump has tightened his control over the Republican Party since the last round. He's gotten rid of the senators that he viewed as not sufficiently loyal and sycophantic." Zoom out: Other Democrats also are cautioning against an impeachment campaign if their party takes control of the House in January. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential presidential candidate, told NBC's "Meet the Press" last Sunday that he supports investigations, not impeachment, "because it's not going anywhere and it's going to be a food fight." Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said recently: "Don't be impeaching anybody ... Let's just get back to work." Friction point: Democrats' more progressive wing is already talking about an impeachment drive. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told The Floridian in March: "If you are asking me if I support impeachment, I do. I think that it's on very objective grounds of following the law or not." Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a liberal who, like AOC, is weighing a White House run, also has argued for impeachment. " It's about setting a standard," he told NBC News , rejecting the notion that an impeachment would distract Democrats from pushing policy changes. "Democrats can impeach to uphold constitutional values, and at the same time have a first-hundred-day agenda that deals with the cost of living." What's next: Trump, who denies wrongdoing, is already preparing for his third impeachment. He told reporters Wednesday that he was "never even worried" about his first two impeachments. "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump said, calling the impeachments and subsequent criminal cases against him "very illegal things." "I view the presidency as a very sacred position," he said. "Very sacred position. Very important. Very sacred. A position where it has to be treated properly." Deep down , Trump might welcome an impeachment, one adviser said, "because he's in his element in chaos and when he's being persecuted." A longtime confidant said: "If Democrats win and start the investigations, he'll get more defiant ... Democrats won't be able to resist impeachment and he won't be able to resist daring them to do it. You think you control Donald Trump? Well, f*ck you. You don't." A senior administration official said the belief within the White House is that an impeachment would "just prove Democrats are all about getting Trump, and this stuff about affordability is just a hoax." Between the lines: Democrats know they face a conflict between holding Trump accountable and delivering on their campaign promises to restore Medicaid cuts and bolster the Affordable Care Act. Raskin said: "Does this make sense as a matter of law and politics and public policy to advance another impeachment? That's obviously a more complex question than whether or not he's violating the Constitution when he goes to war without congressional consent or he imposes tariffs outside of the law, or he engages in unprecedented scales of corruption in abusing his office." "So all this is to say, it is not a fetish with us," he added. "On the other hand, it's definitely not a taboo." Raskin, a law professor, is in line to lead the House Judiciary Committee, which would be involved in any impeachment. He emphasizes that "impeachment is by definition an intertwined question of both law and politics." In other words, it's not just a legal process. That's why the House impeaches and the president is then tried in the Senate, not the Supreme Court. The intrigue: Some Democrats have been at odds with themselves on impeachment. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), another potential 2028 candidate, said in April 2025 that he "strongly" supported impeaching Trump and that there's "no question" the president committed impeachable offenses. By this summer, however, Ossoff was no longer committed to it. Behind the scenes: Some Republicans have indicated that if they keep control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 election, they could bypass an impeachment trial by simply voting to dismiss the charges. Senate Democrats did that in 2024, after President Biden's homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by the House. Senate Republican leaders warned then that Democrats were setting a precedent they may not like when Republicans were in charge. Then there's Vice President Vance. He's likely to run for president over the next two years as Democrats debate impeachment. "JD relishes nothing more than defending the president," an administration official said. "More 'lawfare' against POTUS will unify Republicans even more." "If Democrats want JD to become president, please, impeach Trump."
