events.title: Saudi Arabia faces its toughest moment of war
events.summary: Matthew’s view Riyadh was once the Gulf’s escape route from the Iran war. No longer. Several Western governments are advising against travel to Saudi Arabia. The US requires officials to obtain special approval to use the capital’s airport. I’m hearing of some executives leaving for Doha and the UAE. Here in Riyadh, we now hear booms and see fires that have largely been absent since the Iran conflict began on Feb. 28. This is a jarring reversal: Saudi Arabia has suffered fewer attacks than its Gulf neighbours, its airspace has mostly stayed open, and the kingdom has projected a business-as-usual attitude. That message is getting harder to sustain after Iran-backed Houthi fighters escalated attacks in response to the Saudi-led campaign against them in Yemen. One person was killed in a strike on Riyadh airport, a Saudia Airlines plane was reportedly left in flames , and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Some offices, schools, and the Expo 2030 construction site near the airport were evacuated on Thursday. Foreign governments suggested their citizens remain vigilant, but what can individuals do when threats come suddenly from the sky? Over the next few weeks, Saudi Arabia is hosting the World Petroleum Congress and the Future Investment Initiative, drawing CEOs from the world’s biggest energy and financial companies. While no postponements or cancellations have been announced, security teams are undoubtedly assessing what level of risk is tolerable for the titans of the global economy. Staying away could offend the kingdom, and firms that don’t stand with Saudi Arabia now risk missing out when the economy bounces back. Older residents here repeat a mantra that the country has been through worse, notably when Iraq launched Scud missiles in 1991 during the first Gulf War. But most of those strikes were on military structures. Riyadh was different then, too. It had no ambitions to be a hub for finance, trade, and tourism. Today, it needs stability. It’s harder to sell investors on its vision when the capital is under fire. Notable Explosions “rattled” Riyadh on Thursday, with this week’s Houthi attacks being the deadliest since the war in Yemen was reignited last month, The New York Times reported .

events.title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
events.summary: Everton are currently seventh in the Premier League after seven matches Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control. The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m. In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton 's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter". "The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said. "When TFG became custodians of Everton , the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters. "With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton ." TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window. In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025. Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear. Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong. Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after. The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry. TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward". "Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued. Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out? Published 16 hours ago 'An unspectacular tenure' - analysis The decision of Everton 's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times. A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton 's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players. The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG. It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League. Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners. TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis. Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers. This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure. 'It's come as a shock' - Brown-Finnis Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock". "It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis. "We [ Everton ] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view. "If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence. "I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era." events.title: Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter
events.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock? There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years. With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts. Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression. Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%. Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers. The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026. Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn. "The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW. Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031. Finland: Europe's race for critical raw materials National Coalition rules out tax hikes To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts. While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt. Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts." While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%. With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy. "More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW. Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion. Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion. During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target. A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

events.title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
events.summary: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic , the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not. Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected , citing safety concerns over AI. Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race . Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn. Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn . On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI. SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported. Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

events.title: China and EU trade envoys seek ways to ease tensions over growing imbalances
events.summary: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union are wrapping up two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies BEIJING -- The top trade envoys for China and the European Union were wrapping up two days of talks Friday aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic traveled to Beijing saying it was crucial that the negotiations deliver “tangible outcomes” in rebalancing trade between China and the 27-nation bloc. It was unclear, however, if the two sides would find the will to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($410 billion) last year. China is pushing for the EU to stop blocking its imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington's behest. Sefcovic said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Hurricane Isaias latest: Storm strengthens to Category 2 Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China's global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU's trade deficit with China widened to 103.34 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the April-July quarter, as imports rose to 153.63 billion euros ($172.3 billion) ,while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56.4 billion), according to EU statistics. events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: Vendor roadmaps set the pace of change in most enterprise software estates. Origina argues the business should. Most enterprise software estates run to somebody else’s calendar. End-of-support dates, license model changes and needless upgrades arrive on the vendor’s schedule, and the IT team absorbs them: the migration nobody budgeted for, the re-platforming that displaces a project the business actually asked for, the patch cadence that is really a product roadmap in disguise. Origina, an independent provider of software maintenance and support, puts figures on the pressure. As a rule of thumb, up to 90 percent of IT budgets go on “keeping the lights on”, leaving only 10 percent for anything new. Enterprise software costs, it says, are on course to rise 40 percent by 2027, and most of that increase is driven by vendors rather than by customers. The alternative it argues for is not standing still. It is to decide, on the business’ terms, what changes and when. A system that is stable, compliant and doing its job does not need upgrading because of a vendor-driven deadline. It needs to be supported, secured and kept in step with the business until the business has a reason to move. That reason might be a merger, a new operating model or a real step change in capability. It should not be a support deadline. That is the case for building flexibility into long-term planning from the start, rather than buying it back later at a premium. On the estate’s biggest lines, this is how it looks. Perpetual VMware licenses stay supported for as long as they are useful, instead of moving to a subscription bundle on someone else’s timetable. SAP environments run beyond standard support windows, and modernization programs are planned properly and executed when it makes business sense. Plus, the whole estate is protected against the vulnerabilities that are actually exploited, not the tens of thousands that are merely disclosed. In 2025, 48,000-plus vulnerabilities were published, but only around one percent of these were ever used in an attack. Origina’s OPTAS service proactively identifies, prioritizes and addresses issues before they become a problem. Beyond the budget, one of the constraints most IT leaders feel first is people. The engineers who understand a long-lived SAP estate or a sprawling VMware footprint are scarce, and every unnecessary migration keeps them tied up with work the business never asked for. Independent support helps you to free up resources you can invest in innovation and growth. Control, in the end, is the ability to say not yet, and to mean it. Explore your options: find out how Origina supports VMware and SAP on your timetable, and how OPTAS protects the estate in between. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Chap who took the job left a trail of wreckage – and invaluable case studies – in his incompetent wake Techie was stung by a wasp, held overnight by Chinese police, then trapped in a 13-hour meeting 7 days ago Techie assumed boss knew what they were talking about and killed Exchange by deleting data 12 days ago Project leader thought his team understood the plan, ended up fixing their 'interpretation' of it 15 days ago Your cloud survived everything except the real world 18 days ago Techie fixed Wi-Fi dead zone with a drill 22 days ago Welcome to another installment of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed Friday column which often shares your stories of what happens when incompetent people climb the greasy pole and send their failures straight back down into the lap of tech support. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Preston," who wrote to share his story of working as a field service tech in the late 1990s. "I'd risen to the rank of senior field service engineer and was offered a position in consultancy," Preston told The Register . He turned it down because he liked working at the coal face, and the people he worked with there appreciated his skills. "As soon as I arrived at clients, someone was making me a coffee just as I liked it," Preston explained, "so I turned down the consultancy position." One of Preston's colleagues took the promotion and was soon working on projects such as reconfiguring Windows NT 4.0 and the servers it ran on to handle two CPUs, configuring backup systems, and ensuring uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) were in place to keep things alive. Preston kept doing his own thing, but the character of his job soon changed. "Within weeks, I was getting assigned calls where upgrades had gone wrong, UPSes were failing, and backups were not working." Preston realized the chap who took the promotion was making basic mistakes on almost every job – some of them so bad that one customer refused to work with the newly minted consultant. One of the jobs that eventually landed on Preston's to-fix list saw the consultant wipe a customer database that his backup regime did not protect. At another site, he created a system that pointlessly powered down every day and botched the installation of the UPS that would have saved his bacon. Preston covered as best he could to protect his company rather than the incompetent "consultant." He eventually quit the IT services caper and became a trainer. "I used these incidents as examples of what to look out for when installing and fault finding on customer sites, and also as a lesson on why you should never rely on the person who does a job before you getting things perfectly right." events.title: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
events.summary: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations. Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel. From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent. “Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil prices Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

events.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
events.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres Published 26 October 2025 AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? Published 3 September UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research. Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said. "It's more like a bet on a dream", he added. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create . In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. events.title: Sale rescues landmark WA dairy brands from collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mundella yoghurt returns to shelves as deal revives collapsed WA dairy brands Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company. The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars. Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period. A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves. Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars. Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum. Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh. He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed. "We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market." Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River. Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition. Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation. Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales. There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) "We want to do more than just the WA market," he said. Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres. The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain. WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply. Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. ( ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia ) "Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said. "So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply." Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Top of the Week TSMC and GF inked a $2B manufacturing agreement , under which GF will manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. Volume production is expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. Applied Materials and Intel are expanding their R&D collaboration to develop next-gen transistors, interconnects, and advanced packaging technologies, combining work at Applied’s EPIC Center in Silicon Valley with Intel’s R&D operations in Hillsboro, Oregon. Rapidus launched Rapidus CORE , a global ecosystem framework intended to support customers from chip design through manufacturing for its planned 2nm foundry business. The first phase includes 17 design-service partners. Xanadu and GF formed a multi-year manufacturing partnership to move ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors onto GF’s 300mm production line in Malta, New York. Big hauls Wolfspeed received a conditional commitment for up to $1.5B in 30-year U.S. government financing to expand domestic SiC materials and wide-bandgap power-device production. Vinci raised $250M in Series B funding at a $1.5B valuation to expand its AI-powered physics simulation platform . The platform models thermal, thermo-mechanical, and fluid behavior during design, with simulations reportedly running in minutes rather than hours or days. Oratomic raised $475M for its neutral-atom quantum computing hardware. VEIR raised $110M for superconducting power delivery technology for AI data centers. Atomic Machines launched with $250M for its Matter Compiler system that builds micro-machines from code , including an electromechanical micro-relay to cut power in 800VDC data centers during a fault. Financials TSMC (Sept. revenue) and Samsung (Q3 guidance). Analysis Global semiconductor sales reached $159.7B in August, up 8% from July, with year-to-date sales topping $1T , reports SIA/WSTS . McKinsey expects inference to account for about 60% of AI compute by 2030, driving demand for custom accelerators, HBM, chiplets, advanced packaging, and silicon photonics. Silicon photonics, CPO, and optical networking are emerging as the next U.S.–China semiconductor battleground as AI data centers outgrow electrical interconnects, says Wilson Center , which estimates China accounts for 56% of global optical-transceiver manufacturing capacity. Brookings estimates the U.S. AI buildout could require $10.3T through 2032 for data centers, power, networking and specialized chips, but it warned that increasingly complex financing could obscure financial risks. Lithography ASML and Carl Zeiss researchers outlined a hyper-NA EUV lithography architecture with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75, potentially enabling features as small as 5nm, more than one-third smaller than current high-NA systems. The technology could be ready in about a decade, although commercial production remains uncommitted. Canon says its nanoimprint lithography technology is entering the final stage toward full-scale mass production. DUV immersion lithography is the strongest remaining chokepoint on China’s AI-chip production, contends think tank Center for Technology & Statecraft . It estimates Chinese-owned fabs had accumulated more than 330 DUVi systems by 1Q26 and says continued imports could significantly narrow the U.S.-allied AI-chip manufacturing advantage. The report calls for a China-wide ban on DUVi exports, servicing restrictions and tighter controls on critical components. Memory Samsung is reportedly planning ~$3.9B in investment in memory-chip testing facilities in Vietnam . Netlist and Micron entered into patent license and settlement agreements covering Netlist’s portfolio for server DIMMs and high-bandwidth memory, ending all pending legal proceedings between the companies. Micron faces a potential walkout at its Taiwan facilities after workers voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike over profit sharing. Toshiba plans to invest approximately $380M to double HDD production capacity for AI data centers by fiscal 2027, compared with 2025 levels, reports Nikkei Asia. Security and export controls Arteris won an additional $3.3M through the U.S. government’s Trusted and Assured Microelectronics initiative to expand its third-party IP (3PIP) security assurance program in collaboration with BAE and SiFive . The U.S. DOJ charged the owner of California-based Earthmade Computer with allegedly smuggling more than $300M in export-controlled computer servers to China . Prosecutors allege the servers contained high-end U.S.-manufactured GPUs and were routed through Malaysia and Singapore using false end-user and destination information to evade U.S. export controls. Meanwhile, CSET researchers modeled more than 10 million scenarios for detecting diverted AI chips and found ping-based location verification to be the most cost-effective approach. However, they cautioned that implementation costs and complexity could limit its usefulness, and said that combining PLV with targeted physical inspections could improve enforcement. Recognition Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines was inducted into the National Academy of Engineering for his co-invention of the blue-light-emitting diode and decades of leadership in the semiconductor/EDA industry. In Germany, X-FAB broke ground on a new cleanroom in Erfurt, and Mitutoyo opened a new semiconductor measurement and inspection center in Dresden. HCSS warns that Europe risks losing its strong position in polysilicon unless production capacity grows fast enough to meet rising domestic and global demand. Asia Elephantech plans to open an advanced packaging center in Tokyo in March to support process development, prototyping, and scale-up for AI-server packaging and PCBs. AMD is working with 14 South Korean AI semiconductor and technology companies to develop heterogeneous computing systems that combine AMD CPUs and GPUs with Korean AI processors, reports SBS News. Cadence and Jilin University unveiled their CAE Multiphysics Joint Laboratory in China . The organizations also have a computational fluid dynamics joint lab. events.title: China holiday travel spikes, global funds shift: 5 figures investors are watching in China
events.summary: A Kowloon residential site sale and Hong Kong’s MPF gains shape the week’s market narrative Hong Kong’s property market showed renewed strength as a Kowloon residential site fetched its highest price in nearly five years, while the city’s pension funds posted solid gains despite a September setback. Meanwhile, global investors returned to Chinese equities after years of caution, as US Treasury yields surged to multi-decade highs. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. events.title: Audit firm fined $100,000 by Abu Dhabi's ADGM regulator
events.summary: The Registration Authority of ADGM has imposed fines totalling $100,000 on an audit firm at Abu Dhabi's financial centre over regulatory failings. The action was taken against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers, an ADGM-registered audit firm, and its registered audit principal, Saranga Lalwani, the authority said in a statement on Friday. It has imposed a fine of $65,000 on PKF and $35,000 on Ms Lalwani. The decision was taken after an on-site inspection conducted by the authority to assess PKF’s compliance with ADGM's auditor rules and the quality of its audit work, the statement added. During the inspection, the authority said it identified "significant deficiencies" in an audit conducted for an ADGM-registered entity by PKF and Ms Lalwani. The deficiencies included "failures to conduct the audit and prepare the audit report in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (ISA) as required by the Companies Regulations (Auditors) Rules 2023 and failure to exercise due skill, care and diligence in carrying out the audit", the authority said. The inspection identified that PKF "rebutted the risk of fraud in management override of controls, which is a mandatory fraud risk and cannot be rebutted under ISAs". The firm was also accused of failing to assess fraud risks, failing to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence, inadequate audit documentation, and insufficient evidence demonstrating the audit principal's involvement in the audit process. "Registered auditors and registered audit principals are expected to conduct audits in accordance with applicable professional standards and exercise appropriate skill, care and diligence," the authority said in the statement. "This action reinforces the importance of robust audit practices and demonstrates that failures to meet regulatory requirements will result in appropriate enforcement action." Authorities in the UAE have cracked down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the financial system's integrity and reliability. The Dubai Financial Services Authority this month imposed a Dh401,000 ($109,200) fine on wealth management firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation.

events.title: Frasers Hospitality CEO to step down; COO to lead company and report to Frasers Property
events.summary: Fraser Suites Singapore along River Valley Road, one of the company’s assets. Frasers Hospitality CEO Eu Chin Fen will step down on Jan 1, 2027, after key milestones, including the 2025 privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust and the 2026 portfolio optimisation. Chew Hang Song will lead the lodging business as COO, reporting to Frasers Property group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi, with a focus on global brand growth and third-party management deals. Eric Gan will head hospitality investment and asset management under group investment, supporting an asset-light strategy and stronger capital partnerships across hospitality and living assets. SINGAPORE – Eu Chin Fen will step down as chief executive officer of Frasers Hospitality, effective on Jan 1, 2027, Frasers Property said in a statement on the morning of Oct 9. Chew Hang Song will lead Frasers Hospitality as its chief operating officer, reporting to Frasers Property’s group CEO, Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi. This follows the achievement of strategic milestones: the privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust in 2025 and the completion of its portfolio optimisation in September 2026. Eu, 55, has decided to pursue personal interests, with the hospitality platform now well-positioned for its next state of growth, Frasers Property said. It added: “To sharpen operational focus and support efforts to enhance real estate portfolio value, Frasers Hospitality’s leadership structure will be strategically segmented, aligning with group resources, and reporting into senior group leadership.” Chew’s role will involve driving global brand stewardship for the lodging business, expanding the portfolio through third-party management agreements and overseeing operations at its properties worldwide. Meanwhile, Frasers Hospitality’s current chief financial officer, Eric Gan, will lead hospitality investment and asset management under group investment. He will report to group COO Tony Lombardo. As managing director of group investment, Gan’s focus will be on investment strategies and asset portfolio management across hospitality and the wider living sector. Sirivadhanabhakdi said that the move to house hospitality investment and asset management within group investment aligns with its asset-light strategy for the sector, “connecting (its) real estate platform to institutional capital and enabling (it) to grow (its) capital partnerships more dynamically”. Empowering the lodging business under Chew, meanwhile, allows the team to scale the brand globally through management contracts, he added. Sirivadhanabhakdi said: “(Eu) has helped build a resilient global brand, established trusted partnerships and nurtured a strong hospitality executive team. Our evolved structure builds on that foundation by giving each part of the business clearer focus and optimised resources.” Eu joined the group in 2011. She worked closely with group leadership on the $2.1 billion Frasers Hospitality Trust portfolio optimisation. The stapled group was taken private in October 2025 via a trust scheme of arrangement. Frasers Property closed at 94 cents, down 1.05%, on Oct 9. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Competition authority seeks public views on Eneos Apac’s proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore
events.summary: Chevron Singapore operates under the Caltex brand for retail petrol and diesel. CCS is seeking public feedback on Eneos Apac’s proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore, and will decide if the deal breaches section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore runs fuel retail, storage, terminal and lubricant businesses in Singapore and Vietnam, and would keep the Chevron and Caltex brands if the deal goes ahead. Eneos says the takeover should not harm competition because there are many rivals, low entry barriers, and customers can easily switch suppliers; public submissions close at 5 pm on Oct 16. SINGAPORE – The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) is inviting public feedback on the proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore – a distributor of petroleum products – by Eneos Apac, a subsidiary of energy, resources and materials group Eneos. The authority on Oct 2 accepted the companies’ application for a decision on whether the proposed transaction would infringe Section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore is a subsidiary of Chevron South Asia, which is indirectly wholly owned by Chevron Corp. It is primarily a downstream petroleum company with operations in Singapore and Vietnam. In Singapore, Chevron Singapore engages in the retail distribution of fuels and lubricants. It holds an equity interest in Singapore Refining Company, a 50:50 joint venture with Singapore Petroleum Company. Chevron Singapore’s activities also include fuel storage and terminal operations, and lubricant blending and wholesale. The company operates under the Chevron brand in the Republic. Caltex, for retail petrol and diesel; Delo, for commercial and industrial lubricants; Havoline for passenger vehicle lubricants; Star Mart, for convenience retail offerings at service stations; Texaco, a legacy brand in fuels and lubricants; and Techron and Techron D, for fuel additives. Meanwhile, Eneos is a Japan-based energy, resources and materials group with global operations. In Singapore, it is active in the trading of crude oil, naphtha and refined petroleum products, lubricants blending and wholesale, the supply of marine fuels and solar energy solutions. The company mainly operates under the Eneos brand. If the proposed acquisition were to be completed, Chevron Singapore would continue to operate under the Chevron and Caltex brands. Eneos would “step into Chevron’s current operations in Singapore”, CCS added. Chevron Singapore would continue to source Chevron-branded products and raw materials mostly from Chevron Corp. Eneos Apac believes that it overlaps with Chevron Singapore in the market only for lubricant blending and wholesale supply in the city-state. The proposed transaction will not raise any material competitive concerns, “given the significant number of existing competitors, relatively low barriers to entry and expansion, and ability of customers to multi-source and switch among credible alternative lubricant suppliers in Singapore at minimal cost”. Eneos Apac also submitted that no material vertical effects are anticipated. Chevron Singapore faces significant competitive constraints in its active markets, such as fuel refining, storage and terminal services, retail distribution of fuels and lubricants, it said, while Eneos has a limited market presence in lubricant blending and wholesale in Singapore. CCS invites views from the public on the impact of this proposed acquisition on competition. Submissions – via its online form or through e-mail – will close at 5 pm on Oct 16. events.title: So long, Spokes: GitHub rewrites storage to restore reliability, just in time for agentic hordes
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Octocats claim 35x write improvement There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero 1 day ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 2 days ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 2 days ago OpenAI tries disarming AI angst with cute graphics and always-on agents 10 days ago AI models keep posting screenshots showing sensitive data from inside tech companies 10 days ago Responding to unprecedented demand from AI agents, GitHub is rebuilding its Git storage architecture from scratch. Early tests with the new architecture show a promising 35x write improvement in internal tests. GitHub will need a miracle of that proportion just to keep up with customer demand. The plan involves decoupling writes from reads, offloading maintenance, and letting object storage manage redundancy. Most impressive is that the redesign is happening under the hood, with the goal of a non-disruptive change that won't alter developer workflows, review processes, or security controls. Running an enterprise-grade code repository means supporting “large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today,” wrote Brian Celenza , GitHub principal software engineer, in a blog post describing the updates. Celenza did not offer a timeline for this ambitious migration. When GitHub’s customers shifted their coding focus to AI agents, activity on the platform spiked significantly. Between September 2025 and August 2026, GitHub traffic doubled, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion. In September alone, commits hit 7.38 billion, a 5x increase from September 2025. This shift in traffic is stressing the system. According to the GitHub Availability Report , the service suffered 10 incidents in April alone that degraded performance. Another nine incidents landed in May, with each generating more bad publicity than the previous one. GitHub's current storage architecture, nicknamed Spokes , uses a three-phase commit protocol, storing full repo copies across multiple local disks and requiring a quorum of replicas to acknowledge each write. While this approach ensures strong reliability, it bottlenecks write speed, as every push is bounded by the slowest replica required for quorum. The new architecture writes a commit only once, to Azure Blob Storage , an object store service that automatically handles replication (and hence redundancy) on its own, eliminating the quorum bottleneck. GitHub also gooses performance by separating read requests into their own channel, a job handled by lightweight compute workers. The only coordination between reads and writes is over the reference branch pointers. Maintenance duties – such as compaction and garbage collection — are moved from the serving path to operate as background processes, further reducing system lag. GitHub seems to be on the same page with others in rethinking Git for the agentic age. Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a Git-hosting service called Entire , which offloads agent traffic to mirror repositories, allowing a customer’s core GitHub repos to just serve the core development traffic. SpaceX subsidiary Cursor, which uses Git to back its agent-support service, also refined the storage layer for better performance. Cursor engineers also rejected Spokes’ three-phase commit in favor of uploading pushes into an object storage write-ahead log (WAL), which captured all changes as immutable objects, caching at least one copy on super-speedy solid-state disks. While it's cathartic to hate on a service that often goes down, you have to feel empathy for the GitHub engineers who, when they created the service, couldn’t have guessed what they signed up for.

events.title: Virgin unveils its future cross-Channel train as it gears up to take on Eurostar
events.summary: Group plans to launch services from London in 2030 and hopes to outshine competitor with design inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms Flash interiors, fancy food and maybe even a bar: Virgin has unveiled a mock-up of its future cross-Channel train, with a pledge to create “something genuinely new”. The group is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, with Eurostar facing competition for the first time since the opening of the Channel tunnel. Virgin has ordered 12 high-speed trains from the manufacturer Alstom, matching Eurostar’s for speed at up to 190mph (300km/h) but aiming to outshine the incumbent on design and customer experience. While Virgin’s last stab at reimagining UK train travel may have peaked with the talking toilet seat on its intercity services in 2013, it has said the future trains will draw inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms. Although details are being kept under wraps, it said it would draw on Virgin Atlantic’s airport lounges, or Clubhouses, for “pre-departure and onboard social spaces” with “more flexibility to work, relax or socialise in style”. Food will be influenced by its cruise line menu and the design by its Virgin Hotels brand. Virgin Trains is expecting to introduce 20 daily return services between London, Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam from 2030, adding almost 7.5m seats a year to the cross-Channel network, creating up to 1,000 new jobs. Josh Bayliss, the chief executive of Virgin Group , said: “Virgin has a proud history in UK rail. With our latest venture we are drawing on more than four decades of experience across travel and hospitality to create something genuinely new. “We’re confident that more journeys between the UK and Europe will be made by train. We’re adding capacity for millions more international rail journeys each year, growing the market as a whole. We’re looking forward to seeing our distinctive red and black trains travelling across Europe.” Virgin also hopes to connect its rail and airline networks, potentially bringing passengers from France for Virgin Atlantic flights. It will also wrap the train service into its loyalty platform so that passengers can earn points towards other types of Virgin travel. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Office of Rail and Road on Thursday published an agreement with Eurostar for Virgin to maintain its trains at the Temple Mills international depot near Stratford in east London, with track access in the UK confirmed until at least 2040. Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia is also expected to launch cross-Channel high-speed services. It already runs international trains as far as Paris and recently announced its own €2bn order for 19 new trains from Hitachi, some of which are expected to be based in France and run through the tunnel to London.

events.title: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
events.summary: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive". A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India ’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”. "The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service. The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant. "When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country." The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers. As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards. The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients. In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg. In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans. Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella , the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration. Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students. J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

events.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
events.summary: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external . They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external . O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme. He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly". "I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community. "As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all. "I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally. "And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work. "They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
events.summary: Longbow's co-founders and CEOs Daniel Davey (left) and Mark Tapscott show Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds (left in car) and mayor Richard Parker the Speedster A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire. Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs. Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said. Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it. "So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight." The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car. At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise. Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars. "Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added. People around the world are waiting to buy the limited edition car for around £85,000 The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , external , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry. West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year. Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow. "They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car." Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car. "So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing." events.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
events.summary: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 T he coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies? While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research. Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions: from AlphaFold , which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again? We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that 75% of people agree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth. But it is disappointing that only 36% of the British public believes the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the 10-year plan the government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale that Our Scottish Future has proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK. We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas. Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by the British Business Bank and the national wealth fund . Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Research for the conference has identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovation they need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets. Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “ lost Einsteins ” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius.
