events.title: Data centre operator Firmus pulls blockbuster ASX float after lacklustre demand
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The mega float of data centre operator Firmus has been pulled. It follows poor interest from investors amid concerns about the company's debt and a lack of detail. The company says it will pursue private funding. AI data centre company Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia's biggest share market floats. The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects. Firmus said it would now pursue private market funding while considering other options. "We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said in a statement. Firmus, the AI factory builder backed by chip-making giant Nvidia, was set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997. The company's founders, co-chief executives Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield, targeted a $44 billion valuation, but prospective investors pulled back based on the high sale price of $11 a share and concerns over an AI bubble. Yesterday, reports emerged that Firmus and its advisors were considering reducing the size of the initial public offering (IPO) and lowering the per-share price from $11 to $8.25. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield at Firmus's St Leonards, Launceston site. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Many investors were also focused on Mr Curtis's criminal background — he is a former investment banker who served one year in prison a decade ago for insider trading. With AI infrastructure demand accelerating across the Asia-Pacific, Firmus's website says its broader portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries: Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. It said two sites were operational in Australia and Singapore and five were "under development, targeting ready-for-service over the next 24 months". Its website also spruiks its relationship with US chip giant Nvidia, which has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus. Institutional investors raise doubts Today, after Firmus announced the IPO had been pulled, UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce said it was disappointing. "The ASX needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," he said. Firmus tries to save mega share market float The company is reportedly having to price its shares lower as it closed its books to potential investors abruptly overnight. Ahead of the announcement, he had released an investment update detailing potential investors' doubts about the AI company and why the super fund would not directly invest in it. "Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies," he said. "The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion." Mr Pearce said even though UniSuper was not directly investing in Firmus, UniSuper would own some shares if the float proceeded "because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices". He said the reason UniSuper was doubtful about investing was the high valuation. "At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation. "Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans." Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway yesterday raised concerns over the company's debt levels. Lochlan Holloway is not convinced by the Firmus float. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "The neo-clouds are heavily geared," he wrote in an economic note. "The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans." Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about $US30 billion ($43 billion) of debt, about six times the $US5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028. "Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," Mr Holloway said. CDC was set to build data centres with Firmus but scrapped the deal.

events.title: US disrupts Chinese hacking tools as 7 govts warn of PRC spies stealing sensitive data worldwide
events.summary: The FBI announced that it has seized seven web domains linked to hacking tools allegedly operated by a Chinese security firm called Integrity Technology Group and used by Beijing-backed cyber operatives to scan a South Carolina power company's network and other critical infrastructure systems for vulnerabilities. In a subsequent advisory, the FBI and other government agencies in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Spain warned that Chinese government-linked attackers, enabled by Integrity Tech, are using botnets, malware, and other intrusion tools to target organizations worldwide and steal sensitive data, including from US critical infrastructure networks. “These actors exploit vulnerabilities by using scanning tools, cross-site scripting attacks, and password spraying on Microsoft Exchange servers, while establishing persistence through VPN software and exfiltrating emails and credentials using scripts,” according to the security alert. Based on this activity, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog: CVE-2015-3306 CVE-2015-5477 CVE-2016-3081 CVE-2021-3199 CVE-2023-22894 The court-authorized seizures are the latest in a long series of US law-enforcement attempts to disrupt a Beijing-backed cybercrew called Flax Typhoon and shut down its botnet. From 2021 until its disruption, Flax Typhoon allegedly used a version of this Mirai-based botnet to infect internet-connected devices with malware, scan networks for vulnerabilities, and launch additional cyberattacks, all while hiding the PRC government hackers’ true IP addresses and physical location. The feds allege Integrity Tech developed the botnet and a vulnerability scanner called Microscan, and operated a post-compromise tool called FishHub. The latter allegedly downloaded additional malware to the phishing victims’ networks and stole sensitive data. Court documents, unsealed on Thursday, allege Integrity Tech has contracts with the PRC government, and the feds have long linked Flax Typhoon to the private firm. “Flax Typhoon actors conducted successful computer intrusions against multiple victim entities which had been scanned using the Microscan tool,” according to the court documents. Victims include a university in Hsinchu, Taiwan, that Flax Typhoon compromised in March 2023, and a second university in Puli Township, Taiwan breached in August 2022. “On or about April 26, 2022, and on or about December 29, 2022, Flax Typhoon actors also used the Microscan tool to scan for vulnerabilities on the networks of a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, and at least two Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors,” the documents allege. Integrity Tech accessed Microscan through one of the seized domains, c0cc[.]cc. Meanwhile, five of the seized domains, 98aicai[.]com, 98aicode[.]com, outlook3650[.]com, youtubecard[.]com, and linkedinns[.]net, delivered the FishHub malware as recently as March, and infected about 20 Taiwanese universities. “Based on my training and experience I believe the tool was named FishHub because it facilitated phishing activity,” FBI special agent Adam James said in a seizure warrant affidavit. After FishHub downloaded a file onto victims' computers, that file used the five domains to retrieve additional malicious programs and code. The malware created a file listing, searched for specific files, compressed documents, and then exfiltrated the selected files to an attacker-controlled server. This gave Flax Typhoon remote access to compromised networks. In September 2024, the FBI said Integrity Tech and Flax Typhoon tore down their 260,000-device botnet after the FBI and its international pals went after them. As recently as this year, however, both private sector security researchers and Western governments warned that Chinese hackers continue to turn compromised routers and IoT devices into botnets and break into critical networks. In February, operational technology (OT) security provider Dragos said China’s state-sponsored spies haven't let up on their attempts to compromise America's critical infrastructure, and this includes a group whose activity overlaps with Flax Typhoon. This group focuses on gaining long-term access to OT engineering workstations and exfiltrating operational files, and it targets manufacturing, defense, automotive, electric power, oil and gas, and government organizations across the US, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. In April, a 10-country joint advisory warned that basically every Chinese “Typhoon” group is using botnets “strategically, and at scale.” Some of these covert networks are built and maintained by Chinese infosec companies including Integrity Tech, which also controlled and managed the so-called Raptor Train network, the alert said. In late August, the FBI said that it had disrupted a different botnet and seized domains associated with two platforms that Chinese government-backed operatives allegedly used to target NASA, the US Senate, the Department of Energy, and several other government agencies and critical networks. The DOJ subsequently clarified that not all the named organizations had been compromised.®

events.title: Trump-tied firm helped organize political advisers’ Balkans travel
events.summary: The Scoop Continental, a Washington-based law and lobbying firm with close ties to President Donald Trump’s network, helped arrange a recent trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina by two Trump political advisers, three people familiar with the trip told Semafor. Republika Srpska, whose Russia-friendly Serbian leaders have sought to align themselves with Trump, agreed earlier this year to pay $35,000 monthly to Continental, which would organize “meetings and discussions and establish relationships with key stakeholders in the executive and legislative branches,” according to a Justice Department filing . Since then, former Trump campaign adviser Alex Garcia has helped arrange meetings with White House officials like Walker Barrett, Jarrod Agen and Richard Walters, according to another DOJ filing . A White House official told Semafor that Garcia, who was in Republika Srpska around the same time as LaCivita and Blair, also set up a recent meeting between Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles and a Serbian official from the region. The Balkan trip occurred after Garcia initially reached out to LaCivita, multiple people familiar with the situation said. LaCivita and Blair were there for 48 hours, one source said, to consult on voting equipment ahead of elections on Sunday. Trump on Wednesday signaled his displeasure with LaCivita and Blair’s trip, which was first reported by The New York Times , amid some intraparty criticism that his advisers aren’t as focused as possible on the midterms. But Trump wasn’t particularly harsh about the trip in private, two people familiar with the situation said. “If I’m the president … traveling the country every day and campaigning … I’m rightfully annoyed, right?” one of the people said. “With that being said, do I think James missed a second of work? No.” Two sources said that Trump and Blair had a call following the news, with one calling it “a good conversation.” And while the duo has faced criticism from some corners of the Republican party, others close to Trump are openly defending them. LaCivita and Blair’s trip focused on election integrity rather than political strategy, multiple people said; this year marked Republika Srpska’s first election using new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment. Asked for comment on whether Continental helped organize LaCivita and Blair’s trip, a spokesperson for the firm said only that Garcia was its only employee in Republika Srpska on Oct. 4 as well as its only employee to lobby the US government on its behalf. The spokesperson added that Wiles’ daughter Katie, who also works at Continental , traveled to Republika Srpska in August for a separate reason: helping a US-based company complete “a feasibility study.” After publication of this story, Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for the firm, sent the following statement: “It is wrong for Semafor to report Continental Strategy organized the Election Day trip.” Know More Republika Srpska voters on Sunday decided to keep former President Milorad Dodik’s nationalist party in power. The US last year lifted sanctions on Dodik, who was banned from holding office after violating his country’s peace deal. The Balkans isn’t the only place Continental is looking to cash in on the administration’s agenda abroad: The firm reportedly took on at least a dozen clients in Venezuela after the US captured its former leader earlier this year. Republika Srpska, for its part, has signed lobbying contracts worth at least $9 million since Trump was inaugurated in an effort to curry favor with the administration (though it’s never signed one with Ballard Partners, Susie Wiles’ former firm). So far, it seems to be working: Officials have yet to impose recently enacted sanctions on Serbian politicians despite Congress’ urging. House Democrats already have a plan, reported first by Semafor , to oversee the administration’s Balkans policy if they win a majority next month. Notable LaCivita has also advised another Continental client looking to ingratiate himself with Trump: Albania’s Sali Berisha . Trump this term has embraced a number of foreign governments who have moved to politically align themselves with the conservative or MAGA movement, as CBS and Reuters reported.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Commitment comes as GPUzilla prepares to fortify Uncle Sam's arsenal with at least seven AI-optimized supers Microsoft leans on open weight model from Chinese AI lab to challenge Jev now AWS AgentCore security undone by prompt requesting credentials 11 hours ago Oracle lets AI agents do the work, provided you stay in Big Red's world 16 hours ago Anthropic asks users to stop being mean to Claude 20 hours ago AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI 1 day ago Nvidia on Thursday scraped together some spare change to commit $1 billion — about 1/60th of its quarterly profits — to funding US scientific discovery over the next five years. The commitment , announced during an event in Washington, DC, aims to support the research and development of AI — or is it " super intelligence " now? — in fields including quantum computing, healthcare, and energy security. Nvidia's choice of technologies is not surprising as it has long aspired to fuse AI and high-performance computing. And while LLM training and inference pay Nvidia's bills, the GPU giant has continued to introduce new CUDA libraries specifically for AI-assisted quantum computing, healthcare, drug discovery, and physics simulation. The initiative is part of the US government's broader Genesis Mission , announced late last year by the Trump administration, which aims to use AI to drive the scientific discoveries necessary to ensure the country's continued technological leadership. The program marks Nvidia's return to US supercomputing in a big way. The Department of Energy's (DoE) last flagship supercomputers powered by Nvidia, Summitand Sierra, were commissioned all the way back in 2018. The A100-based Perlmutter system launched in 2021 is also notable, but fell far short of the older systems. And while Nvidia never stopped building supers for the US government, they tended to be significantly smaller than the massive AMD-based platforms like Frontier and El Capitan. That changed last year when Nvidia revealed it would supply the US government with no fewer than seven new supercomputers across the Argonne, Los Alamos, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratories. Argonne will house the 100,000 Blackwell-GPU-based Solstice system. Built in collaboration with Oracle, the machine is largely aimed at emerging AI workloads, which don't depend on ultra-high precision computation and instead can get by with 16, eight or even four bits of precision. That puts Nvidia in a strong position to meet the US government's goals under the Genesis Mission. Over the past few generations of GPUs, Nvidia has traded much of its accelerators' double-precision FP64 grunt in favor of higher throughput at precisions used by more lucrative AI workloads. In the case of its upcoming Vera Rubin platform, Nvidia relies heavily on an FP64 emulation capability based on the Ozaki scheme we looked at in more detail earlier this year . Los Alamos' upcoming Mission and Vision systems will be powered by these same chips and take advantage of Nvidia's Quantum-X800 InfiniBand. FP64 emulation comes with compromises, but for workloads that are predominantly AI-optimized and only occasionally need higher precision, it can be worthwhile for the additional matrix FLOPS. While Nvidia is playing a much bigger role in US scientific computing efforts, it's worth noting that the DoE's biggest super — at least for pure FP64 — will still be powered by AMD. Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Discovery system, which is expected to come online 2029 will be built by HPE's Cray division and feature The House of Zen's FP64-optimized MI430X GPUs and Venice CPUs. Discovery is expected to offer peak theoretical performance somewhere between 3.3 and 8.5 exaFLOPS depending on whether or not Oak Ridge gets a facility power upgrade. Meanwhile, China's LineShine leads the Top500 ranking of Earth's mightiest computers. That system made its debut this northern spring with 2.2 exaFLOPS measured out of a 2.7 exaFLOPS of theoretical performance.

events.title: Kushner, Witkoff to pitch "new ideas" to end Russia-Ukraine war
events.summary: Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet with Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to present "new ideas and proposals" to break the stalemate in the Russia -Ukraine war, U.S. and Ukrainian officials say. Why it matters: The Trump administration is hoping to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the midterm elections and before brutal winter weather grips Ukraine. One of the ideas is a partial ceasefire that halts attacks on energy infrastructure and grain shipments. While Ukraine has said it's willing to take that step, Russia has shown little willingness. "They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop. So the U.S. is trying to mediate with the sides, with the goal of creating a unified proposal," a U.S. source said. Driving the news: Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September. Since then, they've been working with the Russians and Ukrainians on an updated peace initiative. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference in Lisbon Thursday that the war is at a "stalemate." He stressed that the U.S. wants to prevent further escalation of fighting in the coming month and find a way to end the war. Behind the scenes: Witkoff and Kushner met with President Trump Thursday to present the latest U.S. proposal and receive his input ahead of the talks in Miami, which are expected to last two days, a U.S. official said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and deputy national security adviser Mike Needham also attended the meeting. Zoom in: President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence director Rustem Umerov, diplomatic adviser Sergey Kyslytsia and Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia will participate from the Ukrainian side. The U.S. also invited national security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the EU. A U.S. source said the parties will discuss proposals for security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan and other aspects of the conflict. The other side: Zelensky told reporters on Thursday that Ukraine is discussing with the U.S. the possibility of an energy and grain ceasefire. "As for what might be realistic or more realistic, I am not ready to say yet. I do not want to say something and then have Russia, as always, do the opposite out of spite. So let's wait and see," he said. Between the lines: A Ukrainian official said that despite skepticism in Kyiv, the U.S. midterm elections and Russia's need for sanctions relief might lead Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire of some sort. What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner might travel to Moscow later this month for more talks with Putin, a source with knowledge said.

events.title: Pete Hegseth says the public can watch Fort Hood shooter's execution
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the public will be able to watch the execution of the Fort Hood shooter by firing squad. Why it matters: The U.S. hasn't held a public execution in 90 years , and Hegseth's remarks raise questions about how the military would allow people to watch. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, near Killeen, Texas. What they're saying: Hegseth told Real America's Voice Thursday that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be." "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it's public. Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The latest: The Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed, AP reports, but did not name where specifically the stream will be hosted. The Pentagon currently posts speeches and videos on X and YouTube . State of play: The Department of Defense declined to comment on Hegseth's remarks, leaving questions about how the public could watch the execution. The Army has not shared how it intends to conduct the execution, AP reports. It's unclear if Hegseth's remarks mean the execution will be open to public spectators, broadcast on streaming or TV, or made available to select individuals. Zoom out: This would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 . The last U.S. military execution by firing squad was in 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, according to NPR . Firing-squad executions are rare in the U.S. Only Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah authorize the method, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Last year, South Carolina carried out the state's first firing squad execution — the first in the U.S. in 15 years. The last public execution in the U.S. was in 1936, when Rainey Bethea , a Black man convicted of raping a white woman, was hanged in Kentucky.

WIRED has created a tracker to follow America PAC's support in real time. We're going to take you through why these races matter and how Musk is throwing Republicans all of this cash. Zoë Schiffer : We're also going to break down the once obscure philosophy that now seems to be everywhere from X threads to The Economist cover, effective altruism . We'll talk about what this ideology is actually all about, why many AI researchers subscribe to it, and how it has been actively shaping the debate around AI safety. Leah Feiger : And we're going to get into why the designer of Meta's Muse logo has been receiving a ton of backlash. Zoë spoke with her all about it this week and she had a lot to say. Zoë, it's just me and you this week. We've officially pushed Brian off a cliff. Zoë Schiffer : Yeah, we have. The FaceTime chat has gone live. We will not be talking about any tech conferences this week. Leah Feiger : Absolutely not. But he'll be back next week. So at the very least, there's that. OK, Zoë, Elon Musk. He's back. Zoë Schiffer : He's back. He never left for some. Leah Feiger : He never really left, but he is back and so is his wallet . To refresh everyone's memories a little bit, Musk is the founder and main donor of America PAC, a super PAC that was started in 2024 to help elect President Donald Trump to the White House. They succeeded. Trump is in office. The PAC spent more than $260 million to make that happen. This time around for November's midterms, the PAC has been going about it a little bit differently. WIRED created a live tracker to monitor their donations in real time. You can check it out on the WIRED website. And we learned a lot putting this together. Basically, the PAC is donating to the election's most consequential races. They are not focusing obviously on the presidential race. There is no presidential race this year. But they are all in on the most critical Senate races in the country that are really going to decide the makeup of Congress next year. The PAC is primarily pumping money against Democrats as opposed to for Republicans, which is really interesting. For every dollar that America PAC has spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two have gone to oppose a Democrat. And that only becomes more extreme in some of these Senate races, right? In Texas where several Musk companies are based, the group has spent tons and tons of money attacking Democrat James Talarico. We're talking like $9 million. Whereas promoting Ken Paxton, around the one million mark. Similar numbers can be found in the Ohio Senate race, in Iowa, really up and down the board. And these races are not random.

events.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
events.summary: Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training. Explore the Onshape importer guide . Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Have a simulation idea?

events.title: Fears backpacker ballot will leave coastal towns short-staffed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hospitality businesses seek designated area migration agreement to combat backpacker ballot There are concerns about how to fill jobs when the backpacker ballot begins. ( Flickr CC BY-NC-ND 2.0: Jo Christian Oterhals ) Hospitality experts say the backpacker ballot could create significant workforce shortages in holiday towns that rely heavily on seasonal workers. North Coast Hotel Group director Harry Barry says his business hires backpackers because of a local workforce shortage. Business leaders along the NSW coast are looking to negotiate a federal agreement to help fill roles in the regions. For publican Harry Barry, backpackers are the lifeblood of his business. But he says many of his employees are considering returning home after the federal government announced a backpacker ballot , which would effectively cap second-year backpacker visas. "The incentive was a guarantee they could extend their visas by another 12 months," he said. "A lot of them are deciding that there is no guarantee that [they're] going to be earning enough money to pay [their] way. Harry Barry says a designated area migration agreement could help the Coffs Harbour region. ( ABC Coffs Harbour: Claudia Jambor ) The new backpacker ballot will cap annual places at 45,000 for second-year visas if the standard 88 days of regional work are completed. Even fewer third-year places are available. About 57,000 people qualified last year . Mr Barry is among a number of business owners concerned about how the cap will impact their staff. The director of the North Coast Hotel Group runs pubs from Grafton to Taree that employed 80 backpackers over the past two years, with 20 still on his books. "If we're employing 80 backpackers, we're doing it for a reason , and the reason is we can't find local workers to fill the slots," he said. Harry Barry believes the new backpacker ballot will negatively affect the Mid North Coast. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) According to jobs website Seek, there were more than 130 vacancies in the Coffs Harbour region in the industry on Wednesday. To fill the gap left by backpackers leaving, Mr Barry is backing a push to establish the region as a priority area for semi-skilled migrants, also known as a Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA). The DAMA is an agreement between the federal government and a state or regional authority that assists regional areas to fill roles that would otherwise remain empty. It allows skilled migrants, in industries of need, to move to the area for work. Industries include skilled roles in hospitality, agriculture, engineering and more. The agreements are usually in place for five years before they are reviewed. Backpackers help pick fruit across regional NSW. ( ABC Rural: Stephanie Anderson ) There are 13 DAMAs in place across Australia, with one operation in New South Wales; two in South Australia; five in Western Australia; one in the Northern Territory; two in Victoria; and two in Queensland. Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast CEO Madeleine Lawler said the DAMA was not about filling jobs with migrants that could have otherwise employed locals. "The DAMA requires businesses to be able to substantiate that they have been seeking Australians for a long period of time and have not been able to fill these positions with Australians or people locally," she said. A similar agreement in Townsville, in Northern Queensland, brought in an additional 480 workers over three years to fill a skills shortage. Holiday hotspot Cairns has held a DAMA for the past seven years. The agreement, according to the Cairns Chamber of Commerce, was key to keeping the region thriving. CEO Patricia O'Neill said there was a hotel on Thursday Island, which was included in the Cairns agreement, that would shut down without DAMA workforce. Patricia O'Neill says the DAMA has been a lifeline for the Cairns region. ( ABC News: Conor Byrne ) "Government go to [Thursday Island] regularly; there is only one hotel in the place. If they weren't able to apply to attract a chef, that hotel would need to close [because] it can't feed anyone," Ms O'Neill said. "That's how critical a DAMA is to certain parts of an economy up here. "Without having the Far North Queensland DAMA, we would not have a thriving economy; we would not have a workforce to take up jobs." Each area with an agreement has a list of specific jobs, tailored to the region's needs, that can be filled by overseas workers.

events.title: The staggering cost of winning a Senate seat in 2026
events.summary: Source: AdImpact, Census.gov Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios Every voting-age Mainer could get a $167 voucher for home heating oil with what Democrats and Republicans are spending on ads in the Senate race, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. Why it matters: Every senator gets one vote, but Senate seats aren't created equal — and they don't cost the same. Zoom in: Like two years ago , the less-populated states have a dramatically higher dollar-per-voter ratio in 2026. Maine is in first place, followed by Alaska, which is scheduled to be hit with $76 million in ads — enough to suck up most of the state's inventory. Between the lines: Ohio is only in fifth place on the dollar-per-voter metric, but it's on track to host the most expensive Senate race in the country — for the second cycle in a row . Sherrod Brown's comeback bid is proving more expensive than his 2024 race, when he was ousted by now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). And in New Hampshire, where Democratic Senate nominee Chris Pappas has been warning that his race is actually quite close, both parties are spending heavily to reach the state's voters. Data: AdImpact Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The big picture: Both chambers are likely to come down to a handful of races. All year, Republicans warned that Texas would get really expensive if Attorney General Ken Paxton won the primary. They were right. Outside GOP groups spent a mind-blowing $131 million in just 17 days trying to rescue Paxton. And tens of millions more could be on the way. But in North Carolina, where Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), predicted the race could cost $1 billion , the contest looks like it will come in under $200 million. Republican super PACs are abandoning the Senate race there as they reallocate money to redder states. The bottom line: Republicans have a spending advantage, especially when it comes to how many eyeballs they're actually reaching in Texas and Ohio . But neither side has really figured out how to play moneyball and find a way to reach voters with a dramatically smaller budget.

events.title: 'Consumers should feel ripped off': How coffee brands have changed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coffee manufacturers quietly change marketing after price squeeze Coffee brands are changing their marketing due to price pressures. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Major supermarket coffee brands have changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Some companies no longer label their products as "100 per cent arabica" but instead as "coffee", or mix the more expensive arabica beans with cheaper robusta beans. Experts and consumers want companies to flag recipe changes to buyers. Major supermarket coffee brands have quietly changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Labelling of premium arabica coffee beans, prized for their sweeter, more complex flavour, has switched in some cases from "100 per cent arabica" to being described as "coffee", or as a blend with robusta, a more bitter variety of the plant. While the change is legal and does not necessarily mean the coffee is worse, experts say consumers deserve to know when changes are made. Cairns pensioner Brian Rantzau said price was his most important consideration when buying coffee, but he also wanted clear information about changes to the product. "As a pensioner, you've got to mind every dollar," Mr Rantzau said. "It should really tell us what's in it, right?" Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled in price since 2024. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) The price of Mr Rantzau's preferred Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled since early 2024, jumping from $4 per 100 grams to $8. Earlier this year, the product's "100 per cent arabica" description was also changed to simply read "instant coffee". Both versions may appear on supermarket shelves at the same time as stores gradually phase out the old recipe. Coles is phasing out 100 per cent arabica from the label of its Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee. Its website currently shows the old and new labels. ( Supplied: Coles ) Gold Coast mother Vicki Jarvis said she stopped buying the product. "It just kept going up, and now it's $8 a jar, and I just would not pay that," she said. "[But] if they've gone and changed what is actually in it, it should be written on the front of the label to let people know." A Coles spokesperson said product formulations may need to change occasionally in response to ingredient availability and supply conditions. "We work closely with our suppliers to ensure our products continue to meet our quality standards and provide great value for customers," the spokesperson said. Australian food labelling rules do not require coffee companies to identify the species of bean unless they make a specific claim about it. University of Queensland sensory scientist Heather Smyth said consumers had every right to feel ripped off. Heather Smyth says robusta is not a bad bean, but it is more bitter. ( Supplied: UQ ) Professor Smyth said consumers should be told when a product they had previously chosen for a key ingredient had changed. Jason Lilienstein runs a specialty roaster in Toowoomba, Queensland, and has only ever used arabica beans, bought directly from Colombian farmers he has met personally. "Arabica has always been the preferred, high-quality bean," he said. Jason Lilienstein runs specialty roaster Six Of One in Toowoomba. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Robusta is not necessarily bad, he said, but he has not found one good enough for his blends. "I haven't found it of sufficient quality to put in any of our coffee at this stage." He said his customers tended to focus less on the species of bean and more on its flavour and origin. Coffee prices have soared recently, with arabica prices reaching $15.40 a kilogram, while robusta hit $8.73 a kilogram — levels not seen since 1977 — piling pressure onto manufacturers. While prices have fallen about 35 per cent from their peak ahead of what is expected to be a record Brazilian harvest, some say consumers may not see lower prices as other costs continue to rise. Some coffee manufacturers have responded by adjusting the composition of their blends. Australian-owned coffee manufacturer Vittoria's website once prominently promoted its coffee as "100 per cent arabica", stating in 2020: "At Vittoria coffee, we make no excuses, all our coffee is 100 per cent arabica". The Vittoria website compares arabica to robusta beans in 2020. ( Supplied: Wayback Machine/Vittoria ) And in mid-2025, the company's website described robusta as an "inferior quality bean". But a few months later, that message had changed.

events.title: Average long-term US mortgage rate rises to highest level in nearly 3 years
events.summary: Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years. The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage climbed to 7.40% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.30%. The average rate is now the highest it’s been since Nov. 16, 2023, when it was at 7.44%. The housing market has been stuck in a rut this year in large part because of rising mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate increased to 6.73% from 6.60% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.53%. Mortgage rates have been climbing in the months since the start of the U.S. war with Iran in late February. The recent run-up in rates also reflects heightened bond market volatility as surging oil prices due to the war fuel inflation worries. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen to its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation , big government debt loads and other factors. The yield was at 5.29% at midday Thursday on the bond market. That's well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran began. Why are gas prices still high even as traffic improves in the Strait of Hormuz? The 1.42 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional monthly cost of $376 for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate. Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Last month, the National Association of Realtors said that existing home sales fell 2% in August from July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million units. That was their slowest annual pace in more than a year. The sharp rise in mortgage rates has many would-be homebuyers putting their home shopping plans on hold. Mortgage applications, which include loans to buy a home or refinance an existing mortgage, fell for the fifth week in a row last week as mortgage rates kept climbing, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Higher rates are also keeping many homeowners from refinancing their existing mortgage. events.title: There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero
events.summary: Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that Gemini will be "your new single, universal agent for work," a declaration as unassailable as Google's history of consistency, customer service, and long-term product support. Long-term here means a median lifespan of about 4.1 years and a mean lifespan of about 5.4 years across 308 discontinued products and services. That doesn't include enduring successes like Gmail and Search. Perhaps Gemini is destined for that level of longevity. In a blog post adapted from the prepared remarks he spoke at the Gemini at Work 2026 event – and what could be more appropriate for Google than to herald Gemini with a derivative work? – Kurian laid out his vision for an AI service known as Bard only two years ago. Gemini, he said, has your business context – which is to say, data – and thus can be used for various tasks like question answering, content creation, and coding. "It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and brings back something finished — inside the documents, the inbox, and the developer environments you already work in," Kurian said. "It chooses the best model for the job, has built-in cost controls, and most importantly, has the security, administration, and governance required by your company." Kurian's actual remarks at the event were more succinct. "Today, Gemini became an agent," he said. "You give it objectives, not just instructions. It plans the work, uses custom skills and tools, connects to your systems and brings back something finished." You might wonder what role you play in all this as a Google Enterprise customer, when Gemini is planning, executing, and delivering. There's always Minesweeper and hunting for a job that involves physical labor and human dignity. Sundai Pichai, CEO of Google parent Alphabet, opened the Google Cloud event with the Recitation of Self-Reported Statistics, a common ritual in the technocratic liturgy. "Enterprise adoption is moving faster than most people realize," he said. "Nearly 80 percent of Google Cloud customers are using our AI products. And they are not just using it, they're using it intensely. Nearly 500 enterprise customers have each processed over 1 trillion tokens on our platform in the last year." Pichai took time to praise Google's latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, noting that it outperforms rival models Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark with a score of 77.9 percent. And within Google, he said, Gemini 4 Argon has reduced post-submit code rollbacks by 30 percent while increasing agentic code submissions from employees by 35 percent. Kurian then continued the customer success report by citing various claimed productivity gains from Google Cloud customers. Japanese telecom biz NTT Docomo, he said, has saved 450,000 hours annually using data agents. Your mileage may vary. But Kurian's emphasis on the solipsism of Gemini isn't entirely accurate. Gemini is unified in theory. It works within Gmail, Dive, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Chat, and Calendar as a single surface. It can be accessed across iOS, Android, Windows, and Mac desktops, not to mention third-party applications where enabled or during headless operations. It resides in Google Cloud so it retains contextual info. But no agent is an island. Just like the stellar twins for which it's named, Gemini has more than one moving part. "It can dynamically create a roster of sub-agents — temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity — to tackle multi-step tasks," said Kurian, perhaps overestimating the appeal of naming spawned processes. And the Gemini agent is distinct from the various models it may call upon, even if one of those might be Gemini 4 Argon. "It runs each job on the model that fits best — orchestrating across our Gemini family of models and Claude models from Anthropic today, and other leading private and open models in the future — to deliver optimal quality and lower your costs," Kurian explained. During the event, Kurian highlighted how Gemini inherits existing enterprise controls. "Every Gemini agent has an identity of its own, separate from your identity," he said. "Your policies reach it the very same way they reach your people: set the policies once, apply them everywhere rather than agency by agent. You set its budget before it starts and that budget covers the whole cost of the work." That's the promise, but of course the very existence of enterprise cost control mechanisms suggests costs can get out of hand. It was only two months ago that Google introduced flexible billing and cost controls for agents. Managing AI spending, however, remains an unsolved problem. As noted by the Wall Street Journal recently, "Spending on AI Is Becoming Almost Impossible for Businesses to Budget." Back in July, AI cost management company Coworker AI observed there were two Gemini Enterprise products that could easily be confused. Now we're told there's just one. Enjoy it while it lasts. ®

events.title: NASA taps DoE to help it build nuclear space reactors
events.summary: NASA and the Department of Energy have agreed to expand their collaboration on the space agency's nuclear ambitions, as administrator Jared Isaacman pushes ahead with a tight deadline to launch a fission-powered spacecraft to Mars. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’” Isaacman said at a signing ceremony where he and Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed a joint memorandum of understanding. The MOU, the full text of which doesn’t appear to have been published, establishes a framework for collaboration on space nuclear technology. Per NASA, the agreement “unites both agencies” in pursuing its objectives, with work to include research and fuel production, testing, launch integration, and operations. “Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before,” Isaacman added. “The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-poweuing NASA’s objred spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.” NASA has been making big plans to launch nuclear reactors into space since earlier this year when the agency paused work on the orbital Lunar Gateway station in favor of a base on the Moon’s surface. Those plans include a nuclear reactor to power said base, which NASA said on Thursday it intends to have ready for launch by 2030, giving the agency precious little time to meet such an ambitious goal. NASA has provided little evidence the initiative is on track, aside from noting in Thursday's announcement that it is “making steady progress” on Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), the unit it wants to use to power its Moon base. Before then, however, NASA faces an even tighter deadline for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1), which it intends to use to power a nuclear-propelled spacecraft scheduled to launch in December 2028. That’s just over two years away, mind you, and NASA has provided little public evidence of progress on the spacecraft, which it has dubbed "Freedom." NASA provided details [PDF] for SR-1 back in March when it paused work on the Lunar Gateway, describing the spacecraft as being mostly constructed from a repurposed spacecraft bus that NASA had almost completed for a previous project. The reactor would produce more than 20 kilowatts of electricity to power Freedom's electric thrusters on its journey to Mars, where it would deliver three Ingenuity-class helicopters to survey potential future human landing sites. Whether that’ll happen on any sort of timeline that resembles the current one is anyone’s guess, but let’s face it: NASA doesn’t exactly have a great track record for getting things done on time. The Government Accountability Office has been watching NASA’s lunar return ambitions for years, and has been noting for nearly a decade that its timelines were more fantasy than reality. In the past couple of years, the GAO has noted that existing NASA timelines were tight enough that any one mishap could push them back considerably, and massive workforce reductions under the second Trump administration haven’t helped matters. The Artemis missions to return humans to the Moon have also suffered a few hitches. Artemis I and Artemis II faced multiple delays, and NASA has since changed Artemis III's objectives, turning the planned 2027 lunar landing into a demonstration mission in low Earth orbit, in part to address concerns about the readiness of lunar landing systems, including SpaceX's Starship. We need not remind anyone of the saga of Boeing's calamity capsule. Who is going to launch that nuclear reactor in just over two years' time, and will NASA be able to land humans reliably on the Moon's surface by then? We checked in with NASA to get some assurances things were actually on pace, but didn’t hear back. ®

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Regional audiences facing a range of impacts from loss of Network 10 Rosy Smith says it is unfair people in regional areas are losing terrestrial TV channels. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Regional audiences in parts of SA and NSW have mixed reactions to hearing that they will lose Network 10 channels. An expert says advertisers are spending online instead of on broadcast TV, creating an uncertain future. The channels are expected to go off air at midnight. An expert says it would be cheaper for television networks to buy Australians a smart TV with streaming capability than continue to broadcast terrestrial television. WIN Network has announced it will cease broadcasting Network 10 channels, including 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy, in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area markets, after the two networks failed to reach a new broadcast deal . WIN said it was providing the service in these markets was no longer viable, something that reflected "the realities of regional broadcasting". Network 10 says people can still stream its channels online. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) University of Sydney professor of digital communication and culture Terry Flew said TV licences used to be considered "licences to print money", but streaming had up-ended the model. "Traditional broadcasters around Australia and around the world are feeling the pinch," he said. "The cost of delivering the terrestrial service is now greater than the returns that are coming from the advertising share, and that is impacting on regional areas." Network 10 said audiences could continue to access its content online and via its app. WIN Network says the infrastructure costs of maintaining regional terrestrial TV are high. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) Professor Flew said commercial broadcasters had already seen about 20-30 per cent of their audience move to streaming platforms. He said audiences would need to adapt to the changing landscape. Terry Flew says the economics of broadcast TV have changed significantly. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) "You would then need to connect up all those homes with a modem, and people would need to become familiar with how to use the television in a different way. "There may be an opportunity for local or state government to get involved in providing services in that way." For some, the decision will not have much of an impact on how they consume media. Limestone Coast resident Talie Teakle, 54, said she had not had an aerial connected to her TV for about 17 years. Mount Gambier's Talie Teakle streams her shows, but worries about what losing terrestrial channels will mean for others. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) She said for many people, the flexibility of on-demand streaming was preferable to scheduled broadcasts. "Life is so busy, if I've got free time I want to be able to watch what I want, when I want to watch it," she said. "I don't want to be at the whim of a schedule where you're waiting for a weekly show to come on." Rosy Smith says she and other seniors will not move to streaming their shows. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) However, Mount Gambier's Rosy Smith said she was a regular free-to-air TV watcher, and it was an "absolute shame" to lose channels. She said the majority of people she had spoken to at the city's senior citizens' club would be impacted by the "unfair" decision. "There's a lot of people that don't want to go down that track," she said. "It's just another blow to the regional community, having had things and then it's taken away from you. events.title: An air-con firm building AI, a hygiene business going regional: How home-grown SMEs are turning decades of expertise into new revenue
events.summary: With guidance from Enterprise Singapore and SME Centres, these firms are packaging their know-how into AI tools, overseas ventures and services they can sell Innoflex founder and managing director Kelvin Gan (centre) is turning two decades of engineering know-how into digital tools that could open up new service and revenue opportunities. Twenty years ago, this home-grown firm was merely a five-man air-conditioning contractor. Today, Innoflex has close to 100 employees, takes on multimillion-dollar projects – and is developing its own digital and AI tools. Its ZEGGO CoolHub brings equipment records, maintenance history and fault reports onto one platform, while ZEGG-BOT, an AI-enabled assistant, helps technicians retrieve information and identify possible causes of faults using everyday language. It is a significant shift for the company, and reflects its ambition to turn two decades of engineering know-how into a new source of growth. The innovations were developed as a means to address a challenge that emerged as the company grew. As Innoflex took on larger and more complex projects, manual reporting, fragmented records and reliance on individual employees’ experience became increasingly difficult to manage. These projects included maintenance work across SBS Transit’s interchanges, transport hubs and depots; air-conditioning and ventilation works at SMRT stations; and servicing about 700 units across CapitaLand’s portfolio. That pushed the company to look beyond fixing internal inefficiencies and reconsider the role it wanted to play for customers. Innoflex founder and managing director Kelvin Gan says: “Instead of being a contractor, we want to be a solutions provider, using technology to solve our customers’ problems.” Technology offered a way to do that. But coming up with the idea was easier than putting it into practice. Innoflex initially envisioned its digital transformation as one large project, with multiple AI and digital functions developed simultaneously. Gan soon realised that this would demand substantial money and manpower – many a hurdle that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often face. To help SMEs navigate such challenges, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) works with trade associations and chambers to strengthen and build capabilities of business advisors at SME Centres, enabling them to provide more effective and personalised support for companies. Business advisors at these SME Centres work with companies to assess their needs and growth plans, and extend support in areas including capability development and internationalisation too. Such support would enable businesses to be connected with relevant expertise, partners and support programmes. “As a small and open economy, Singapore can stay relevant and competitive only if our businesses continue to build capabilities, innovate and internationalise. SMEs anchor growth and create good jobs, which is why strengthening them is key,” says Audrey Lok, executive director of Enterprise Experience at EnterpriseSG. “Through the trade associations and SME Centres, our partners amplify EnterpriseSG’s efforts by bringing industry expertise, trusted networks and on-the-ground insights to SMEs. This multiplier effect allows us to reach more businesses and deliver more targeted support, enabling our SMEs to stay competitive and seize opportunities for growth.” Building new capabilities for the next stage of growth For Innoflex, the way forward came after it approached the SME Centre at the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEC@ASME) in 2024. Business advisor Steven Wong helped Innoflex break down its plans into steps to better manage its digital transformation. This involved assessing what could realistically be executed and implemented, and also helped the company identify where to start. The first phase focused on digitalising analogue data and signals, human servicing procedures and error codings. Phase 2, which is now under way, involves merging all digital data onto one platform. At Civil Service Club @ Tessensohn, Innoflex’s digital tools help facility teams monitor equipment, spot faults earlier and plan maintenance more efficiently. Innoflex’s head of sustainability Dr Ng Kong Jee, who worked closely with Wong, says: “Because of Steven’s advice, we managed to get Phase 1 working and already implemented on site, and now we’re on Phase 2.” EnterpriseSG’s Enterprise Development Grant (now streamlined into the EDGE Grant) also supported the company in engaging technology partners, organising its operational data and testing the system in practice. What started as a solution to Innoflex’s own operational challenges could eventually become a new source of revenue. Managing director Gan wants to offer services such as energy optimisation and predictive maintenance throughout a building’s operations, and eventually take these solutions to regional markets.

events.title: Singapore’s cheque cut-off: Why this property player is switching to e-payments now
events.summary: With banks set to stop processing Singapore dollar corporate cheques from Jan 1, 2027, City Developments Limited has adopted the electronic deferred payment option that has made collections faster and more reliable CDL’s early adoption of e-payment methods like EDP+ has made payment collection for its property sales faster. Buying a property in Singapore has traditionally meant homebuyers writing physical cheques, while developers manually verify and match each one against the sale – a slow, paper-heavy process on both sides. City Developments Limited (CDL) has moved away from it, and with much success. The developer’s e-payment journey began as early as 2018, when it introduced FAST (Fast and Secure Transfers) for homebuyers at The Tapestry development in Tampines. That early move set the stage for CDL to become one of the early adopters of the Electronic Deferred Payment (EDP and EDP+) system when it launched in 2025 – a transition that, as it turns out, was also well-timed. With e-payments growing more convenient and widespread across the economy in recent years, cheque usage has also seen a sharp decline. As such, all banks in Singapore will stop processing Singapore dollar-denominated corporate cheques from Jan 1, 2027. Ahead of that deadline, businesses and consumers here are being encouraged to switch to e-payment alternatives such as EDP and EDP+. Both let payers make deferred payments instead of using future-dated cheques, for instance, to fulfil contractual requirements such as buying a home for individuals or making supplier payments for businesses. The two solutions were introduced to give individuals and businesses the option of making deferred payments with notifications to recipients, complementing existing options such as PayNow, GIRO (General Interbank Recurring Order), FAST and MEPS+ (MAS Electronic Payment System). For CDL, the shift to the latest e-payments has already created a win-win for the company, its clients and partner banks. The developer now uses EDP+ for sales bookings and progressive payments on its property transactions. “EDP+ provides a sustainable, more efficient alternative to cheques, which have traditionally been used for property sales collections,” says CDL’s group general manager Chia Ngiang Hong. “It improves payment collection, reduces the manual administrative effort associated with cheque handling, while enhancing payment tracking and reconciliation.” EDP vs EDP+: What is the difference? EDP and EDP+ are two e-payment solutions introduced on July 28, 2025, that let businesses and individuals make deferred payments in place of cheques. They complement existing options such as PayNow, FAST, GIRO and MEPS+. The key difference between the two lies in when funds are deducted from the payer’s account. EDP: Funds are deducted from the payer’s account only when the payee requests payment, that is, upon presentment of the EDP. EDP+: Funds are deducted immediately from the payer’s account upon issuance of the EDP+, ensuring the amount cannot be used for other transactions. This reduces the risk of non-payment due to insufficient funds in the payer’s account, providing greater assurance to payees as compared to EDP. The challenges and benefits of switching to EDP+ CDL’s move to EDP+ builds on its digital payment journey that began in 2018. Chia called it a “natural progression”. By working closely with its banking partners, CDL was able to align operational processes for successful implementation. One key challenge was adapting to the different ways banks process incoming EDP+ payments. As collections must comply with CDL’s existing banking controls and mandate requirements, the company collaborated with its banking partners to ensure the smooth collection of funds while maintaining appropriate governance and oversight. Homebuyers can opt for e-payments via EDP+ for Lucerne Grand, CDL’s new launch at Lakeside Drive. That groundwork paid off in three ways. The first is lower risk with less hassle. Because EDP+ funds are deducted and set aside upon issuance, CDL gets greater assurance of payment, reducing the risk of insufficient funds and unsuccessful collections – while also saving the time and effort of having to chase clients for replacement payments. The second is easier tracking and matching. With payment details captured electronically, CDL can more easily identify who made a payment and match it to the correct transaction, improving the accuracy of its bank reconciliation and giving the finance team better visibility and control over incoming payments. EDP+’s presentment feature, accessed through the bank’s digital banking platform, enables CDL’s finance team to receive incoming EDP+ payments while providing clear visibility of the payer, payment amount and payment purpose. The third benefit reaches beyond the balance sheet: moving away from paper cheques complements CDL’s sustainability and digitalisation goals.

events.title: Coca-Cola looks to sell Costa Coffee
events.summary: The Scoop Coca-Cola is seeking to unwind its $5 billion acquisition of a British coffeehouse, months after a sales process faltered earlier this year. The American beverage conglomerate is once again exploring a sale of Costa Coffee, according to people familiar with the matter. Coca-Cola acquired Costa for $5.1 billion in 2018 , but has struggled to grow the business meaningfully. It explored selling Costa in late 2025, before calling off the sales process earlier this year after a tepid response from private-equity bidders, the Financial Times reported in January . At least one strategic acquirer mulled what a deal for Costa would look like before passing due to valuation and strategic issues, one of the people said. It couldn’t be determined what price Coca-Cola might seek for the asset were it to market it more actively again. Coca-Cola’s on-again, off-again efforts to sell Costa mean it might again choose to wait. Coca-Cola did not return a request for comment. Know More Costa Coffee has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland and employs 20,000 people. The coffee chain is targeting younger consumers by adding more iced drinks and matcha to its menus. Coca-Cola bought Costa from British hospitality company Whitbread. The business lost nearly £20 million in 2023 and 2024 combined. Costa reopened a number of its revamped high street outlets in early 2026, around the same time as Coca-Cola reportedly abandoned its plans to sell the chain. Costa’s chief executive Philippe Schillee told the Guardian that the company’s new Hertfordshire headquarters, which will open in January 2027 with capacity for 300 workers, “really signals our confidence in the business.”

events.title: She Designed Meta’s New AI Logo. Then Came the Hate
events.summary: Bay Area lettering artist Jessica Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse , it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me. Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.” The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision: “For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote . She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help. “Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.” Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances. Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal. We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole. This interview has been edited for clarity and length. Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job? Jesscia Hische : The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year. So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle. What were you hired to do, specifically? I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.” The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M. It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks. What did the team tell you they wanted to change? They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight. Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.” How much do you get paid for a project like this? I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.
