events.title: The five takes that will define this midterm campaign
events.summary: David’s view Prick up your ears, and you can hear it — the sound of many different kinds of Democrats grabbing credit for midterm victories that aren’t official yet. There’s Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, assessing that when (not if) Abdul El-Sayed wins his Senate race in Michigan, the left will “break open the entire political calculus in America” — i.e., that progressives like them can win the Midwest. There’s Pete Buttigieg, making sure we know how many states he’s campaigned in (37) and how many candidates he’d endorsed (more than 100). At this time in any campaign cycle, groups, candidates, and strategists pepper reporters with early claims that they were right. The election, they say, will be a referendum on issue, a validation of spending strategy, proof that ideas moved votes. These takes aren’t immaculate. I’ve never deleted the October 2017 email from a strategist who was ready to explain why Ralph Northam lost the election for governor of Virginia. In fact, Northam won easily, and that strategist got strategically quiet. As preposterous as it is, though, the pre-spin cycle matters, because anyone not ready to contextualize what happened to their benefit will lose face. It mattered in 2020, when centrist Democrats burst out to blame “defund the police” activists for their party underperforming the final polls. It mattered after President Donald Trump’s win in 2024, when Sen. Bernie Sanders instantly blamed defeat on the party having “abandoned the working class.” That quick analysis shaped the conversation. Populism won. This is the Sanders project — progressives’ entire project, really. The goal of recruiting swing-seat populists and getting them through primaries was to prove, as Ocasio-Cortez said, that their kind can win anywhere, which should matter for 2028. This theory may be tough to sell. One of its proof points was supposed to be Maine, where Graham Platner humiliated the party establishment, then himself. Progressives won the insta-caucus that replaced him, nominating Troy Jackson to face GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and Sanders will campaign for Jackson this weekend after some internal grumbling about whether consultants not approved by the left were ruining his campaign. Michigan’s the ballgame now. An El-Sayed win would, for progressives, be the story of the midterms. Most of the movement’s primary victories came in safe seats, but to take control of the 2028 story, they want to be talking about El-Sayed winning, Will Lawrence flipping back a mid-Michigan district, and Randy Villegas unseating Rep. David Valadao in California. They want to say that hand-wringing moderates were wrong, and pure populism can flip or hold swing seats. But if El-Sayed becomes the first Democrat to lose a Michigan Senate seat this century, progressives will enter 2028 with empty hands. Gerrymandering didn’t matter . This will be the biggest conclusion if Republicans don’t hold the House. And they’re already conceding partial defeat. “We’re not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told Axios this week. Indeed, Democrats are competing for most of the seats that Republicans tried to lift beyond their reach z– three in Texas, three in Florida, one in North Carolina, one in Ohio, one in Alabama, and as of this week, one in Tennessee. When Trump first urged Texas to eliminate five Democratic districts, the most ambitious response was that Democrats could moderate and compete for them anyway. That did happen. Four of the Democrats whose seats turned redder voted with Republicans on a recent transgender health proposal; a fifth, Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is running the most critical ads about “transgender ideology” of any Democratic incumbent. While it might not decide who controls the House, gerrymandering did matter. It won’t have mattered enough if most of the remapped districts don’t flip. Anti-trans politics stopped working. This is a complicated topic to spin; both LGBTQ rights groups and more cautious Democratic strategists are trying to set themselves up for it. “I hope that the headline coming out of November 4 is that equality voters won and anti-trans ads lost,” Kelly Robinson, the president of the Human Rights Campaign, told reporters on Monday. Robinson wants that to be proven by victories for candidates who followed her group’s playbook, of responding to GOP attacks on a candidate’s gender voting record by answering them and pivoting. A small group of Democrats, like Kaptur, have used the language that activists find offensive; the HRC is ready to point to those defeats as evidence that using a conservative frame won’t win votes. [Insert 2028 Candidate] was the strongest surrogate. There’ll be fast post-midterm calculations of which Democrats and Republicans endorsed, and campaigned for, the most winners in congressional races. The model for taking a scorecard into a presidential primary comes from Richard Nixon, who refurbished his reputation by campaigning across the country for Republicans in 1966 and got some credit for a good GOP year. But every would-be president has approached this differently. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., has endorsed scores of candidates, some of them extreme longshots. He’s not going for a batting average; he’s trying to show people that his politics, and the attention he got by releasing the Epstein files, give him broad appeal. Buttigieg has gotten the word out that he can draw crowds in Republican districts, and that the candidates are happy to have him. So has Sen. Mark Kelly; he doesn’t have Buttigieg’s reach but he’s made it known that Democrats in the toughest seats are happy to campaign with the astronaut from a swing state. And isn’t it convenient that Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the Democratic Governors Association, has to keep going back to Nevada? events.title: Is ‘abundance’ really dead?
events.summary: The News Whatever happened to “ abundance ,” the pro-growth movement that many Democrats were going to hitch a ride on this election cycle? They did embrace its ideas. They just don’t use the “a-word” that much. In ads and across swing districts, Democrats are running on having “built more affordable housing,” supported “all-of-the-above energy,” and sliced through “bureaucracy and red tape” without mentioning “abundance” at all. Back home, some are talking about the permitting reform bill they’re trying to push through Congress, and the housing bill they already did. “Resource development is about our survival,” former Rep. Mary Peltola says in one of her ads, highlighting how she defied climate activists to support Alaska’s Willow oil-drilling project.This year, after progressive activists accused the loose “abundance” movement, which favors targeted deregulation to spur growth, of trying to steer Democrats away from populism, groups working with local electeds forged ahead armed with polling showing how their ideas fit into the “affordability” framework that most candidate were running on. “That early criticism of ‘abundance’ being a flash in the pan was a bad faith argument from people worried about what a powerful argument it was,” said Derek Kaufman, the founder and CEO of Inclusive Abundance. “I look at New York, where I live, where you have Gov. [Kathy] Hochul Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani changing environmental reviews for urban infill; you have Mamdani doing his version of DOGE, which he called COGE.” In the Los Angeles mayoral race, Kaufman continued, “the more progressive-coded candidate is all about building housing to bring down costs.” Know More The criticism of the “abundance” concept got a wide airing in 2025. Last spring, after Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s “Abundance” hit the New York Times bestseller list, progressives attacked it as a dangerous off-ramp from populism — which could actually win elections.Skeptics commissioned their own polls to argue that “abundance” was a dead end. Last spring, Demand Progress tested a version of an anti-bureaucracy “abundance” message against a “populist” message that saw the latter winning out. Four months later, Groundwork Action released data that found “excessive bureaucracy,” while a concern for some voters, “ranks far behind other concerns and tackling it does not strike voters as a direct response to the problem of affordability.” To critics, the absence of the word “abundance” on the campaign trail is a sign of victory. Those sympathetic to the movement argue that’s not the case — and that there was never a binary choice at hand between progressive ideology and the ideas abundance advocates stand for. “I don’t use the word ‘abundance’ when I’m campaigning,” said Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., “but I say all the time that when people think that the system is rigged against them, they’re right. It is. And a lot of the reason is what we’ve layered into government, where really well-intended ideas have the opposite effect.” David’s view Democrats are feeling very good about next month’s elections, and the jockeying is already underway about which faction made it happen. Progressives hope to power a Democratic victory in the House that sees them pick up more seats — and influence — in the next Congress. When “abundance” critics went after the movement, they were trying to win the argument then as well as the argument of the future. They saw a coalition of techies and liberals who were trying to prevent what they wanted: A move to the left and away from deep-pocketed donors. They view “abundists” taking credit for Mamdani’s victory as opportunists trying to deny democratic socialists a major governing success. But the non-socialists have made a modicum of impact, even if “abundance” has faded from Democrats’ lexicon. Thompson got Mamdani to agree with some of the “abundance” principles, and both agreed that the left can’t credibly compete with the new right if people believe progressive governments are tied down by interest groups and can’t build. The argument continues. Room for Disagreement David Segal, whose group Demand Progress commissioned the first abundance-skeptical poll, argued that the abundance movement is all but dead. “Having a primary message that is populist and then having a couple of lines about zoning or permitting reform is ‘offering a sop to abundists,’” he said. “It’s not ‘running on abundance.’ And it’s totally fine to do that, but it’s just not what Abundance (™) was arguing for when they rolled out their project.” Notable In Politico, Riley Rogerson broke news of another “abundance”-pilled caucus in the House looking for a way to fund more big projects.

events.title: Why France is a warning sign for the markets
events.summary: The good news about the epic shifts in global bond markets is that they mostly reflect economic fundamentals, not the kinds of panicky swings seen in a crisis. The bad news is that there's a risk the disruptions metastasize into a broader crisis in an era of fractured politics across major democracies. The big picture: Turmoil in the streets this week in France is the latest sign of hazards that await elected leaders who try to address yawning fiscal deficits head-on. They are squeezed between voters who want to maintain public benefit levels and tax levels and a bond market that is resetting long-term interest rates higher — meaning that carrying on with wide deficits will come at a greater and greater cost to service debt. That's why even what has been a relatively orderly repricing so far carries risks that are bigger than just high mortgage or corporate borrowing rates. Driving the news: The relentless upward march of bond yields continued Wednesday morning. The French 10-year yield soared 0.18 percentage point, to 4.93%. French yields are also surging relative to other countries that use the euro, especially Germany — the kind of fragmentation seen in the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s that originated in Greece . But France is not alone. U.K. 10-year yields are up 0.12 point, to 5.49%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is up 0.08 point Wednesday morning, reaching 5.36%, the highest since 2002. Reality check: These are massive moves in markets that form the bedrock of global financial markets. And yet they don't appear to be driven by the kind of crisis dynamics and forced selling that fueled bond market volatility in the 2008 crisis, the 2014 Treasury flash crash and the March 2020 pandemic. Rather, they've been driven by bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and deficit-running sovereign governments, exacerbated by surging energy prices that increase inflation risk. What they're saying: "When you look at outright yield levels and/or spreads, a lot of this is still quite rational, and within the realm of what fair valuation should be, just given where nominal growth is and where we are in the cycle," Kunal Shah, the co-CEO of Goldman Sachs International, tells Axios. "At this point, I still wouldn't say that we're anywhere close to the point of this being a broad financial stability risk or issue," says Shah, who is also co-head of fixed income, currency and commodities. "What policymakers in Europe have shown us, though, is that when there's broader issues on contagion and/or disorderly functioning markets, that's when they can be quick to respond." "Whilst the move in spreads has been very quick and sharp, in the broader context, we're still nowhere close to where we had got to in that previous European crisis," he says. "Financial conditions are tightening, but it's still not, I'd say, flashing red to the point that you need a backstop from the policymakers." Yes, but: The European Central Bank has more powerful tools than it did in 2010 to address imbalances between European countries, and has shown willingness to use them. But it can't do much about the fundamentals of governments spending consistently far more than they raise in taxes. And the global nature of the yield surge shows the common fiscal challenge across major economies. State of play: In France, there have been violent clashes with police as teachers and students protest proposed wage freezes and school funding cuts. In the U.K., a central political dispute is over the future of the "triple lock" pension adjustment mechanism, which all but guarantees pension costs will grow faster than the overall economy. The U.S. Social Security trust fund is on track to be exhausted in 2032 . The rate adjustment of the last several weeks will increase already-onerous debt service costs for all advanced countries. Of note: Those forces can create destabilizing effects for business even apart from the impact on rates. Shah, for example, says that U.K. governments lurching from budget to budget has made it hard for businesses making long-term decisions. "I hope that at some point we'll be able to break out of this cycle, because it does stifle confidence and it just makes planning for the long term very hard," Shah says.

events.title: Unions look beyond their rolls to build a new movement
events.summary: The Scoop Every Thursday afternoon, a cadre of state AFL-CIO leaders meets on Zoom to advance a shared project: the “Contract with Working Americans,” a populist economic platform they devised independently of the national AFL-CIO. These calls are a new organizing tactic for labor, which historically leads top down from Washington, and the goal is new, too: to mobilize not only workers who belong to unions, but the many more American workers who do not. “We’re trying to connect two segments of a group that, quite frankly, should be naturally aligned, but just haven’t,” said Derrick Osobase, vice president of Communications Workers of America District 6, which covers Texas. “We are actively talking to working-class people who are not affiliated with the union, and wrapping them into an agenda that they have said will make their lives different.” The idea for the “contract” was born of a paradox: Union membership has declined from 20% of all workers in 1983 to 10% last year, even as union popularity hovers at 90-year highs. Seventy-one percent of US adults approve of unions, according to Gallup, including 52% of Republicans. The widening gap between those figures is where organizers see an opportunity. “For years the labor movement, for understandable reasons, has fought for a narrower set of issues,” said Francis Eanes, executive director of the Maine Labor Climate Council. “But I think it’s made it easy for some folks to say we’re just another special interest out there fighting for our own.” Skeptics of labor, he said, say a union is “a private welfare state that provides benefits to its members and no one else. I think it’s an unfair characterization, but it’s not entirely unfair.” The Gallup numbers suggest Americans of different political shades seem to be concluding that private welfare states aren’t such a bad idea. In a moment of declining trust in Congress, political parties, the media and many other institutions, labor activists believe a union-led movement whose stated aim is to agitate for the benefit of all workers could have real juice in setting a new national agenda as audacious as Newt Gingrich’s 1994 “ Contract with America ,” which helped produce a sweeping congressional majority for Republicans that year. “Both political parties are wildly unpopular. Unions are more popular than ever,” said Matt Schlobohm, executive director of the Maine AFL-CIO. “It is really important that we — working people, the labor movement — define and put out an agenda and demand it. Or somebody else will define it for us, and it’ll be culture wars, or it’ll be some mealy-mouth opportunity agenda.” The main tenets of the “Contract with Working Americans” were born out of a series of canvassing surveys led by state AFL-CIOs and affiliates. But there is no single document; iterations of it vary somewhat from state to state, to account for local trades and industries. (The national AFL-CIO did not respond to a request for comment.) The “contract” framework was inspired by negotiated union contracts and is meant to establish policy commitments from candidates in exchange for the movement’s support. All versions include a set of economic priorities: Signatories must support lowering prescription drug costs by expanding the government’s power to negotiate directly with companies, expanding healthcare coverage, capping childcare costs, bringing down the price of gas, and raising the minimum wage. The contracts adopt a populist tone throughout. They include shared language demanding a congressional stock trading ban and a ban on lobbying by elected officials after leaving office; a tax on billionaires; and, in a time of rising AI anxiety, a ban on AI surveillance, to prevent “robots deciding your paycheck, hiring and firing you, or monitoring your work.” The language does not include identity- or criminal justice-specific provisions, and largely steers clear of climate topics. Several candidates with national profiles have signed on to versions of the contract so far this cycle, including in Texas, where Democrats hope that Senate nominee James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa could make the state ground zero for a Blue Wave next month. Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, delivered a public “ Pledge to Working Mainers ” adopting the demands in Maine’s contract. Independent Alaska candidate Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and teacher challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich, told Semafor he supports the ideas in the contract, though there isn’t an Alaska-specific version of the contract to sign. “This is about an agenda that delivers for the hardworking people of this country, by lowering costs, making sure hardworking people get the value of their hard work, and building a system where billionaires and big corporations play by the same rules we do,” Hill said in a statement. Another state AFL-CIO, and its endorsed candidate for statewide office, have agreed to sign on as soon as this week, and more are circling. No Republicans have backed one of these contracts. Organizers in North Carolina and Maine said that the campaigns for Republican Michael Whatley and Sen. Susan Collins had not responded to their outreach. Still, organizers said they see progress. In interviews, most said they believe labor has long been too aligned with the Democratic Party, leading to a kind of “mutual malaise,” in the words of North Carolina AFL-CIO President Braxton Winston. Eanes touted the contract’s potential to inject what he saw a bit of virtuous transactionalism back into the democratic process by energizing votes around specific policy demands, building back a kind of feedback loop that unions have down to a science. “They have committed. We’re going to hold them to the fact that this contract has to be an essential part of how they govern,” said Osobase of Hinojosa and Talarico, though he declined to say whether that could entail supporting primary challengers in the future if either candidate gets elected and fails to deliver. Know More State AFL-CIOs and affiliates conducted thousands of surveys of union members and non-union workers over 2024 and 2025, gleaning insights that were then distilled down to the bullet points that appear in the contracts. The Maine, North Carolina, and Texas AFL-CIOs and their affiliates have knocked hundreds of thousands of doors already this cycle, presenting voters with the contract and where the candidates stand. “This project for us is about reviving the best of the labor movement,” Eanes said. “If you go over the arc of the last 200 years, we win more when we’re fighting for everyone: When the demands are broader, when the demands speak to the needs of all working people, that’s where we have the most power and resonance, and frankly, at a moment when most people don’t trust any institution, they still see organized labor as something that can be trusted.” The contract’s most striking divergence from progressive ideological c

events.title: Raskin seeks to preserve Trump's D.C. "propaganda" in Smithsonian
events.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) introduced legislation Wednesday that would direct the Smithsonian to preserve and display artifacts he said reflect the rise of "governmental propaganda" under President Trump . Why it matters: The bill will almost certainly fail in a Republican-controlled Congress. But it could preview how Democrats would scrutinize the president's use of taxpayer dollars to promote his image if they regain control in November. Trump's drive to remake D.C.'s physical and cultural landscape in his image can be seen in banners bearing his face on government buildings and attempts to rebrand institutions with his name . The administration also unveiled a plan last month to post warnings accusing Smithsonian leaders of pushing "personal, radical ideologies." Driving the news: Raskin's bill directs the secretary of the Smithsonian to collect and display Trump's sprawling portraits hung outside of federal agencies at the Museum of American History. It also calls for preserving signage or "artifacts" related to Trump's planned warning signs accusing the museum of "Ideological Capture." The proposed new exhibit would also include narratives from Americans "who resisted and opposed the rise in authoritarianism." It also calls for signage stating, in part, "Donald Trump ordered the installation of these signs without any Congressional authorization as required by the Constitution." What they're saying: " Unlike President Trump's project of censoring, whitewashing and fictionalizing American history, my legislation will forever preserve his manifestations of authoritarian narcissism and his propagandistic assault on American history and American democracy," Raskin said in a statement. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The Smithsonian has been caught in the crosshairs of the president's D.C. residency and his government-wide DEI purge that has targeted so-called "woke ideology." Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his retirement after more than three decades at the world's largest museum, education and research complex. events.title: Hyperscalers won't stop spending until shareholders make them
events.summary: Liz’s view The bull market of the early 2010s was called the most hated rally in history. This one may be a close second. Back then, investors underestimated the power and determination of the Federal Reserve to prop up a flagging economy. Flatlining corporate earnings, European debt bombs, and runaway government spending disappeared into a sea of free money. Today’s problem is hyperscalers spending themselves into oblivion, spreading inflation well beyond Silicon Valley and obscuring problems nearly everywhere else. The S&P 500 hit another record yesterday, even as oil stays trapped in the Gulf and Europe tilts toward another debt crisis. The rally is driven by just a handful of AI companies. Some of them have the earnings to back it up — Goldman Sachs expects Nvidia and Micron alone to account for a third of the S&P 500’s earnings growth in the current quarter — but the return on their investments is far from certain, and far from now. Alan Greenspan’s declaration that the Fed can’t deflate a bubble without wrecking the economy is far from economic canon , but it’s holding up in the AI era. Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella aren’t slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and won’t stop spending until their shareholders make them. Their shareholders are very happy. You see the problem. Notable “Increasingly, the market is running on one engine,” The Wall Street Journal wrote of the AI boom, while “ just about everything else is going down .”

events.title: New Skydance CEO Kreiz will be Ellison’s enforcer
events.summary: One thing was clear on Skydance’s first day of life: Beneath David Ellison’s velvet glove is Ynon Kreiz’s iron fist. To earn his $40-odd million payout to help run the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., Kreiz will have to serve as a Tom Wambsgans-ian pain sponge — the executor and cost-cutter behind Ellison’s lofty vision boards. After Ellison told Skydance’s assembled employees at a town-hall meeting Tuesday that “there is something magical about” movie-making, Kreiz stated plainly “ultimately, our success will be determined by performance,” according to prepared remarks viewed by Semafor. Investors are warily eying Skydance’s freshly downgraded debt , and layoffs are coming. There’s only so far Hollywood and Washington connections can take Ellison before the reality of managing a debt-laden media giant forces him to prove he can actually run one. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Bessent's reassurances fall flat for investors
events.summary: Scott Bessent isn’t worried. The market is. The US Treasury secretary has been trying to reassure investors that economic growth and budget restraint can put the US government’s financial house in order. But he’s 0-for-3 on his 3-3-3 plan of increasing oil production, growing the economy, and cutting the deficit. His bond buyback program landed as a curious half-step — big enough to suggest concern but too small to make a difference. Tempers are flaring, WSJ reports . Cracks are showing in the riskiest corners of the credit markets, always the first to surface confidence gaps. Take the loan market, where the amount of deeply distressed loans (those made to low-rated companies trading at 60 cents on the dollar or less) has ballooned to a level not seen since March 2020, as JPMorgan strategists pointed out this week. The biggest concentration of these highly distressed loans, of course, is in the technology sector, where SaaSpocalypse fears have eased among stock investors but not sandbag-packing credit investors. Rising global bond yields and Fed tightening haven’t helped. If Bessent “is the house now,” investors are calling his bluff. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: SpaceX looks to $40 billion debt raise to buy chips
events.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is the in-betweener in the AI capex wars. SpaceX’s reported $40 billion debt raise to buy Nvidia chips shows it is stuck between mature tech giants like Google and Meta and startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose private status tends to forgive their inability to pay their own bills . SpaceX carries five times more debt than Alphabet, and three times more debt than Meta, relative to their respective profits, and while money from Starlink helps prop up SpaceX’s cash-guzzling rocket business, it isn’t nearly the cash cow that rivals’ ad businesses are. It needs to borrow because it’s spending more on AI than it’s taking in from the rest of its businesses. By going public in June, SpaceX locked itself out of the raise-and-pray venture capital world. But its stock price’s sideways lurch since then makes it unattractive to issue new shares to pay for its growing AI tab. Its BBB credit rating is two notches below Meta and Alphabet, and a tougher sell with blue-chip bond funds; enter Apollo, which has a pot of money to match seemingly every risk out there ( including cash-strapped governments! ). Oracle finds itself in a similar position. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Mixed outlook for energy expenditures this winter
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook We expect energy expenditures this winter to vary because of diverging trends in energy prices among fuels and regional variation in forecast temperatures. We expect that lower prices for natural gas and propane will drive decreases in expenditures this year for the half of U.S. households heating with those fuels. Higher prices for electricity and heating oil drive increased expenditures for households heating with those fuels in our forecast. Although we expect national average temperatures to be similar to last winter, our forecast assumes warmer temperatures in the Northeast, following a relatively cold winter last year, and much colder temperatures in the West, following an unusually warm winter last year. Temperatures in the Midwest and South are similar to last year. Homes that use heating oil as their main heating fuel—about 3% of U.S. homes, which are mostly in the Northeast—could see the largest increase in spending this year. We expect a 21% increase in spending on heating oil compared with last winter, driven by increasing global distillate prices. We forecast the price of heating oil will average 34% more this winter than last winter, but warmer forecast temperatures are expected to partly offset our forecast increase in prices. We expect the more than 40% of homes heating with electricity will experience a 4% increase in electricity bills on average. We expect energy expenditures will decrease on average by 9% in homes heating with natural gas and by 3% in those heating with propane. Distillate dynamics Global distillate fuel production, which includes heating oil production, has dropped because of reduced global refining activity. Lower production has caused rising international prices, driving up both the cost to import distillate to the United States and the demand for distillate exports from the United States. Through the first seven months of 2026, U.S. distillate exports increased 20% over the same period last year, with much of the increased volumes sent to Europe. With more costly U.S. imports and higher demand for U.S. exports, U.S. distillate fuel stocks are low heading into winter. We expect inventories will be about 11% below the five-year average in the fourth quarter of 2026. events.summary: This White Paper gives robotics researchers and engineers an overview of a new large-scale motion capture dataset built to close the data gap limiting humanoid robot learning. It also shows how policies trained on the dataset transfer to a real humanoid robot. What you will learn about: Why humanoid robot learning, a central problem in embodied AI and Physical AI, needs data that internet video and existing motion capture datasets cannot provide. How FrameNet , a linguistic framework for human action, can guide motion capture collection to systematically cover a broad range of whole-body motion. Why synchronized object trajectories and meshes make human-object interaction data useful for teaching robots real-world tasks such as carrying, pushing, and pulling. How reinforcement learning policies trained on this motion capture data improve with scale, and how sim-to-real transfer carries them onto a physical humanoid robot. events.title: ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests
events.summary: A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “ Rey ,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing , which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines . The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing. On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile , in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups. Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p . Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “ Umbreon ” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks. A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left. As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft , a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough. ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules. In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government. Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records. ‘REY’ MEANS KING, AS IN ROYAL According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities. Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks. In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight , a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion. “We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.” A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.” Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines , which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed. However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey , his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees. Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims. Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p. Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today. MURDER FOR HIRE? Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. events.summary: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism Hollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech. Netflix is no longer a lone disruptor: historic studio MGM is now the property of Amazon’s Jeff Bezos; David Ellison’s takeover of Paramount and subsequent Warner Bros merger was supported by his tech giant father; and Apple TV has acted as a patron for multiple film-maker passion projects. Everyone, including trendy auteur-factory A24, is tying themselves financially to AI. Item 2: Minutes of 17 March Legal Sub-Committee The minutes of the meeting of 17 March 2026 were approved. Item 3: ISDA Update – FX Definitions & Non-Deliverables (ISDA – Ann Battle and Jonathan Martin) The discussion focused on a comprehensive update on the 2026 FX Definitions, covering the transition from the 1998 definitions, key substantive changes, SWIFT implementation, and supporting materials for firms. Program Timeline and SWIFT Transition: The four-year program launched in 2024 is now in implementation phase, with a SWIFT change request submitted ahead of their June 4th deadline. SWIFT rulebook changes are expected over the summer and transition to the new FX Definitions in November 2027 (after which the 1998 definitions will cease to apply). Consolidation and Digital Publication: The 2026 FX Definitions create a single, fully digital and versioned framework that can be updated and maintained centrally, including matrix-based templates for non-deliverable transactions, simplifying operations and reducing reliance on master confirmations for vanilla trades. Key Substantive Changes: Introduction of three default disruption events, alignment of the calculation agent standard with 2021 rates definitions (including a good faith/commercially reasonable standard), and optional provisions such as calendar adjustment events. Business Day Framework and Automated Exercise: Streamlined and harmonised business day concept, plus a new fully automated exercise option for FX options based on published rates. Implementation Materials and Outreach: A suite of materials are available and forthcoming for firms, including the FX definitions brochure, an industry implementation roadmap, a plain English guide, annotated confirmation templates, and an optional master confirmation bridge agreement. The team is coordinating with the implementation steering committee and planning dealer outreach to clients, with educational webinars and FAQs to support the transition. Foreign Law Agreements and SWIFT Application: The group noted uncertainties regarding the application of the 2026 FX Definitions to non-English and non-New York law governed agreements, particularly in relation to SWIFT messaging and local banking associations. Discussions between ISDA and local banking associations are ongoing. Item 4: Competition Law Guidance Refresh Non material amendments have been made to the competition law guidance. Review and comments were invited from the group, particularly to the introductory paragraph and references to the Sub Committees. Item 5: Approval of Terms of Reference and Deputy Chair Appointment It was noted that most substantive changes to the subcommittee terms of reference relate to the operation of the legal subcommittee and the introduction of the deputy chair role. The group was invited to provide any final comments to the Secretariat. The Chair confirmed the appointment of the Deputy Chair (Tamsin Rolls) with no objections from the group. Item 6: Topics for discussion at Future Meetings The group considered revisiting legal issues relating to the use of AI in the FX markets, particularly its application in algorithmic trading and related competition law and market practices.

events.title: "The beginning of a new scientific paradigm": Zuckerberg's Biohub, U.S. and Google build virtual cell
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub is partnering with Google and the federal government in its ambitious effort to use AI for generating vast quantities of biological data that can predict how cells behave. Why it matters: The ultimate goal is an AI model that lets scientists test potential experiments virtually, helping them identify the most promising ones before spending the time and money to perform them in the lab. AI is capable of understanding proteins and other pieces of biology, but modeling an entire living cell is orders of magnitude more complex — and researchers don't yet have enough of the right data to do it. Driving the news: Biohub, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, Meta and a collection of scientific organizations are collaborating to create and standardize data for what Biohub calls a "universal virtual cell." The big picture: The goal is to use AI to explore many more scientific questions in biology virtually, allowing scientists to reserve expensive lab work for experiments most likely to teach them something important. "If we can put more and more reasoning and intelligence into every single question that we actually ask in the lab, the value of those empirical results will be far greater," Biohub head of science Alex Rives told Axios. Much of AI's recent progress has come from combining better algorithms, more computing power and enormous amounts of data. Biology presents an additional challenge: Much of the information AI needs doesn't exist yet and has to be painstakingly measured from the physical world. "We're at the beginning of a new scientific paradigm with AI," Rives said. Yes, but: Biology is harder than many other AI domains because researchers need what Rives calls "empirical AI" — models that learn from biological evidence and can accurately predict what happens in the physical world. "The big challenge in biology is to bridge that gap between compute and the digital world and the real physical world of biology and life," Rives said. "The way to do that is through data." Such models could eventually help scientists investigate fundamental questions such as how aging and regeneration work — or medical questions such as which molecular mechanisms are responsible for Alzheimer's disease. How it works: The first phase will create a broad map of cellular biology, gathering different kinds of information about cells and how they respond to changes. Further out, Rives envisions models that could examine an individual's disease and predict its molecular causes and the best way to intervene. The intrigue: The commercial partners will have one year of exclusive access to the data they develop before it is shared publicly. Rives said the temporary advantage is intended to give companies a reason to contribute money while still ensuring the resulting data becomes an open scientific resource. "We have to have some incentive for commercial players to be a part of this, and the embargo period creates that," Rives said. "But it's a one-year embargo. So what that means is that very rapidly, data becomes available broadly to scientific efforts." Zoom in: The effort involves $1.8 billion in funding, data, computing and measurement technology. DOE plans to invest more than $500 million over five years in biological measurement, modeling and computing, while NIH is bringing datasets and other resources resulting from more than $500 million in previous federal investment. Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta are collectively investing another $300 million, while Biohub previously committed $500 million to the effort. Flashback: When Biohub announced its initial $500 million effort in April, Rives told Axios one of the biggest unanswered questions was whether cellular biology would exhibit the same kind of "scaling laws" seen elsewhere in AI — with models becoming predictably better as they are trained on increasing amounts of data. What we're watching: Rives thinks researchers won't have to wait particularly long to find out whether the bet is working. Within a year of having the first large-scale dataset, he said, researchers should be able to train models, measure their capabilities and determine which kinds of additional biological data make them better. "It's worked in every field, and it works in biology too," Rives said, pointing to AI's progress in protein biology.

events.title: Mubadala's Solutions+ expects to double Dh1.5bn contribution to Abu Dhabi GDP
events.summary: Mubadala's business management services unit Solutions+ contributed about Dh1.5 billion ($408.4 million) to Abu Dhabi's economy in 2025 and expects this to double this year, its chief executive has said. The figure forms part of Mubadala's wider Dh45 billion portfolio contribution to the emirate's GDP. Solutions+ has been able to grow by 53 times since it was formed as Mubadala Business Management Services in 2014, Nasir Al Nabhani told The National on the sidelines of the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday. “We invested in people and technology, and we have grown significantly. We have healthy cash [flow and] healthy net profit, so we have a healthy organisation,” he told The National in an interview. The privately held company, which does not disclose its financials, has also been able to exceed its goal of becoming a billion-dollar company, which it first revealed in 2023 , as it accelerated its acquisitions strategy. The company grew by about 20 per cent in 2022, an achievement that was “beyond its targets”, Mr Al Nabhani previously said. Solutions+ is in the midst of a five-year growth plan that was introduced during its rebranding in 2023. During that span, it welcomed seven companies into its fold, with three more to be acquired “very soon”, he said. “All the acquisitions that we have done in the last three years, based on the [five-year] strategy, will give us also another 100 per cent of growth.” Solutions+ provides digital business services for sectors including business process outsourcing, finance, procurement, facilities management, and environmental, social and government. Initially, its services were dedicated to companies under Mubadala, the sovereign wealth fund of Abu Dhabi. Solutions+ has more than 50 government and enterprise clients, and its services have helped them save more than Dh300 million, according to its website. It has also developed Weave, a software-as-a-service solution designed to simplify HR and enterprise management. The company is also increasingly improving the use of AI on its services. Mr Al Nabhani said Solutions+ and its partners are testing new large language models, the underlying algorithm of generative AI. They are expected to introduce a new one by the first quarter of 2027, he added. At AI Everything, the company signed agreements with Tahaluf Al Emarat Technical Solutions to boost AI collaboration and Saal.ai to accelerate the adoption of enterprise data platform solutions. These are part of a broader strategy to grow Solutions+'s business locally and abroad, Mr Al Nabhani said. The company currently has a presence in countries including Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Pakistan, Tunisia and Uganda. “We are trying to explore what could be or what could add value to us and to our clients,” Mr Al Nabhani said. Meanwhile, Mubadala, whose $385 billion portfolio spans six continents across asset classes, also continues to build its AI portfolio. Last week, it signed an agreement with the US company Together AI to explore investment opportunities in AI infrastructure in the UAE.

events.title: Ethiopia renews push for Red sea access
events.summary: Ethiopia’s prime minister reignited the issue of sea access for his landlocked country, potentially further inflaming regional tensions amid renewed fighting in its northern Tigray region. After being sworn in for a second full term, Abiy Ahmed told parliament his government would work diligently to ensure Ethiopia had “an outlet to the sea.” Abiy, who has described this as an existential issue for his country, was not specific but neighboring Eritrea’s Red Sea port of Assab has long been seen by some in the government as a possible prize. It was part of Ethiopia until Eritrea seceded in the 1990s, leaving Ethiopia without a coastline. In a statement prior to Abiy’s remarks, Eritrea, along with Egypt, Somalia, and Sudan, said control of the Red Sea was the “exclusive responsibility” of countries that border it. The tensions over maritime access come with Ethiopia locked in a domestic conflict, as well: An alliance of rebel groups have pledged to overthrow the government four years after the end of a civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people died. — Damian Zane

events.title: South Africa under pressure to provide $600M fuel relief
events.summary: South Africa is facing growing pressure from labor unions and business groups to provide around $600 million in fuel relief, after the Iran war drove petrol prices to record highs in the continent’s biggest economy. The calls heap pressure on the coalition government to loosen its purse strings, threatening to undermine its reputation for fiscal discipline just as Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana prepares to present his three-year fiscal plan later this month . South Africa’s biggest labor federation, Cosatu, described the price shock, which sent a liter of fuel above 30 rand (almost $2) for the first time, as “ a cost of living crisis ” because workers spend nearly a third of their wages on transport. In response, the central bank has raised its main interest rate twice this year and warned in its monetary policy review this week that it has adopted a “ firefighting ” stance before energy prices spill over into broader inflation. The raised borrowing costs apply a secondary squeeze on households and businesses demanding fiscal relief. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: China is coming, slowly, for the dollar
events.summary: China’s competitor to the dollar-denominated system that zips money between global banks saw record daily volume in August. A spike last spring, as the Iran war sent sanctioned companies looking for a way around Washington, now looks less like a blip and more like a permanent, if small, leg-up for Beijing’s efforts to build a parallel system of financial plumbing. This isn’t the death of the dollar. New data from Atlantic Council researchers Jessie Yin and Lize de Kruijf shared first with Semafor, shows the greenback still underpins most global trade and foreign-exchange transactions. (Try converting Turkish lira to Indian rupees without going through the greenback.) “The top line numbers all remain stable,” said Josh Lipsky, the Atlantic Council’s chair of international economics. “But look underneath the hood and there’s some worrying signs.” China’s efforts to dethrone the dollar have so far mostly been a curiosity. Renminbi’s place in global central-bank reserve coffers has actually fallen since 2022, despite Beijing shoveling its currency into developing economies through central-bank swap lines. But crises can reset the board: The number of direct participants in Beijing’s cross-border interbank payment system has more than doubled since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the resulting weaponization of Western financial networks to freeze Russian assets. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: US futures slip as oil prices and bond yields rise with markets awaiting latest Fed minutes
events.summary: U.S. futures are lower as oil prices tick higher and the bond market climbs ahead of the release of the Federal Reserve’s latest minutes U.S. futures are retreating and bond yields are climbing again after a barrel of oil ticked back above $100 per barrel Wednesday. Much of the focus on Wall Street will be on the release of minutes from the last meeting of the Federal Reserve, where the nation's benchmark interest rate was hiked for the first time in three years. Futures for the S & P 500 dipped 0.1% a day after reaching a record 7,818.93. Despite worries over the Iran war , high inflation and pressures from the bond market , the index at the heart of many 401(k) accounts has soared 23% since hitting a trough in late March. Futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.3%, while Nasdaq futures declined 0.4%. Crude prices rebounded early Wednesday. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 1.3% to $101.88. That’s about $55 more than a barrel cost at this time last year. U.S. benchmark crude rose 0.6% to $89.99 per barrel. Yemen's Houthi rebels used ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones, to attack military facilities and airports in Saudi Arabia , the rebels’ military spokesman, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on social media Wednesday. He didn’t provide evidence for the claim. Also attacked were Abha airport, military facilities in Khamis Mushait and other “critical sites” in the cities of Najran and Asir, according to Saree. And after falling back slightly this week, bond yields are on the rise again. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 5.33%, while the 30-year Treasury climbed to 5.71%. Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Hurricane Isaias latest: Storm strengthens to Category 2 Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The Fed releases the minutes from its September meeting when U.S. central bank officials raised the key interest rate. The minutes may provide clues about where the Fed, and interest rates, are heading. Earnings season is also just around the corner and PepsiCo will report its quarterly results Thursday. Delta Air Lines posts earnings Friday and several of the country’s biggest banks release quarterly performances next week. Analysts expect companies in the S & P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30% in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to data provider FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25%. Investors have grown leery of how much growth is being driven by companies in the artificial intelligence race. Those companies can take a hit when it becomes more difficult to borrow, and the 10-year Treasury can be an indicator of credit costs ahead. events.title: Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction
events.summary: Long-standing factors contributing to job satisfaction, such as feeling appreciated, still matter more than the type of workplace format. Luis Villasmil on Unsplash , CC BY The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more flexible arrangements , such as hybrid or remote work. But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that workplace factors like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office. To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person. These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers. As a researcher of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar Jason Schloetzer that analyzed responses from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager. Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest. In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy. The workplace behind the work arrangement Semi- or fully remote workers may appear more satisfied . But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue. Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately. A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable. We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work. Burnout and happiness are different questions Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion. Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report , 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely. Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience. Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an American Medical Association survey in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages. The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession. Meanwhile, separate Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines. Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations. Those problems require attention wherever employees work. Working apart can carry social costs The expression “work-life balance” implies that it’s healthy to engage in social activity with friends and family outside work. But as other research of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job. Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them. Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, according to new research published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst. As more people have flexible work options, it hasn’t translated into more time with friends and family but more time alone. events.title: The Download: weight-loss drugs slowing aging and carbon dioxide batteries
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process. Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.  The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results? Read the full story on what the new findings reveal about GLP-1 drugs and aging . —Antonio Regalado 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries Energy Dome is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Solar and wind are among the cheapest and quickest ways to add electricity to the grid. But they’re subject to variations in weather patterns, so supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome has an unusual solution: massive batteries that use compressed carbon dioxide to store energy for when the grid needs it. Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new. Utilities have used compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world. Here’s how the company is using carbon dioxide to store renewable energy . —Casey Crownhart Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from mobile flood barriers and electric buses to next-generation nuclear reactors. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason —Thore Graepel, a core member of DeepMind’s AlphaGo team Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol. AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch. It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks.  This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture . events.title: The 5 future vehicles you need to watch for, according to Edmunds
events.summary: Automakers will debut some interesting new models in the next six months Fall is typically when automakers release the majority of their models for the new year. Most will be continuations of prior designs, but there’s also a good number that are all-new or getting major redesigns. If you’re thinking about buying a new vehicle in the next six months, it can be useful to know which ones have major changes or offer notable breakthroughs. To give you an inside scoop on what’s coming down the pike in the next few months, the automotive experts at Edmunds have picked five vehicles that promise to be well worth the wait. Nissan’s best-selling model is getting its first full redesign since 2021, and it’s a significant one. The fourth-generation Rogue small SUV debuts with a new hybrid powertrain called E-Power that works more like an electric vehicle than a traditional hybrid. A small gas engine acts as a generator, recharging a battery that powers the electric motors driving the Rogue. The result is reduced noise and quicker acceleration compared to the regular Rogue, Nissan says. Nissan also estimates that the Rogue Hybrid will get 38 mpg in combined city/highway driving. That’s a bit less than what the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4 hybrids can do, but it’s still very good for a small SUV. Starting price: $37,065, including destination fees The Highlander undergoes a massive change for 2028, becoming an all-electric three-row SUV with a quoted range of up to 320 miles. Buyers who still want a gas- or hybrid-powered three-row Toyota SUV will need to look at the larger Grand Highlander. But you needn’t step up to the bigger version to get a reasonably comfortable third row, even for adults. Edmunds’ first drive in the new all-electric Highlander showed the new version’s way-back seat to be much more comfortable than the outgoing model’s. Besides the Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Kia EV9, there aren’t many three-row EVs aimed at bigger families, so we’re excited to see Toyota offering an all-new alternative. At the same time Audi is sunsetting the longstanding A8 flagship sedan, it’s adding a new full-size three-row SUV. The 2027 Q9 is the largest vehicle Audi has ever built, and it’s aimed squarely at rival German stalwarts like the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS. Power comes from a 429-horsepower turbocharged V6. Inside, there’s seating for seven or a more premium six-passenger layout with second-row captain’s chairs. The Q9’s third-row seating area is considerably roomier than the one in the Q7, which also gets a redesign this year. Audi has also fitted the Q9 with all of its latest technology and driver assist features. Starting price: $89,095, including destination No 2027 model has generated more buzz among budget-conscious shoppers than the Slate Truck, the debut model from an American startup automotive company. The Truck is a bare-bones two-seat electric pickup that’s smaller than a Ford Maverick. By design, it comes without factory paint or even an infotainment touchscreen. Instead, buyers are encouraged to personalize it to their liking, up to and including the option to turn the cargo bed into a seating area and effectively turn the Truck into a five-seat SUV. The Slate Truck is an intriguing option for affordable vehicle, but go in with your eyes wide open: It lacks many features you might take for granted in other vehicles, and its estimated range of just 205 miles is a concern. Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Hurricane Isaias latest: Storm strengthens to Category 2 Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Starting price: $26,400, including destination Chevrolet’s full-size truck is getting its first redesign since 2019, and that should make it a more capable rival to the Ford F-150, Ram 1500 and Toyota Tacoma. The 2027 Silverado 1500 brings a bolder exterior design, a new interior and a standard 16.3-inch touchscreen. Two new V8 engine options join the carryover turbocharged four-cylinder and diesel six-cylinder. The 5.7-liter V8 produces 402 horsepower, while the larger 6.2-liter V8 cranks out 481 horsepower. Both are more powerful than the Silverado’s previous V8s. Expect Super Cruise — GM’s hands-free driving technology — to be available on top trims. And like all full-size trucks, there will be many variants — seven to be exact, topping out at more than $80,000 for the off-road-oriented ZR2 or the luxurious High Country. The new model year is jam-packed with big updates for some of the most popular vehicles on the market. These models we listed above will have some significant advantages over a vehicle in the here and now. Buyers shopping for new wheels will have a lot of exciting options to choose from in the next few months. This story was provided to The Associated Press by the automotive website Edmunds . Josh Jacquot is a contributor at Edmunds.

events.title: DR Congo uncovers $20B in payments to ineligible mining suppliers
events.summary: The News Fourteen major mining companies in DR Congo paid at least $20 billion to ineligible subcontractors between 2020 and 2025, the country’s subcontracting regulator told Semafor, citing recently completed checks. These findings at mining businesses, among them subsidiaries of Swiss commodities giant Glencore, Ivanhoe Mines and Chinese-Congolese joint-venture Sicomines, have prompted the regulator to plan tougher inspections this month to tackle breaches of subcontracting rules. These include the longstanding use of Congolese figureheads to disguise foreign control. Glencore declined to comment. Ivanhoe Mines and Sicomines did not respond to Semafor’s requests for comment by publication time. The regulator’s move comes as the country courts new mining investment, including from the US, and seeks to ensure that Congolese partners genuinely own and help run the businesses supplying its mines, in line with its laws. “We are open to partnership. But we don’t want people to come just for an extractive economy and leave us with holes,” Juan Ted Beleshayi, head of the Authority for the Regulation of Subcontracting in the Private Sector, told Semafor. In recent weeks, he has ordered miners to terminate about 1,800 subcontracts with suppliers lacking valid registration certificates. These include contracts with 1,540 suppliers at two subsidiaries of Glencore, alongside those involving Ivanhoe Mines, Eurasian Resources Group and Sicomines. “We really only carried out a simple check,” said Beleshayi, who took charge of the agency just over three months ago. He said he had completed checks begun under his predecessor. This month’s inspections would be “very detailed and rigorous,” said Beleshayi. Inspectors will check who owns the suppliers on paper, who calls the shots and who controls the bank accounts. Companies who fail to comply with the regulator’s decisions could face closure, he said. Know More Subcontracting represents billions of dollars to the Congolese economy — in 2025, 167 major companies declared $3.7 billion in contracts. The regulatory agency registers mining suppliers, which typically handle transport, machinery maintenance and construction among other work, and enforces rules based on a 2017 law that requires Congolese investors to own at least 51% of those businesses, with foreign ownership capped at 49%. Chinese companies dominate DR Congo’s copper and cobalt mines and have often faced criticism from the regulator for shutting Congolese businesses out of subcontracting work. Beleshayi’s predecessor, Miguel Kashal, accused Sicomines, in 2023 of keeping all its subcontracts in Chinese hands. Three years ago, Sicomines pledged to give Congolese suppliers its secondary work. A company representative said that a misunderstanding over subcontracting rules had been resolved. Beleshayi told Semafor his own inspections had found the same pattern. Sicomines did not respond to this claim. “We’re not saying foreigners have to leave. We just want a 49-51 split,” Beleshayi said. Limited financing and technical skills prevent Congolese suppliers from handling major mining contracts, researcher Fridolin Kimonge told Semafor. Ownership checks and contract cancellations alone cannot address those weaknesses. “It is not enough to cancel; there has to be a plan behind it,” Beleshayi said. Temporary exemptions would allow foreign suppliers to help Congolese businesses become partners or competitors, he said. “We will look for Congolese who understand American culture or can adapt to it, to build companies together,” he said of incoming US companies. Ruben’s view Like many African countries, DR Congo struggles to enforce laws that exist on paper. Part of the problem with its subcontracting law is finding replacements for the suppliers who break it. Congolese businesses often lack the financing and technical skills to take over major mining contracts, limiting how far the regulator can act without disrupting operations. Washington’s push to loosen China’s grip on Congolese minerals could give the regulator more options. Beleshayi expects American suppliers to accompany new US mining investments and form businesses with Congolese partners. If those companies can deliver the work and meet the ownership rules, existing suppliers would face competitors capable of replacing them. “Yes, absolutely,” he said when I asked whether that prospect could pressure companies already operating in DR Congo to comply. Conflict in mining regions, disputed licenses, slow permitting, and unpredictable enforcement have long deterred Western investors, while Chinese operators have been better able to absorb those risks. DR Congo’s recent reforms and Beleshayi’s crackdown could help signal to the US and European companies it is courting that the country is becoming a more reliable place to do business. Room for Disagreement Transparency has long been a central demand in efforts to improve DR Congo’s mining governance and local ownership alone offers no guarantee that contracts benefit ordinary Congolese, say critics. In a 2020 study of six mining companies, researcher Kimonge found that DR Congo’s subcontracting law required majority Congolese ownership but provided no mechanism to trace where the money invested in those businesses came from. He warned that gaps in the rules also allowed political and administrative officials to own suppliers and steer contracts toward their own businesses. “The situation has not improved much,” he told Semafor. Mining governance analyst Jean Pierre Okenda called repeated denunciations of figureheads as “populist rhetoric” that does not go far enough and urged the regulator to publish suppliers’ real owners and their ties to officials. Otherwise, he warned, replacement contracts could go to another set of politically connected businesses. Notable DR Congo has launched a geological survey aimed at improving knowledge of its vast mineral reserves ​to reduce exploration risk and attract investment into underexplored regions.
